Projects.Highlights:
Burn boundary maps included in report (in file).
Ryegrass seeding experiment conducted after burn (in Aguanga file)
Seeding ryegrass at 3 different application rates failed to have a significant effect on the total vegetative cover present on the site after one year. Poor success of the seeding was likely due to steep slopes, the inland climatic zone and elevation of the study area, and the amount of water repellant soil. The timing and intensity of early season storm events probably has as much of an impact on the success or failure of seeding as does any of the other factors mentioned above.
Cost for 1st year monitoring was $2500, total suppression costs were $2,500,000, and rehab costs were $13,000. Monitoring represents less than 0.10% of the total cost of the incident.

Narrative and burn intensity maps included in the file.
In the most severely burned areas, road cuts and fills lost all vegetation. Ditchline and culvert plugging would increase as a result of surface ravel from outslopes and the "lip" of soil above cuts, as the slopes erode back.
Aerial seeding mix for high intensity burn areas: Annual ryegrass 5 lbs/acre, white clover 3 lbs/acre, and Birdsfoot trefoil 5 lbs/acre. Used seed coated with lime (all seed), to improve ballistics and establishment. Coating would increase the weight of grass seed about 100%. Both Trefoil and clover were inoculated. Channel seeding mix: Annual rye 3 lbs/acre, perennial rye 3 lbs/acre, Dutch or New Zealand white clover, 2 lbs/acre, Birdsfoot trefoil 5 lbs/acre, and Dwarf orchard grass 4 lbs/acre. Fertilize at 200 lbs/acre with 16-20-0-14. Channel planting: Red alder or other suitable hardwood spp. to be planted spring of 1988, in and adjacent to channel sediment deposits. Plant one row each side of channel within 10 ft of bank on 10-ft spacing, approximately 1000 trees per mile. Road revegetation (25 ft strip along toes of outslopes and selected out faces of high intensity burn areas). Seed mix: tall fescue 7 lbs/acre, orchard grass 8 lbs/acre, Alsike clover 4 lbs/acre, hybrid perennial ryegrass 5 lbs/acre. Fertilize at 300 lbs/acre with 16-20-0-14 and use neutralizer (lime or dolomite) at 300 lbs/acre. Mulch with wood fibre at 3000 lbs/acre. Applied in two applications, 1 - mulch includes seed, fertilizer, neutralizer, and up to one half of the wood fibre. Second application included the remainder of the wood fibre mulch.

Actually, there was no BAER report because of the small fire size, the chapparal vegetation type, and situation high in the watershed. No treatment was done. Most information is from News clippings and suppression notes
George Robertson mentioned this fire because, although small and received no slurry nor fertilizer, it did cause a measurable spike in the nitrate levels downstream. Little soil was lost and the rise in N only lasted a week. D. Salizar of DEQ is the contact for this nitrate/stream information
In searches for fire info, I discovered a press release that indicated that the fire was put out using waste water effluent from the city of Sedona.
A Type I team was sent in to take care of this potentially explosive fire and kept it under control. Fear was that it would enter Oak Creek canyon and run.

Projects.Highlights:
Most unique feature of fire was its proximity to the community area comprised of El Portal, Rancheria Flat, and Indian Flat. Plus the fire burned extremely hot on 75% of its area.
"Other" treatment included debris basin , dam built with rock-filled gabions.
Straw mulching at 2 tons/acre was only used on steep slopes located above roads.
Silt fence monitoring: (Rob Griffith 8-6-91) Silt fence #1 - granitic derived soil, no treatment 4.26 tons/acre erosion 1991, 3.1 tons/acre 92 (decreased erosion rate)
Silt fence #2 - granitic derived soil, seeded with cereal barley, 1.46 tons/acre eroded 1991, 2 tons/acre 92 (approx. same erosion rate)
Silt fence #3 - granitic derived soils upper half dominated by rock outcrop, seeded with cereal barley, 1.07 tons/acre eroded 1991 (failed in 92)
Silt fence #4 - soils derived from metamorphic rock in chaparral system, no treatment, 9.07 tons, acre eroded 1991, but only 5.43 tons/acre in 92. (decreased erosion rate)
Have report by DeGraff that monitors the effects of storm event lasting from Feb 27 to Mar 4 1991. (in file - color photos in report of dams) Debris basin rapidly filled with debris after an intense period of rainfall during the storm. Little debris had gathered in the basin under normal intensities during the storm. Timing of the debris basin filling suggested a debris flow origin. If the material was simply water-transported sediment and ash, it would tend to gradually fill the basin over the three day period from the start of the storm thru Sunday. Conclusions of report; closed debris basins can provide a significant level of protection to property and life where debris flows or heavy sediment loads are anticipated. The design volume for such structures should allow for the loss of volume resulting from trapped sediment which cannot be removed due to inability to extract it or to avoid damage to the dam. Check dams constructed from pre-fabricated silt fences were suitable for only ephemeral streams where silt and ash were expected. They are not appropriate for channels where debris flows or heavy sediment loads are expected. Wildfires represent a natural disaster. As such, it is not possible to prevent all disastrous consequences. This is especially true in an environment where geomorphic processes are capable of generating disastrous consequences under natural conditions.
Also have report of Frank Rauchschwalbe that monitored success of grass seeding in July of 1993, the 3rd year. No barley occurred on any of the plots in 1993, and only a few scattered plants were noted between plots on four of the five transects. Conclusion, while some cereal barley still remained in the area, it has demonstrated it's anticipated non-persistence.

Roads and Trail Treatments:
There is a need to increase the size of some existing drainage structures to prevent the structures from washing out. In some cases grouted rock spillways will need to be installed to handle the additional flows and bed load. There are also undermined drainage structures that need to be replaced or reinstalled to handle the additional runoff. The outlets of drainage structures need to be protected from erosion by installing loose rock riprap energy dissipaters. There are some cases were additional intercepting dips and over side drainage structures will need to be installed between existing structures to decrease the distances between existing cross drains to remove flows off the road way before they start cutting the roadbed.
In addition to these prescriptions, the road bed will need to be graded to maximize the drainage flow lines to allow for additional bed loads, debris, and flows; intercepting dips will need to be deepened to handle additional flows and silt; inlets to culverts and over side drainage flumes will require cleaning of all loose vegetation, debris, and silt to maximize their efficiency; earth berms channeling flows will need to be reinforced; lead off ditch lines will need to deepened.

Projects.Highlights:
No treatment. Decision on not to seed was based on; the time of year the fire burned (not being able to establish ground cover until next spring), question of seeding success because of the rocky basalt soils, and the distance to streams with T & E species.
Money for monitoring of fire was asked for on this fire. Included in $8600 of BAER costs. Currently being processed, so do not if allowed or not. Planned monitoring included: initial monitoring would be in fall and done as soon as funding was approved. A 2nd monitoring trip would be done in May or June. A 3rd monitoring trip would be done just after the summer monsoons in Sept. A zig-zag pebble transect would be setup in Deep Cr. to determine the conditions of the creek bottom. At least two Daubenmire plots would be setup within the fire to monitor ground cover, with metal stakes marking the boundaries. One would be setup within the high mixed conifer vegetation type, and the other in the ponderosa pine type. Both of these would be set on slopes >30%. Photo points would be set up near these plots with metal stakes marking the locations. Soil erosion plots using an erosion bridge would be set up near these plots to estimate soil erosion. GPS locations would be taken of the plots and photo points. Several soil samples would be taken and sent to a lab to test how much viable seed is in the soil. These soil samples would only be taken one time in the fall.
Cost breakdown for monitoring included in the report (in file).

Projects.VegType: chaparral
Projects.Highlights:
All information for this fire is from a USDA FS publication (1978?) titled Burn Area Rehabilitation Activity Review. Battle is one of the many fires described and reviewed for effects of fire rehabilitation techniques.
Treatment was aerial seeding between June17-July3 with weeping lovegrass, sand dropseed, sideoats grama, and burnet (the lbs/ac, seeds/ft2, % mix, PLS/ft2, etc are all on pg. 32) The review team visited the burn in January 1977 (5 growing seasons). Resprouting chaparral had made normal expected regrowth and no seeded species were visible. **a report "Preliminary Battle Fire Erosion Survey" by James Williams, Watershed Scientist and Sherman Radtke, Soil Scientist was prepared in April 1973... |... |... | who might have it???? This report said seed germination was low, possibly due to light rain before seeding that encrusted the ash. They also noted problems in dispersing large seed such as sideoats grama by the helicopter [also noted by Steve McWilliams of SantaFe] "According to this study, by the second growing season the production of grasses and forbs was 55 lbs./acre dry wt. It is interesting to note that 27 pounds or 49 percent was weeping lovegrass, the only seeded species. By the third growing season it accounted for 32 percent of the production of grasses and forbs. Also by the third growing season the shrub canopy cover was close to 30 percent, which represents about 50 percent of the preburn shrub cover. When you combine the grasses and forbs with the pounds of shrub regrowth, the seeded weeping lovegrass accounts for less than 5% of the production during the second growing season." -and the first year the seedlings are able to do very little to lessen the amount of seed loss [so why bother]

Estimated Hydrologic Response: Model predictions indicate that peak flows at selected poursheds (the drainage basins for each pourpoint) increased by a magnitude of 1.3 to 1.7 from pre-fire to post-fire. The largest increases occurred in the Wilson Creek and Indian Creek poursheds. These drainages are in the southwest portion of the fire where the greatest proportions of moderate and high soil burn severity occurred. Moderate and high burn severities within these two poursheds occur intermittently throughout the drainages, including within the channels. The other modeled drainages, all of which are larger than these two, will experience smaller degrees of initial watershed responses.
Eighty-two (82) previously recorded eligible and unevaluated cultural resources fell within low burn severity of the Battle Mountain Complex. Additionally, low intensity fire has been utilized by indigenous people in the Blue Mountains to enhance the yield of culturally significant plant species (First Foods). It would be expected that fire of this severity would have a positive impact on First Food resources. Moderate and high severity burns may thermally alter artifact characteristics, lead to increased erosion which may expose and destabilize subsurface archaeological features or cover up surface archaeological features. Medium and high intensity fire has affected 11 eligible or unevaluated properties including pre-contact and historic archaeological sites. The overall proportion of moderate and high burn severity within the Battle Mountain Complex footprint is small and risk to cultural resources determined to be low. The relationship between soil burn severity, projected watershed response, and site type and their probability of damages or loss as a result to changed conditions is considered to be possible. Immediate threats to the NRHP eligible and unevaluated cultural resources fall within natural/physical (i.e., erosion, fallen trees, cattle activity) and cultural/human (i.e., looting and vandalism) processes. The magnitude of consequences is minor due to expected localized effects with exception of a predicted increase in erosion in high and moderate SBS areas.

The Bear Fire was lightning caused and burned within a perimeter of 350 acres. The majority of acres burned were backburned acres by the Forest Service in an effort to prevent fire spreading across FR 231 and prevent further loss of ponderosa pine forests and associated resource values and to protect a private parcel of land located about 1/2 to 3 miles NE of fire perimeter. No acres burned on Private property.
Almost all acres burned on Terrestrial Ecosystem Survey map unit 546 in ponderosa pine gamble oak vegetation type on soils that are relatively flat and therefore have slight erosion hazard. Most burned acres (about 75%) were dominated by a mosaic of unburned and low severity (about a 50/50 % split). Only about 1% (4 acres) burned in high burn severity while about 24% (85 acres) burned with moderate severity and some in a mosaic with low burn severity. Most moderate burn severity acres occur on map unit 546 and post-fire runoff is not expected to be higher than tolerable limits and water runoff would be similar to preburned conditions and therefore, is not expected to cause appreciable on-site or downslope resource damage. Only .2 miles of stream courses are present within the burned perimeter.

Fire Suppression costs includes Beaver Lakes, Siah Lake, Hopeful II, Wendover, and Bears Oil. The Lolo portion of the Hopeful II Fire was $2,720,619. The Clearwater portion of these fires is $14,720,600.
Note on adjusted design flow: "For design storm analysis, we used a 15 minute, 25 year storm that occurred in Sleeping Child Creek. This storm produced a 110 cfsm runoff in a 1.8 mi2 burned watershed (Site 14), which was greater than a 500 year runoff. This watershed was selected for the design storm because the runoff was water only (not debris) and the watershed was small (Less than 2 Mi2), where impacts are most likely to roads or other facilities.
Road drainage in watersheds less than 2 Mi2 should be designed to handle these flows. In watersheds 5 to 20 mi2, the design storm should be approximately 23 cfsm (Parrett and Others, Fire Hydrology, 7/2003)."
The 2500-8 asked for funding to upgrade 7 culverts. Actually, the number of culverts that were upgraded with the funding was more like 18. Anne Connor, current Forest Hydrologist could provide more accurate estimates.
After three years of visual monitoring on the Pleasant Fire, one area of high elevation was not vegetatively recovering. The Clearwater did an aerial application of wood straw that worked quite well. Jim Mital, Forest Soil Scientist can provide the acres and costs.

Projects.Highlights:
In risk assessment: High value properties below and within burn area were at risk from sediment flows and floodwaters. Average upper channel slopes were in excess of 65% and were where most of the runoff would originate. The seeding that is done after fire would only have a positive effect on the slopes 40% or less. Due to the mostly "low" to "moderate" nature of the burn which generally had minor effects on the soil, the number of grass/herb seeds in the soil, and sprouting characteristics of the vegetation, seeding would normally not be recommended for the general burn area. Because of the extremely steep slopes and loose soil in the upper burn areas, it is unlikely that seed would remain on these upper slopes under heavy precipitation. However, it is possible for germination to occur if there were a series of light rains.
Forest supervisor picked alternative treatment which included seeding.

Projects.Highlights:
Contour felling - felled trees on the contour at 40 ft intervals on high intensity burn areas.
Trail work - large log waterbar structures were placed on ORV trails to reduce the effects of water erosion.
In channel tree felling - fell large trees along 2.4 miles of White Cr. for maintaining channel stability, and reducing erosion and velocity of floodwaters.
Fire resistance: Fire-killed trees can be grouped into 3 categories (visual observation): 1. Black scorched bole and limbs, needles consumed. 2. Heat scorched, brown needles still attached. 3. Green needles, bole mostly unscorched, basal girdling caused by ground fire.
Seeding options : (from Paula Brooks, botanist) 1. No seeding (this option chosen) a. Although there are areas of the fire that are mapped at high intensity, these areas were not totally devastated by the fire. Within the fire perimeter there were signs of living roots of perennial sedges and grasses in many spots. b. Some scientific studies have indicated that seeding may be detrimental to reestablishment of native plants. Concerns include the inability of natives to recolonize sites that have been heavily seeded, increased fire danger from fine fuels produced by grasses, difficulty in reforesting heavily seeded sites, and increased rodent activity. Unless conditions are just right, no seed of any kind will sprout in the fall, nothing will begin to come up until the 1st spring after the fire. c. In light of the new emphasis on ecosystem management, we need to reassess our inclination to alter natural processes. Erosion and fires are both natural processes, to try to circumvent the natural progression from bare soil to complete cover may have implications we don't even realize.
d. The plant associations that burned heavily in this fire are naturally adapted to stand replacement fires. Much of the hotly burned areas are lodgepole pine, grouse huckleberry, and pinegrass plant associations. There is a very good chance that the pinegrass, eld sedge, huckleberry, and other species will resprout and grow vigorously as soon as next summer.
2. Using native species for restoration seeding
a. There is no commercial stock of most species that would grow well on the site. The species that would be recommended include: pinegrass, elk sedge, lupine, northwestern sedge, Ross sedge, and wild strawberry.
B. Any commercial seed that may be available of these species would not be from locally collected seed. There is a regional direction, and logic agrees, that if native seed is to be used for projects it needs to be originally collected in the local area. This relates to polluting the gene pool of native plants with genes from plants from many miles away, and also there may be problems of adaptation.
C. Commercial seed of native plants is prohibitively expensive. (an important point here is that if we are going to try to use natives for fire rehabilitation projects, we need to start stockpiling and contract growing seed now, so it is available and reasonably priced when these emergency needs emerge.
3. Non-persistent grasses
a This alternative was the preferred alternative for the group if the decision was made to seed. It recommends using grass species that will grow well and provide cover the first one to three yrs. after the fire. Then they will naturally fade out of the ecosystem and allow native plants to recolonize in the 2nd and 3rd years and beyond. Soft white winter wheat seems to be the best species to use for this purpose. Two big assumptions are made in this alternative: the wheat really does go away in 2 to 5 years, and the native plants will indeed be able to recolonize the site within that time. There is some uncertainty as to whether either of these assumptions are correct. Some literature indicates that even short-lived annuals inhibit the recolonization of sites by natives, and if the fire was really hot the natives may not resprout or be able to recolonize the area in that short of a time.
4. Persistent perennial grasses (Treatment that has been traditionally used on the forest. Involves using aerial application of high rates of traditional sod-forming grasses. These mixes usually include orchard grass, hard fescue, intermediate wheatgrass, smooth brome, a legume, and often small burnet. Once these grasses are established, they will persist on the site until the trees are able to provide a thick canopy to shade them out.
a. The solid grass cover provided by non-natives changes the site characteristics for many years (possibly forever). Once the grass is established it is very hard for natives and conifers to recolonize the site.
b. In light of the current extreme fire year, even commonly used grasses are daily becoming more expensive and difficult to find in any quantity.
c. If ecosystem management is our mandate, we have no reason to be altering natural processes like erosion and natural plant succession. In addition, the Regional office has recently sent out direction to try to use native plants for all projects whenever it is feasible. Seeding non-native grasses goes against this direction.
d. There is conflicting information on how valuable this tactic really is in preventing erosion caused by fires. It usually takes at least two years to get good cover established and by then most of the natural erosion has already occurred (some studies claim that the majority of erosion occurs within the first year after a fire.

Projects.Highlights:
Good treatment narrative in file.
Rationale used to support the decision not to seed the burned area as follows;
1. The effects of grass seeding on peak flows and sediment reduction are uncertain and depend on evenly spaced, low to moderate amounts of rainfall during initial post-fire storms. Seeding will not reduce erosion and runoff from heavy precipitation that occurs early in the rainy season.
2. Seeding can increase infiltration rates which were lowered during wildfire due to the creation of a hydrophobic layer. Higher infiltration rates can have both positive and negative impacts. Positive impacts include reduced surface erosion created by rilling, sheetwash, and gullying. Disadvantages include potential increases in mass movement (primarily shallow debris sliding) (Ruby 1987, Spittler 1995, Booker et al., 1993).
3. Seeding can reduce native plant species density, cover, and diversity which in some situations can reduce a system's long-term hillslope stability (Keeler-Wolf 1995), Stone 1993, Rice 1975).
4. Grass seeding can only affect surface erosion processes (I.e. rilling and gullying). It is likely that between 1/5 and 1/3 of the erosion in southern CA watersheds results from surface erosion. Seeding will have little impact where the major source of sediment is dry ravel or mass wasting. Similarly, downstream sediment yield may not be significantly reduced by seeding if there is very high sediment storage in stream channels that is mobilized by very high peak flows. If infiltration rates are significantly increased by seeding through interruption of the hydrophobic layer, erosion of channel deposits could be affected by grass seeding. (Rice 1975, Spittler 1995).
5. On average, about 70% of the long-term sedimentation from the watershed occurs during the first year after the fire (Rice 1975).
6. Due to climactic conditions in many instances, seeding efforts achieve little soil stabilization during the first year except to establish a cover that may be effective in the following seasons (Rice 1975).
7. Based on observations of vegetative recovery rates on the Reservoir Fire which burned under similar conditions and intensities, there appears to be sufficient viable seed bank left in the soil. Ground cover on the Reservoir burned area established on a majority of the area in only one growing season after the fire.
8. Seeding success and effectiveness are closely associated with site productivity. Only better sites should be considered as a priority for seeding; poorer sites should not be considered. The best sites have fine-grained soils, dark color, and usually slopes less than 50%. Poorer sites have harsh exposure, slopes greater than 50% with mobile surfaces, no definite soil development, and high natural erosion rates (Ruby and Griffith 1994). Using this criteria, the Canyon II burned area would be classified as a poor site.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Four sites were examined through GIS exercises by the BAER archaeologist and modeling analysis by the team... s soil scientists and hydrologists to determine if potential post-fire effects or proposed BAER treatments could impact sites. Four cultural sites, associated with the railroad tie cutting industry, are located within or adjacent to the burned area. These sites were also within the fire perimeter for the East Fork Fire in 2002 and conditions at that time were documented. The degree to which they were previously affected by the East Fork Fire, and their overall condition at that time were taken into consideration. This included whether the cabin structures burned down, or were recorded as being highly decomposed, and if archaeological potential remains. Two sites are within the current Beulah Fire perimeter and may have been affected by the fire, unfortunately, this was unable to be field verified. There are 2 sites located outside the burn area, but adjacent to the main East Fork Bear River stream channel coming off the fire. As such, all 4 sites are potentially at risk for post-fire effects and were evaluated. Using the BEAR Risk Assessment indicated threats to sites were possible to unlikely with post fire risk magnitude of consequences that were minor to moderate. Sites had low to very low assessments for post-fire risks from debris flow, soil erosion, hydrological response. Therefore, no post-fire BAER treatments are recommended for the cultural resources evaluated. Additionally, none of the BAER treatments have the potential to affect these sites or any other unidentified cultural resources.

Projects.Highlights:
Erosion potential estimate of 80 tons/acre is based on an average loss of 1/2 inch of soil during a high intensity, infrequent storm (10-50 year return interval). Natural soil building processes were estimated to replace 1/2 inch in less than 100 years. The soil loss is within the range of soil loss due to natural fire/erosion cycles that historically characterize this landscape. Under normal snow melt conditions erosion is estimated at only 1 ton/acre.
Sediment potential. Sediment potential is estimated for the infrequent high-intensity storm at 860 cu yds/sq.mile , for normal snow melt conditions it is estimated at 10 cu yds/sq mile. Most intense burns were in upper 1/3 of watershed, with only a few acres of riparian area burned.

Projects.Highlights:
E. Sediment Potential: 27,000 cubic yards / square mile. Results are from Disturbed WEPP. Modeled high severity fire in the uplands and riparian; 20-45% slope; 20-45% ground cover; 0-30% rock; Fenn modified climate. This is a worse case analysis. Most of the fire will have no increase in erosion or sediment.
H. Adjusted Design Flow, (cfs per square mile): 110 cfsm. For design storm analysis, we used a 15 minute, 25 year storm that occurred in Sleeping Child Creek in 2001. This storm produced a 110 cfsm runoff in a 1.8 mi2 burned watershed (Site 14), which was greater than a 500 year runoff event. This watershed was selected for the design storm because the runoff was water only (not debris) and the watershed was small (Less than 2 Mi2), where impacts are most likely. It is possible, that the Black Canyon Fire could receive a similar storm with similar watershed response where burn intensities are high, however there are no facilities that could be threatened. Storm runoff should be adjusted downward in watersheds where burn intensity is less than high. Road drainage in watersheds less than 2 Mi2 should be designed to handle these flows. In watersheds 5 to 20 mi2, the design storm should be approximately 23 cfsm (Parrett and Others, Fire Hydrology, 7/2003).
E. Cost of No-Action (Including Loss): The usual cost/benefit analysis was not conducted for the proposed treatments since it is very difficult to place a monetary value on the invasion of a burned area and the associated loss of ecosystem composition, structure, and function caused by a noxious weed, spotted knapweed. The potential cost would be the invasion of hundreds of acres of knapweed displacing the native plant communities.
F. Cost of Selected Alternative (Including Loss): The monetary cost of the produced treatments is minimal IF action is taken immediately next spring to release the bio-control insects and conduct follow-up monitoring on the suppression weed treatments. If weed invasion is observed, further, immediate treatments (rapid detection, early response techniques) must be implemented.

Projects.Highlights: Non-native Invasive Plants Monitoring should occur both before and after the monsoon season and into the next growing season, as well as identification of any new infestations from BAER treatment activities. A recommended schedule range would be 5-10 visits, starting in September (after monsoons) and resuming in April and May to develop current baseline, mid-late June prior to seasonal monsoons and finally in the following September after the second monsoons. Monitoring should occur along the roads and trails that were used as suppression lines. Areas specifically identified for monitoring include suppression lines, FSR 107, 107D, and 107A. Information collected should include species, area extent of infestation, and approximate percent of infestation (i.e., sparse, dense, very dense, percentage, etc.). Photo points should be collected. Geospatial locations of infestations should be documented and put into the corporate databases including NRIS. Funding for EDRR is requested in the treatment narrative. Monitoring will include two previously recorded sites. Regular monitoring and inspection after heavy rain and flood events will monitor any damage, and document efficacy of the seeding upslope and on the site directly. Funding is requested in the treatment narrative. Wildlife Wildlife biologists will continue to monitor and evaluate impacts to the MSO Critical Habitat and Recovery Habitat. Two (2) additional visits will be made to the area, one immediately pre-monsoon and one immediately post-monsoon season, and monitoring to accepted protocol will take place in 2025. Changes and impacts will be documented in the report and photos. No funding is requested.

Projects.Highlights:
Roads and Trail Treatments on NFS Lands:
Cooperators and permittees specifically requested that the San Bernardino National Forest keep the two system roads described in this section open for their travel for the next several years so closure is not an option. These roads are needed by the BNSF and UP Rail-roads, pipeline companies and Southern Cal. Edison to reach their service roads. This access is required by OSHA as a safety measure for these utilities. These same cooperators are spending tens of thousands of dollars to improve drainage on their service roads that are under special use permit.
Numerous road drainage structures will be impacted by the fire. The major concern is the capability of the structures to carry increased debris, silt, and additional runoff caused by the lack of ground cover and hydrophobic soil conditions. The failure of drainage structures and flows and debris overtopping the roadway would result in damage to the road surface, embankment, and areas downstream of the drainage structure, In addition there will be slides which will result in temporary road closure. These hazards will exist to some extent throughout the recovery period, but will be the most extreme during the first two to three years following the burn.
The following mitigation measures will generally work for most of the overflow conditions throughout the burn area, however a more detailed site-specific analysis may reveal different or more cost effective solution which can be implemented at that time.
There are sections of insloped road that will suffer erosion and cutting due to debris and silt plugging the toe ditch lines, thereby forcing surface runoff to run down the roadway for long distances. Mitigation includes installing intercepting dips with overside drainage structures at closer intervals between existing cross drains to remove the flows off the roadway.
There is a need to increase the size of some existing drainage structures to handle the increased runoff and debris flows.
There is a need to increase the capacity of corrugated metal pipe used as cross drains for natural drainages. The installation of metal end sections at the inlets of corrugated metal culverts will assist in handling the increased flows. In addition, there is a need to construct a route to direct high flows safely over the top of embankments at a defined low point, and the installation of overside drainage structures to carry the runoff down embankment to an appropriate discharge point to minimize gullying.
The installation of energy dissipaters at the outlets of drainage structures need to be installed to decrease flow velocity, erosion, and undercutting of the structures and fills.
There are intercept dips and lead off ditches that need to have metal drainage structures installed to prevent down cutting of the road embankment where the water leaves the roadway.
In addition to the above prescriptions, the following work needs to be competed immediately prior to the next rain. The inlet and catch basins of culverts will require cleaning of all loose debris and silt which has the potential to restrict culvert openings. All drainage structures need to be cleaned. Road surfaces need to be graded to ensure all earthen drainage features (intercept dips, road surface cross sloped for proper drainage, earth berms channeling flows) are functioning properly.
As part of the rehabilitation effort, a storm patrol and emergency warning plan will need to be developed and implemented jointly with all of the affected transportation and utility companies that are subject to damage to their facilities caused by high runoffs as a result of the fire. The Contingency Plan will set up a procedure for monitoring and surveillance of weather conditions, and will set into motion different levels of actions to be taken by the road agencies and utility companies depending on the level of severity of the predicted or actual situation.
For more information, see the road logs in the specialist reports section of this report.
A one-mile section of the Pacific Crest Trail in the mouth of Crowder Canyon will need to be temporarily relocated due to the extreme possibility of hikers and other users getting caught in flash floods. The Pacific Crest Trail is located so that it goes through a large Freeway culvert under I-15 and then under a railroad bridge. Crowder Canyon drains through the culvert and under the bridge. The culvert is at the mouth of the canyon and at the apex of the alluvial fan... in the most dangerous place for a trail to be located. This would become the single most dangerous place for a hiker to be while inside the Blue Cut and Louisiana burns during a thunderstorm. The trail must be rerouted to save lives. Hikers will be subjected to an order of magnitude more danger now than before the fires due to the much greater amounts of water and sand that will be going through the culvert and under the railroad bridge. There is no chance of closing the Pacific Crest Trail but it can be temporarily relocated. Informational signs and brochures will be printed, posted and handed out to trail users regarding the risk. Dry ravel is causing rocks and soil to move down over the trail and this will need to be removed.

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, only rehabilitation report
Seed mix prescribed for the steep southerly escarpment (about 300 acres): Intermediate wheatgrass 5 lbs/acre, slender wheatgrass 5 lbs/acre, hard fescue 1 lb/acre, timothy 1 lb/acre, and dwarf yellow sweet clover 0.5 lbs/acre. Seed mix for remainder of burned area: Orchardgrass 3 lbs/acre, timothy 1 lb/acre, hard fescue 1 lb/acre, and White Dutch clover 0.5 lbs/acre.
Pubescent wheatgrass is commonly used on burned sites in the Okanogan even though it is a rhizomatous grass. In this case, intermediate wheatgrass was substituted, but it too can be somewhat rhizomatous.
Review 1 yr later: The grass had become well established one yr following seeding. All species were present including yellow sweet clover and white Dutch clover which quite often are failures. Water bars on roads were poorly constructed. They were not deep enough and all that was done was to pile a berm downslope from the water bar to provide a dam. The water bars should have been installed deeper into the roadbed. Also there was little indication of outlets for the waterbars.

There were 29.1 miles of non-fish streams within the fire perimeter and 6.5 miles of fisheries streams.
The emergency treatment objectives are to: 1. Prevent impairment of ecosystem function from the invasion of spotted knapweed into the burned area (which had been weed-free prior to the wildfire) through the release of biological control agents. 2. Weed monitoring would be conducted to identify areas where weed invasion may occur primarily along Roads 485 and 500 and Trails 48 and 230. 3. Reduce erosion and sedimentation from Trail 48 through the construction of waterbars and check dams which will divert, and dissipate runoff flowing down the trail tread. This will protect watersheds by lessening the force and concentration of water flowing downstream.

Projects.Highlights:
Seed mix @ 3 lbs/acre included mountain brome 30%, slender wheatgrass 50%, little bluestem 10%, Woods rose 5%, and yellow sweet clover 5%.
Seed was applied by helicopter on severe to moderately burned areas on steep slopes.
Observations of visual monitoring of fire on 9-13-94:
Contour felling: Observed that where logs were felled on the contour, two features were important in the effectiveness of these structures: 1) Logs must be placed correctly on the contour. Where logs were not placed correctly on the contour, water was channeled along the log resulting in increased erosion, and 2) gaps under logs must be filled. Where gaps under felled logs were not filled, the logs did not trap sediment effectively and in many cases appeared to contribute to channelization of water. Log dams: Log should be cut so that the ends of the log do not extend up the side slope. This can channel water along the log and cause increased erosion. Gaps under the log structures should be blocked, preferably by seating the log into the channel bottom as much as possible. In this way, water is slowed by the log allowing sediment to drop out and erosive forces to decrease.
Sites on gentle to steep slopes which had burned at low to medium intensity were found to have good vegetative cover, some sites having 85-95% ground cover by herbaceous species. The species were primarily those already present on the site. Species included Ribes, Robinis, Rosa, Quercus, Rubus, and Holodiscus, all of which were resprouting from perennial root stalks. Oxalis, Geranium, Solanum, Silene, Tradescantia, Lathyrus, Stellaria, and Hydrophyllum were growing from volunteer seeds or perennial root stalks. No yellow sweet clover was present on the site (was in rehab seed mix).
On sites that burned at high intensity, herbaceous ground cover was not present or was present at very low levels of 2-5% cover.

Projects.WtrQualThrtDescr: Threat of sedimentation to streams and the City of Bend's water supply in Bridge Cr. The fishery resource in Tumalo Cr. Is also threatened.
Projects.Highlights:
Article included in file: McCammon and Hughes, Fire rehab in the Bend municipal watershed.
Comprehensive narrative (hydrology, vegetative management, silviculture, soils) and map included in file. Main focus was threat to the Bend Municipal water supply.
Observations: North aspects and valley bottoms burned hotter. South aspects had: 1) more brush, rock talus slopes and bedrock outcrops, 2) less intense burns, and 3) manzanita and ceanothus brush fields overall had lowest burn intensities.
Seeding (helicopter): Tetrapode annual ryegrass was recommended because it would give a quick cover in the fall and would provide the best possible protection in the spring, whereas slow developing perennial grasses would not provide cover in the fall. Nor would it do any good to use perennials in mix with rye, as ryegrass is strongly allelopathic when used in mixes at rates greater than 3 lbs per acre.
Ryegrass seed was applied at 10 lbs/acre (50 seeds/sq.ft.). Total cost - $10/acre (approx 1600 acres). An area of the Bend Municipal Watershed was seeded at 20 lbs/acre.
Hand application of hard fescue and intermediate wheatgrass was recommended as a filter strip along the major stream courses.
Fertilizer recommended was ammonium nitrate-sulfate (30-0-0-6). Objective of fertilization is to give the grass seeding a fast start without encouraging the shrubs that will come from seed, root, and crown sprouting. Believed that by using nitrogen fertilizer in both the nitrate form (for the fall) and the sulfate form (for next spring) that growth of ryegrass would be promoted without encouraging brush regeneration. Applied at 200 lbs/acre.
Riparian planting was done along the streamside in an area completely destroyed by the hot burn. Adaptable species found in the nearby riparian area included: Swamp currant (Ribes lacustre), Black currant (Ribes petiolare), Baldhip rose (Rose gymnocarpa), Menzies spires (Spirea menziesii), Grouse whortleberry (Vaccinium scoparium), Big whortleberry (Viccinium membranaceum), Saskatoon serviceberry (Amelanchier alnifolia), Thinleaf alder, mountain ash, willow, quaking aspen, black cottonwood, sedge, tufted hairgrass, lodgepole pine, Englemann spruce, grand fir, and Pacific red elder.
Rehabilitation review: (9-26-80) Lack of success in the grass seeding effort, even though there was 1.1 inches of rain. Only spots which appeared to germinate were locations where water was trapped in small concavities or behind debris. Possible that germinated seed was affected by winter cold and was very susceptible to frost-heave and drought. Riparian plantings of the streambanks were not needed , as there was adequate resprouting of natural riparian vegetation along the streams.
Log terraces were reviewed after the Sept. 1 thunderstorm. 63% of the terraces were effective in retarding sediment movement. The remaining 37% were either partially effective or did not experience sediment flow. Common failures of the terraces were : 1) flow under the terrace, and 2) terrace was not placed close enough to contour to slow flow. Log terraces - tree diam. 6-12 inches, terraces placed on the contour in rows with a 1.5 to 2 ft gap between adjacent terraces. The rolls were to be offset in relation to each other so that any flow passing between the terraces of one row would be intercepted by the row immediately downslope. The logs were secured behind existing stumps or staked with 3 ft metal stakes. Logs were sealed with debris and soil at surface. The rows of terraces were placed 10 ft apart on slopes exceeding 50%, 15 ft apart on slopes between 31 to 50%, and 20 ft apart on slopes less than 30%.
The Sept. 1 storm produced very high turbidities in Bridge Cr. Turbidity graphs showing peaks are included in file. The stream returned to near natural turbidity levels within 24 hrs of the fire. The vast majority of the turbidity in the stream was caused by ash and fine organic debris. During high turbidity, the water supply system to Bend was shut off for about 24 hrs.
In an attempt to improve the germination of grass seed and to break down the hydrophobic soil conditions, the south aspect slopes above Bridge Cr. Were irrigated. Thirteen sprinklers were supplied by a backpack pump which drew water from Bridge Cr.. Each sprinkler produced a 100 ft diameter and was allowed to run until the upper 1 inch of soil was wet. If surface flow was noticed, the sprinkler was shut down or moved. The irrigation project was terminated when the log terrace project began. Approximately 1 acre ft of water was applied in 7 days at a cost of $900.

Projects.Highlights:
This fire was treated in three phases - one before any problems, one after a large storm July 12, 1996, and again after additional storms in August and September. Two people lost their lives in July, and several home, bridges, and roads were lost. Total cost over $1,800,000.
The July event was estimated to be 13000 cfs at a point where the estimated 100 year flood was 675 cfs, so a flood 20X bigger than the 100 yr occurred.

Projects.Highlights:
Included in file is a reseeding evaluation concerning coated vs uncoated seed, also monitoring report for the third year after the fire. Also included in file is the report, "The Cachuma Burn Revisited" by Esplin and Shackelford.
Conclusions: Ryegrass grew and then diminished in the vegetation community as expected. 83% reduction on the seeded plots as it was replaced by native species.
There were a wide variety of plant species in both seeded and unseeded plots
Data indicated that chamise seedlings can possibly be partially controlled by seeding ryegrass after a wildfire almost as effectively as if it had been sprayed with a herbicide.
In the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th winter storm periods the amount of bare soil averaged 25% less on the seeded sites than on the control, assuming a straight line curve, going into the 2nd winter, the control had 10% more bare ground than the seeded areas, 50% more going into the 3rd year and exactly the same going into the 4th.
In the 4th growing season, there was 20% less live vegetation in the seeded than in the unseeded areas. But because of the litter cover, the amount of bare soil is currently the same on seeded and unseeded areas.
Coated vs. uncoated seed. More species diversity occurred on the uncoated seed sites than on the coated seed sites.
Lana vetch could not be evaluated. Either competition was too great for the vetch to become established, or its life cycle was completed earlier leaving little evidence by early summer.
At rates seeded, coated annual ryegrass out-competes most of the native successional species.
In the unintentionally skipped, burned chaparral bands, greater species diversity occurs, but ground cover was not adequate to control erosion by the second rainy season.
Two conclusions from application:
1) The aircraft needs to disperse coated and uncoated seeds in tighter patterns or from higher elevation to attain more uniform coverage. 2) Uniform coverage may not be as desirable as the effect unintentionally achieved. Banding provided cross-slope alternating sites of soil stabilizing cover and of protected natural secondary succession; the best of two worlds.

Projects.Highlights:
No treatment reasons:
Revegetation of the area with short-lived non-natives was expected to be difficult due to short growing seasons and cold soil conditions. Native seed stock from local seed stock was not available. The entire burned area was within the Strawberry Wilderness. The fire was situated at the top end of the drainage and burned at low fire intensities along the stream channels. Considering the small portion of the drainage affected, the mosaic of fire intensities, the low probability of sediment reaching channels in excess of carrying capacity, and low success rates in establishing non-native vegetation, it was believed that the natural recovery of the burned area would adequately protect the fish habitat concerns.

The treatment "Road Drainage Reconstruction" was not broken out in cost per item. This is what was provided:
Road Drainage Reconstruction General Description: The roads surveyed within the Caribou fire were found to have issues with their drainage system due to the expected increase in flows. The minimal treatments required to remedy these issues are: 1. Drain Dips (with or without armor) ... Roadway dips modify the road drainage by altering the template and allowing surface flows to run off the road to prevent any excessive erosion of the surface. The armor consisting of rip rap is placed where runoff could possibly cause erosion to the road surface and fillslope. 2. Culvert Cleaning ... Includes the cleanout of catch basin culvert inlets, outlets, and the drop inlets. Also included is the replacement of lids covering the drop inlets. Cleaning culvert pipes and replacing the missing and damaged lids over the drop inlets will enable the drainage system to pass flows more intended design flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 3. Culvert Repair - Using mechanical means to open up culverts to improve flow or cutting off sections too damaged to repair. This will improve culvert flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 4. Catch Basin Expansion ... Expanding existing catch basins in size and remove debris in the channel above the inlet. The expanded catch basins will handle more sediment and removing debris will reduce the chance of the culvert plugging. 5. Fill Size Reduction ... Reduce the fill volume over undersized culverts and construct a channel over the culvert. The channel will normally have rip rap to protect the remaining fill. This keeps the flow and sediment in the channel and reduces road related sediment and total fill failure. 6. Fill Slope Protection ... Place geotextile and rip rap on fill slopes where water flow over the fill is expected. This will reduce erosion and sediment delivery down stream. 7. Ditch Cleaning ... The cleanout of drainage ditches is required to remove debris that impede the flow or deflect it out of the ditch onto the road surface. Clean ditches will ensure that the flow reaches drainage structures. 8. Roadway slope improvement ... Out sloping or in sloping the road surface to ensure the flow goes into a drainage structure or is allowed to sheet off outside edge of the road without concentrating the water. This reduces road related sediment. 9. Culvert Additions ... Add additional culverts to drainage fills where the expected increased flow is more than the existing culvert can handle. Also allows replacement of fire damaged pipes and down drains to maintain existing drainage capacity and flow dissipation.

Projects.Highlights:
This one of the most complex and expensive BAER undertakings imaginable. I couldn't begin to summarize all the information included in the final report. However I will summarize some of the pertinent observation the Greg Kuyumjian made in the final BAER report.
Seeding: Seeding was at a prescribed rate of 36 lbs/ac (60 PLS ft/2). Tests indicated about 1/2 the PLS specifications. Best results were on bare soil before needlecast or under applied mulch. Intense rainfall on June 28,2000 washed away much of the seed on the south side of the fire, which were retreated. Straw wattles: Did not work as a stand alone treatment, and felt best use was in conjunction with contour logs. Straw mulch: This was identified as the single most effective treatment of all BAER actions. Observations of manually applied, 2 inch thick cover of straw resulted in a 90% reduction of sediment export when compared to controls! Also was observed to have reduced hydrophobicity. Aerial hydro mulching: Trees intercepted 40% of the mulch and much washed away. Doubling of the application rate appeared successful in one area. Contour felling: Felt this treatment was a failure due to poor soil/tree contact, sometimes worsened conditions by concentrating flow. Log erosion barriers: Observed to be successful but too few were installed due to cost and lack of oversight. Dredging of Los Alamos Reservoir: Never took place and uncertain of status. Channel clearing: Results were favorable as no downstream structures were damaged. Channel tree falling: Of limited use in very specific circumstances. Needs constant supervision. Low head dams, catchments and grade controls: These were constructed of straw, rock or logs. This treatment was determined to be a failure for several reasons. Sites were not carefully selected and captured large drainage areas. Inadequate oversight of crews was a problem. A 24" culvert was plugged downstream due to straw traveling downstream. Trash racks: Wood racks were a failure while metal ones succeeded. Large trash racks actually acted as a grade control structure.2 large steel racks were located too near the culvert inlet and plugged, causing the road to be overtopped. Racks need regular maintenance to be successful.

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report No treatment recommendation - The ID team felt that the Chamise would resprout and provide the necessary ground cover and that the conifer forest would be salvaged logged creating slash for ground cover
Intense thunderstorm (5 inches in an hour) in the China Burn area led to the Bridge Gulch flood. Good narrative and evaluation of flood included in the file. This intense rainfall event caused significant surface erosion on many of the hillslopes, and caused debris torrents to flow down at least 4 intermittent channels which flow into Bridge Gulch and Hayfork Cr. Observation: majority of the surface erosion came from burned slopes formerly covered by chamise brush fields. There was approximately 40% ground cover, which was predominantly forbs. It appeared that the rainfall rapidly infiltrated a gravel and organic matter layer which was about 2 inches thick. The soil below the gravel was much less permeable therefore the water flowed across the soil/gravel interface. Due to the amount of precipitation, there was enough water along the interface to lift the gravel off the soil surface. This caused the surface of entire slopes to flow down into minor swales and collect in the larger ephemeral channels.
It appeared that the soils in the chamise fields were somewhat hydrophobic, both due to being very dry and having organic residues related to the chamise. Where forbs were present, their roots were effective in retaining the gravel. Lower on the slopes, the material flowed over grass covered areas without eroding the soil. There was little evidence of significant erosion within unlogged burned conifer and oak stands. It was apparent that large quantities of water had streamed across the hillslopes, but little soil erosion occurred.
Ephemeral and intermittent stream channels were severely eroded. All unconsolidated alluvium, including sand, gravel, cobbles, boulders, and woody material was blow out of the drainages.
A mall risk was taken by not seeding the burned area, but no one could have anticipated a storm of this magnitude occurring.

Projects.Highlights:
Treatments: Wetting agent - was used to lessen water repellency on 100 acres of high intensity burn with high erosion hazard (hydrophobic soils). Agent used was "Naiad". Treatment not tested, so not funded by BAER.
Seed test of natives in soil after fire for viability (in file)
Road protection - Due to the high mileage of roads within the burn, the high number of specific structures and locations of concern, and the high number of types of specific treatment types needed, just a general cost per mile of road is shown on the 2500-8 form. Treatments included: intercepting relief dips, catch basin clearing and cleaning, ditch cleaning snorkel pipe inlets, spot rocking for water energy dissipation, rocked crossings, and trash/debris racks. Copies of "Road winterization and monitoring" and "Road management" are in file.
Field Observations on 1/10/93 - mid-winter survey (in file) On Jan. 9 and 10, the 3rd in a series of warm "pineapple express" storms passed thru. Objectives of observations was to observe hydrology in action. Slope failures and rockfall were observed in d.g. material along Ice House Rd. Water running in drainages was dark brown and turned very dark brown for a period of 5 minutes, possibly the result of a storm cell that had just passed thru likely causing a bank failure or small debris slide into the drainage. Most of the observed straw bale check dams were washed out on Fry Cr. Some of the small log dams were still in place but water was usually moving under them (the streams had downcut below the logs in most cases). In general, the tributaries to the American River were much cleaner looking outside of the fire area and within the fire area on the south side of the canyon. Most erosion was occurring on the north side of the canyon within the burn area. Within the burn area, there were also differences in turbidity. Areas that had much vegetative groundcover such as bear clover had noticeably cleaner-looking flows than in areas where there was little ground cover.
Visual monitoring of 3-23-93 (in file) and also 8-18-1994g In some of the areas where burn intensities were moderate, bear clover was sprouting. Density of barley seeding varied from very sparse and no barley cover to good density and vigor. At lower elevations, there was some basal sprouting of deerbrush.

The fire started by lightning on September 3, 2024. The Forest managed the fire for resource objectives. The fire is in the Fall Creek Aspen Improvement Project Area, which has aspen regeneration objectives, completed NEPA identifying prescribed fire treatments, and past prescribed fire accomplishments. It provided the opportunity to further restore fire as an ecological process to achieve aspen regeneration in the watershed. The Forest Fire Duty Officer briefed the Deputy Reginal Forester on the fire, its proximity to the project area, and the possible watershed benefits. It was decided to manage the fire and to treat acres meeting objectives of the Fall Creek Aspen Improvement Project. The fire burned in a mosaic pattern with single tree and group tree torching; there was no sustained crown fire. The fire burned small groups of conifers where aspen was present, which should result in aspen regeneration in targeted areas. Given the nature of the fire and our use of it to meet objectives from the Fall Creek Aspen Improvement Project, the Forest has determined that there are no unacceptable risks to any BAER-related critical values. No emergency response actions are proposed and there are no BAER assessment costs.

Projects.Highlights:
Seeding mixture was soft winter wheat and sheep fescue at a combined rate of 43 lbs/acre. About 10 acres were hand seeded along the Kettle Crest Trail to avoid Phacelia franklinii sites (sensitive sp). Aerial seeding of the high intensity burned areas was started Sept. 19 and completed Sept. 22. Heavy application rates were used because of the steepness of the slope and the weight of the wheat seed. About 1900 acres seeded.
Temporary range fencing and cattle guards were installed to prevent cattle from entering the Lambert grazing allotment.
Old culvert was not removed but left in place and a drivable drain drip was constructed just north of the old culvert. This was done because removal would create a drivable mud hole.
Silt fences (about 2000 ft) were installed in swales to control sediment flow from intensely burned side slopes.
Monitoring: Four treatment plots were set up off the 2165-300 road to test the effectiveness of seeding. The plots were to be monitored by the forest botanist. On Nov. 3, reports were that the fescue had sprouted on the middle slopes of Lambert Creek. The wheat had not sprouted yet.

The BAER survey report for this fire (is extensive and comprehensive): it shows what all should be considered especially in the hydrologic area (although it all might not be needed in the report). The hydrologic report by West Zone Hydrologist Gregory Lesch includes sections on probable return frequencies for 13 different storm sizes and durations. It discusses by landtype association how much of precip can be expected as streamflow, the probability of overland flow, and the amount of buffering in the delivery of stormflow to stream flow.
Identified areas at high risk of erosion based on the following criteria: 1) sensitive landtypes with moderately high and high ratings for surface erosion and/or debris slides, 2) slope class categories 40-60% and >60%, 3) burn intensity moderate or high.

Projects.Highlights:
Map of burn area included with report.
Seed mix applied at 7.5 lbs/acre. (seeds PLS/acre) Weeping lovegrass 1/2 lb/ac (17), Needle and thread - Stipa comata 2 lbs/ac (1), Sideoats grama 1 lbs/ac (1), Siberian wheatgrass 3 lbs/ac. (9), and Yellow sweetclover 1 lb/ac (6).
From disturbed area rehabilitation review report: Native herbaceous and woody species responded quickly and out-paced the planted species which responded more slowly perhaps due to drought conditions. However, weeping and Lehman lovegrass appeared to be spreading in spite of a diverse and otherwise adequate component of native forbs and grasses. The lower elevation Coyote fire recovered best the first two years in areas where the catch of seed species appeared to have been poor. However, recovery did not have to compete with use by large herbivores except for a small number of deer.
Flew seed on and had 1/2" of rain in 1 wk but no rain after that for the rest of the summer. In spring the area looked like a moonscape. But 2 years later had got moisture, and side oats gramma (Bocu) was knee high (granitic soils with limestone cap).

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, only a burned area survey
Major concern was to stabilize the soil against wind erosion. A high degree of wind erosion was already occurring just a week after the fire. Productivity of some soils, especially those only 1 to 2 feet deep over bedrock could be materially decreased by soil loss. In the event rains have not caused crusting of the soil surface, it was recommended that any available organic material such as wood chips or straw or felled snags be placed as to reduce wind velocity near the ground. "Listing" or constructing small ridges was also recommended on abandoned roads and firelines.
Fire burned within a larger burn that occurred about 1925, about the same time the area was being logged. Heavy logging and fire have altered the site to the extent that successful reforestation may not be achieved. Recent reforestation efforts using superior stock, and tubed trees have not been successful. The area has become primarily a grass-shrub vegetation.
Fire was divided into 4 areas. Area 1 and 2 with 5% lava rock outcrop was suited to seeding with a range land drill. Seed mix was: standard crested wheatgrass 6 lbs/acre and annual ryegrass 2 lbs/acre. Areas 3 and 4 had a high occurrence of rock outcrop (40-70%) and seeding with the range land drill was not feasible. Manzanita would probably be the first plant to be re-established in these areas. Aerial seeding by helicopter was recommended. Seed mix was: crested wheatgrass 6 lbs/acre, annual ryegrass 2 lbs/acre, and hard fescue 2 lbs/acre. Fertilizer applied to area was 200 lbs 16-20-0 per acre. Seeding of grass by range land drill was delayed until fall rains settled and firmed up the soil. Normal recommendations are to seed ahead of fall rains, but on these ashy, sandy single-grained structured soils depth of planting cannot be controlled. The soil was very dry and literally ankle deep and wind erosion was severe. Seed would be buried or blown away if planted under these conditions.
The burn perimeter was fenced to protect it from livestock grazing as it lies in a cattle allotment. Needs to maintained for 2 years.

Projects.Highlights:
Monitoring of crater fire rehab: (4-30-92)
Area was seeded with winter wheat which was followed by a thunderstorm event in late fall. At 4-30, seeding success was not spectacular. Some seed sprout was evident along the stream bottom. Site revisited on 6-16 and wheat was growing vigorously. Natural vegetation was also responding well. Willows and alders in the riparian areas are resprouting.
Conclusions:
Seeding did not provide any immediate overwinter benefit in terms of preventing soil mobilization, but did have effects on reducing soil erosion in the following year.
It may have been beneficial to have mulched or placed erosion control blankets on steeper slopes adjacent to the stream
It will be beneficial in the future to mulch, hydromulch, or place blankets in unstable areas to prevent soil mobilization when the probability of a winter storm is high.

Two rehab events: 1. After fire rehab 1976 2. After flash flooding 1977 funded by flood funds.
Seed mix recommendations: seeding was done in October of 1976 Treatment A - cereal rye 35 lbs/acre, sweet clover 2 lbs/acre, orchard grass 6 lbs/acre (in draw bottoms, hot burn) Treatment B - orchardgrass 4 lbs/acre, hard fescue 4 lbs/acre, intermediate wheat 6 lbs/acre (hot burned scattered conifer with brush understory) Treatment C - hard fescue 4 lbs/acre, cereal rye 35 lbs/acre, ceanothus 2 lbs/acre (conifer) Treatment CT - hard fescue 4 lbs/acre, cereal rye 35 lbs/acre, bitterbrush 2 lbs/acre (big game thermal cover) Treatment D - crested wheatgrass 10 lbs/acre, hard fescue 2 lbs/acre. (grassland)
Fertilized with 50 lbs N/acre using ammonium nitrate-sulfate. Fertilized 2812 acres, only seeded 1673 acres. In 1977, two separate high intensity storm cells impacted the canyon in 1977, the summer following the fire. The Entiat River subwatershed experienced two flood volumes of 4000 cfs in a 6 week period. 1977 treatments: Contour terraces were accomplished by several means to achieve vegetation establishment. These were done after an intense rainfall in the area resulted in crusted soils that were not expected to accept seed and germinate without some type of site prep. Trenches were constructed on slopes <40% by two mechanical methods: 1. Using the blade of a tractor, and 2. Using a Holt reversible plow. In both cases, the trenches were shallow - a maximum of 1 ft deep. Trenching with the Holt reversible plow moved less topsoil and appeared to be the best of the 2 methods.
On steeper slopes, contour trenches were constructed by 3 methods: 1. By felling snags on the contour, staking, and filling in any holes under the snags (40-50% slopes). Utilized existing snags under 10 inch dbh, leaving 12 to 18 inch stumps to act as anchors for log trenches. 2. Trenches constructed by hand (50-70% slopes). Trenches were a few inches deep and less than a ft wide. Conducted on slopes where there were frequent unvegetated rills over 2 inches deep. 660,000 lineal ft were dug by hand. 3. Trenches were constructed by hand. Burlap was buried to decrease the chance for trenches to breach on 50-70% slopes Results were successful in all 3 treatments.
Areas where contour trenches were constructed were seeded with perennial grass and fertilized. In addition to this, a very good cover of cheatgrass seeded in naturally in the spring. The cheatgrass offers some protection from surface erosion, though it does replace the need for deeper rooted perennial grasses. The cheatgrass should be valuable in holding seed and fertilizer in place., considerably reducing the need for more contour terracing.
Aerial seeding and fertilizer were applied to McKinstry Canyon on steep south facing slopes (100%). They figured that any attempt to scarify the steep slopes would probably do more harm than good.
In ephemeral channels, where felling snags parallel and into the channels has been successful in catching sloughed material, it is important to establish willow or other shrub species, which can survive partial inundation by slough material. This needs to be done as soon as possible peak flows may erode away the trapped soil.
Treatment of gullied ephemeral channels (4 to 10 ft deep) - plug gullies with large snags to catch bank slough and build up the channel bottom. Snags should be arranged and obstructions added to maximize sediment trap efficiency. Plant bottoms with grass and fertilizer and shrubs.
Approximately 2900 cubic yards were hauled and used in building the rock dams. On June 13, 1977, the Crum Canyon burn area was subjected to a high intensity thunderstorm that led to flash flooding and watershed damage. Another high intensity thunderstorm hit the area on July 25, 1977 stripping tons of topsoil off the slopes. Funds for rehabilitation from the floods was requested from the Flood Control Act of 1950.
Second seeding of 1977: seed mixes used. 1. Cereal rye 30 lbs/acre, Fairway crested wheatgrass 12 lbs/acre, Nordon crested wheatgrass 6 lbs/acre, and florida broadleaf mustard 5 lbs/acre. 2. Cereal rye 30 lbs/acre, Fairway crested wheat 4 lbs/acre, Nordon crested wheat 5 lbs/acre, Florida broadleaf mustard 1 lb/acre, Sherman big blue 1 lb/acre, flax 0.19 lbs/acre, bachelor button 0.15 lbs/acre, buckwheat 0.13 lbs/acre, Penstemon 0.1 lbs/acre, and balsam root 0.5 lbs/acre.
Seeded over 3,000 acres, but fertilized over 6000 acres.

Projects.Highlights:
Very thorough narrative with maps included in file. Also the BAER seeding accomplishment report for the Crystal Peak and Cottonwood fires with a chronological record of every step in the seeding process (in file). Article - "Restlessness among the natives (an essay on the appropriate use of "native plants" is in separate file.
Land - straw wattles were placed along the contour to trap small amounts of sediment, but more importantly to shorten slope lengths on steeper slopes. They were placed in a checkerboard pattern.
Seeding (in activity section)
Channel treatments - rock checkdams were used extensively because of the availability of native material. In areas of less available rock, straw bale check dams were used.
Stream bank armoring - functioned well in small ephemeral drainages and near the heads of larger ephemeral/intermittent drainages. But where there were steep gradients and high flows after storm, bank armoring was largely buried by the sloughing off of upslope materials.
Rock dams failed on steep gradients where there were high velocity flows. On milder gradients, it appeared that sediment loading behind the dams was within the dam's capacity. Willows came in naturally behind rock dams without any staking.
Cottonwood fire (no 2500-8), soil erosion monitoring compared with Crystal Peak fire. Fire was on the eastside of the Sierra (pine stands).. Eastside much drier than west. Ceanothus velutinus (tobacco brush, snowbrush) was on N-facing moisture slopes, recovered after fire, but not enough to protect the soil. Benefit of using cereal barley was that it was thick enough to limit cheat grass expansion and spread Cheat grass and other noxious weeds are major problems in this area, so getting something established quickly after fire may be important Riparian vegetation sprouted within one month after fire even though duff was gone, only ash left. Cottonwood fire burned in an area considered a transitory range. Grazing allotments on contractual agreements (lease). Cattle were allowed back in one year after the fire. This was bad for the cottonwoods and aspens, as the cattle came in and ate off the terminal buds. Also the burn reduces wildlife habitat. By bringing cattle back in, increases competition and puts pressure on wildlife survival. Good contact for Cottonwood fire is John Kennedy (Sierraville Ranger Distr). Monitoring exists of the timber salvage effort. Little BAER rehab done.
Master's thesis by Steven Jacobsen looked at channel treatments, compared areas with no treatments to those with, and also compared the Cottonwood fire with the Crystal Peak fire. Do have a copy of his thesis proposal on post fire erosion. Observations to be studied included erosion from runoff on two different parent materials. He observed that in Hoke Valley on primarily granitic soils with high permeability and rapid infiltration, rilling was negligible; whereas in volcanic areas with much lower permeability and slower infiltration, there was greater overland flow resulting in increased rilling.
Crystal Peak fire - burned area all drained into Truckee R., Reno's water supply, so much political pressure to treat fire.
Heritage resources - fire burned over historic sites including the Donner trail. Resource crews were able to go in and document.

Projects.Highlights: This fire does not warrant a watershed emergency. The fire occurred mainly on 1-5% slopes with a low to moderate erosion hazard potential. Most of the area has an adequate amount of effective surface cover to limit erosion to within the tolerance levels,. The physical properties of these soils produce seasonal surface cracking and cause subsoil drying . Revegetation potential is limited by the surface cracking and ponding. Upland soils are shallow and rock fragments will further limit revegetation success. The surface hydrophobic conditions resulting in reduced infiltration is expected to self mitigate within the next several months with the monsoon rains.

Cultural and Heritage Resources (CR):There is one NRHP eligible pre-contact cultural resource located within an area modeled as high risk for post-fire erosion. The probability of damage or loss is very likely due to the site... s location within an area modeled as high probability for post-fire erosion, with potential impacts including loss of subsurface deposits, partial destruction from debris flows, as well as increased vulnerability to looting or vandalism if exposed. The magnitude of consequence is major, as such damage could irreversibly alter the site... s integrity and result in its removal from the National Register of Historic Places. The risk rating is very high. Other BAER treatments are expected to reduce the risk to this resource. b. There are 12 eligible or unevaluated historic or pre-contact cultural resources located in areas modeled as having a moderate risk of erosion. The probability of damage or loss is likely due to post-fire processes such as falling hazard trees and moderate erosion, which may impact structures or expose cultural features, increasing the risk of looting or vandalism. The magnitude of consequence is moderate, as many of these resources lack diagnostic tools tied to specific cultural periods and are common within the broader cultural landscape, reducing the potential loss of significant historical information. The risk rating is high. BAER treatments were considered but are not recommended due to the inability to effectively manage the immediate risk to the resources. c. There are six eligible or unevaluated historic or pre-contact cultural resources located in areas of unburned/very low to low SBS. The probability of damage or loss is possible due to the low risk of erosion, as the sites are located in areas with minimal anticipated sedimentation, flooding, or debris flow, and below slopes with low burn severity. The magnitude of consequence is minor, given the sparse cultural material, and the commonality of these site types within the surrounding landscape. The risk rating is low. BAER treatments are not recommended.

Projects.Highlights:
Included in file is the implementation plan and an excellent accomplishment report
Log terraces - need to get more ground contact with the logs on the slope. At least 70-80% of the log length needs to be in direct contact for the terrace to be effective. Need to buck logs more often to get them to fit the contour of the ground better. Need to trim limbs/staubs that are holding the logs up off of the ground. Chinking the logs on the upslope side is effective, but chinked material needs to be in contact with the ground.
Seed mixes (pure live seed per sq. ft. in paratheses) Seed mix for forested area: later orchardgrass 4 lbs/acre (48), white clover 1 lb/acre (18), and winter wheat 19 lbs/acre (5). Seed mix for non-forested areas: Ephraim crested wheatgrass 6 lbs/acre (34), Durar hard fescue 4.5 lbs/acre (58), Ladak alfalfa 1 lb/acre (5), and winter wheat 15 lbs/acre (5). Seed mix for channel: intermediate wheatgrass 20 lbs/ acre (20), sweetclover 4 lbs/acre (24), and winter wheat 15 lbs/acre (5) Legumes were inoculated that had a viability of at least 2 months. Fertilization for both: 48 lbs/ac of actual N and at least 9 lbs/ac of sulfur. Reason for fertilization - intense burn where all the downed woody material, understory vegetation, and duff layer was consumed. As a result, the soil's ability for nutrient cycling was drastically impaired necessitating a heavy application of fertilizer. Used two helicopters, one for seed and one for fertilizer.
Fires occurring in annual precipitation zones of less than 20 inches are particularly low in soil moisture due to heavy evaporation and transpirational losses. Assuming normal annual precipitation, the first available moisture following the fire is utilized to satisfy the soil moisture deficit. Regardless of the soil type, once the vegetation is removed and the soil deficit satisfied, the fact remains that the second post fire spring season has historically been the most critical regarding soil erosion and potential sediment delivery. Hydrologic recovery is a long term process, especially in low rainfall areas. Watersheds in this hydrologically unstable condition are often at the mercy of climatic conditions.
Rehabilitation efforts in the fall of 1970 were highly successful. Ocular estimates of ground cover ranged from a low of 20% on untreated areas to a high of 80% on treated areas. The wheat provided an immediate ground cover which would be replaced by the seeded perennial species. Channel structures in the broad alluvial valleys were successful, but structures installed in narrow V shaped valleys were severely damaged (especially by the 8-19-89 storm - 2 inches in 40 min).
Rock check dams - after the 8-19-89 storm, all were filled to capacity with sediment. Each dam trapped from 2000 to 10000 cubic yards of sediment. Sediment was removed from the impounded areas and most dams were altered to increase storage capacity. Check dams were not designed to impound stream but to reduce flow velocities - allowing sediment to settle.
Flood event of 8-19-89 Climatic factors caused the flooding (rainfall intensity and duration - 2 inches in 40 min). The extent of flood damage resulted from several factors. The steepness of slope, soil stability, road density (during intense rainfalls, roads have a tendency to accumulate runoff regardless of good water management practices), integrity of ground cover, storm intensity and duration, uniformity of slope and degree of interception by tree canopy. These factors are intensified after fire. Historic flooding events in north central Washington have not always been fire related. Isolated flooding in major subwatersheds occur as a result of unusual climatic-associated events. The coincidence of high intensity storm cell flooding from wildfire areas of large areal extent - to date has no scientific merit.
