Projects.Highlights:
Narrative (Dome fire assessment) included in file.
Additional treatment was recommended in the interim report. This consisted of hand seeding, contour felling, and fencing. These treatments followed storms of the summer, fall, and winter. Re-assessment was performed by Pete Stewart and Earl Ruby. Additional funding requested was needed due to failure of the original treatments as a result of high intensity storms. $31,900 was spent on hand-seeding 100 acres. $23,400 on log terraces $4,000 on fencing $21,000 on rock check dams
Total amounts on page 4 reflect the additional treatments.
Aerial seeding: helicopter seeding of high intensity burn areas: Seed mix: (Popos/Psmeg), in (seeds/sq ft) - Annual rye 38% (15), slender wheatgrass 25% (10), sideoats grama 10% (4), Little bluestem 5% (2), Mountain brome 20% (8), and Purple prairie clover 2% (1). Seed mix (Pipos/Pied) - Annual rye 38% (15), slender wheatgrass 25% (10), sideoats grama 25% (10), Little blue stem 5% (2), Indian ricegrass 5% (2), and Purple prairie clover 2% (1). Mixes were considered native to this part of the Santa Fe National Forest except for the annual rye. Experience with annual rye on other Forest projects indicated that the rye will sprout fast and provide quick cover, but will not persist beyond a few years.
No additional information on why the aerial seeding failed (possibly as a result of high intensity and localized storms) Interim request for additional funding was within the one year time frame and was to cover the failure of these treatments. Additional treatments included seeding 100 acres and construction of 150 log terraces.
Hand seeding mix: Annual rye 50%, Mountain brome 25%, and sideoats grama 25% resulting in 25 seeds/sq ft PLS This was done on 100 acres following the construction of log terraces.
Contour felling: Initially asked for 3000 acres of felling at a cost of $150,000, but were refused due to lack of proven benefits with this activity. In additional treatments, asked for log terracing instead. Log terraces were constructed on 100 acres within the high burn intensity burn area. Current conditions were 300+ stems per acre of various sized boles. This treatment would place approximately 40 6-8 inch diameter tree stems per acre on the ground parallel to the contour of the slope. Only burned trees would be used and the logs would be backfilled with soil on the upslope side to prevent water flow beneath the log.
Two loose rock check dams were built to prevent downcutting of the channel and to provide partial storage of flood sediments and to stabilize the gully forming in the upper headwaters of Capulin Canyon.
Statement from Reggie Fletcher (Regional Ecologist) - stand replacement fires in ponderosa pine forest are not considered normal or needed for natural processes.
Earl Ruby observations: Typical weather patterns for northern New Mexico is early-season rains (March-April) that taper off to near-zero rain by mid-May. The early rains are typically followed by a 6 to 8 week drought (mid-May to mid-July) with no effective rain and dry lightning events. The spring drought is typically followed by "monsoon rains" in July, and continuing into early Fall. The typical rain pattern supports an early growing season, followed by drought, followed by a later growing season. The resident vegetation communities have adapted to the local weather patterns. However, wildfires are often seeded with species that are not adapted to the local weather, and are therefore only partially effective to ineffective as burn stabilizers. Thus a fallback treatment (e.g. contour terracing) needs to be considered.
Straw bale check dams need to be put high in watershed because they are not very strong.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. The Nez Perce National Historic Trail (#40; 0.5 miles) and Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail (#25; 0.6 miles) are within the burned area. The cultural resources of the trail routes are threatened by degradation of trail tread, erosion of soil in and around the trail area, and/or exposure of possible cultural materials or features along the trail sections that would then be at risk of damage or looting. The Nez Perce National Historic Trail probability of damage or loss is unlikely due to the route is more of a corridor of historic travel than a defined trail on the landscape and magnitude of consequence major because the damage or loss of cultural resources are irreversible. The risk rating is INTERMEDIATE, no treatment recommended. The Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail probability of damage or loss is possible due to the steep nature of the trail, moderate burn severities, and erodible soils and the possibility that cultural material could be exposed along the tread if eroded; the magnitude of consequence is major because the damage or loss of cultural resources are irreversible. The risk rating is HIGH. BAER treatments are recommended. See treatment T1 ... Trail Drainage Stabilization. b. NFSR 500, also known as the Lolo Motorway, runs along the Lochsa divide from Lolo Pass to its terminus on the USFR 100 Road near Kamiah Idaho. This roughly 110 mile road was constructed in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps to support motorized traffic along the same travel corridor shared by the Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail, the Nez Perce (Nimiipu) Historic trail and the Bird-Traux Trail. In a number of places, these trails and the road converge and diverge, depending on the landform. This road retains character and integrity to the time period in which it was constructed, with numerous CCC sites having been recorded along its length. The fire burned over about 0.8 miles of the road. Road could be damaged from increased runoff and raveling onto the road/ditch. The probability of damage or loss is unlikely, though larger storms could create enough increased runoff for erosion. The magnitude of consequence is moderate because it is a small segment of road that, if damaged, would not change the historic character of the road. The risk rating is LOW, no BAER treatment recommended. c. The Bird-Traux Trail, first constructed in the mid-1800s as an attempt to create a wagon road from Virgina City, Montana, to Pierce, Idaho, runs along the ridgetops north of the East fire, with a 0.4-mile section passing though the burn area. The feature is threatened by erosion of trail tread, cultural materials/artifacts along the trail at risk of looting due to exposure after the light to moderate burn through the area. Site visit on 9/29/25 showed this section of trail to be faint, passing through a previously burned area. Possibility of damage or loss of integrity due to these factors is unlikely due to the affected section of trail being located along a gentle slope, already impacted by previous fire activity. No artifacts or cultural features observed during site visit along burned sections. The magnitude of consequence is moderate because the small section of trail within the burn area is faint, the localized section... s integrity not effecting the overall importance of the feature along its entire length. The risk rating is LOW, no treatment is recommended.

Projects.Highlights:
Seeding was done on 200 acres of steep and intensely burned land. Seed was applied in strips 25 ft. wide and 75 ft apart.
Fence was constructed to keep cattle off meadows until burned vegetation was re-established. Recovery of the meadows was rapid; a lush, dense cover was present by late spring of 1982.
Culvert cleanout to prevent drainage problems, and placement of ground cover/sediment catchments below dips on bare slopes
Construction of gully plugs in meadows to prevent head cutting. Cedar poles were used. Treatment was successful in halting the cut.
Followup to work on steep slopes - following the summer storm events, attempts were made to stabilize the steep slopes that were eroding severely. Sub merchantable poles were dropped contour to the slope, and trenches were dug on the contour. Unfortunately, neither of these treatments was very successful, mainly because the drainage network (gullies and rills) had already been established.

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, but rehab narrative included in file. Seed mix: orchard grass 8 lbs/acre (80 seeds/sq ft), creeping red fescue 7 lbs/acre (80 seeds/sq ft), and cereal rye 25 lbs/acre (10 seeds/sq ft) 260 acres total to be seeded @ $4692.00 Fertilizer application to accompany the grass seed - 74,500 lbs of urea @ $9,400.00 It was felt that a fertilizer application (fall of 1975) would enhance the growth of the cereal rye and any residual or native sproutings. Since the area receives approximately 150 inches of precipitation each year (mostly in the winter months) and leaching can be expected, it was suggested that 96 lbs/acre of available N be applied. Fertilization effects would be short-term due to the lack of depth of the soils and high precipitation rates. A second application at the same quantities in the spring of 1976 (better fall of 76) was felt to be necessary for seedling establishment and vigor.
Dry ravel was significant after the fire.
Streams in the burned area experience extremely high peak flows twice a year. A peak in Dec. is the result of rainfall runoff, and the peak in March is due to the occurrence of snowmelt runoff.
Fire retardant was mixed near the shoreline of the Wynoochee Reservoir. It is believed that the retardant is not toxic, but can go into suspension. It was recommended to cover the retardant with soil. It is expected that the clay in the soil will serve to bind the chemical components of the retardant.

This is a wilderness fire.
Sediment Potential: 22,300 cubic yards / square mile. Results are from Disturbed WEPP. Modeled high severity fire in the uplands and riparian; 10-30% slope; 20-50% ground cover; 10-30% rock; Fenn modified climate. This is a worse case analysis. Most of the fire will have no increase in erosion or sediment.
Adjusted Design Flow, (cfs per square mile): 110 cfsm. For design storm analysis, we used a 15 minute, 25 year storm that occurred in Sleeping Child Creek. This storm produced a 110 cfsm runoff in a 1.8 mi2 burned watershed (Site 14), which was greater than a 500 year runoff. This watershed was selected for the design storm because the runoff was water only (not debris) and the watershed was small (Less than 2 Mi2), where impacts are most likely to roads or other facilities.
Road drainage in watersheds less than 2 Mi2 should be designed to handle these flows. In watersheds 5 to 20 mi2, the design storm should be approximately 23 cfsm (Parrett and Others, Fire Hydrology, 7/2003).

Projects.Highlights:
All treatments were confined to slopes no greater than 40%.
Decisions on where to aerially grass seed were based on germination tests of soil samples taken from high burn intensity areas.
Results indicated soils from grasslands had a high % of germinants, so these areas were not seeded.
Soil samples from brush and conifer areas had varying germination rates, ranging from 0 to 10 plants per plot for ten days and 30 plants per plot for 30 days in chaparral. Native seed germination on timber soils was 0 after 10 days and 10 seeds germinating after 30 days.
Since there was varying results on chaparral soils after 10 days, it was decided to seed those areas on slopes less than 40%.
The team decided not to seed the timber areas.
Dramatic increase in rehabilitation costs from the initial to the final report.
Where log erosion barriers were placed correctly, they were catching sediment. It was noted that water would run down the log and concentrate at the end resulting in downhill rilling. They were not as effective as mulching. Not a lot of soil behind them. Improvements may be to put wings on the logs, use shorter length (4 to 6 ft).
Straw bale check dams had a 90% survival rate after the first storm. Structures that were below a recently logged area of private property were completely full of sediment. Structures in other areas were storing sediment at a range of 75 to 100% of their capacities. They were used downstream from the straw wattles. All were built with energy dissipation below the dams
Pre- and post-fire stream gauges water quality studies were conducted by the Lake County flood Control District (Tom Smith). Reports are available (do not have)

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report.
From "Burn restoration report" July 1970: High water usually occurs from spring snowmelt, with the crest appearing in May, but can occur later. Low flow periods are in early October and mid-February as a result of drought and freezing. Runoff is usually by runoff percolating through the soil to the streams. Water seldom appears on the ground surface as overland flow unless concentrated by man's activities. Because of the coarse-textured soil, the streams are usually clear, have low, suspended sediment, and a high bed load.
High intensity summer storms occasionally occur in the area. Storms are more likely to be more intense over blackened areas than over the adjacent forested areas, particularly within the orographic effect of mountains. Chinook winds over a snowpack, with the resulting runoff, is not a rare occurrence in the area.
About once every ten years, under normal conditions, a wet spring causes small soil mass failures. In the burned areas, at least a 25% increase in moisture will be available in the soil and streams.
The soil water balance over most of the forest is delicate. Mass failures can occur in these areas when fire reduces transpiration and contour terracing (which increases infiltration) is used as a treatment. The low liquid limit of the soil results in many small mass failures whenever the amounts of water are increased. This type of failure in cutbanks is one of the prime road maintenance problems on the Forest road system. Along roads, the removal of vegetation has "added" water to the soil matrix, resulting in failures. The vegetative ash which overlies the ground in hard burned areas will readily absorb water and, when saturated, will flow across the nonwettable scorched soil underneath. The potential for debris flows from snowmelt in these conditions is high.
From Okanogan Fire Rehab plan: It was strongly recommended that at least one plot study on the burn be established as a control to evaluate the effects of fertilization vs nonfertilization on broadcast seeding. The following data was to be collected: 1. Seed mixture used, 2. Mixture application rate/acre, 3. Method of application, 4. Time of application in relation to seasonal moisture trends, 5. Type of fertilizer used, 6. When was fertilizer applied, and 7. The fertilizer application rate/acre.
Seed mix for burn Low elevation (<5600 ft) - orchard grass 3 lbs/acre, smooth brome 4 lbs/acre, hard fescue 3 lbs/acre, timothy 2 lbs/acre, and pubescent wheatgrass 3 lbs/acre, and yellow sweet clover 1lb/acre. High elevation (>5600 ft) - fescue 3 lbs/acre, hard fescue 3 lbs/acre, perennial ryegrasses 2 lbs/acre, white clover 2 lbs/acre, timothy 3 lbs/acre, and orchard grass 3 lbs/acre. 85% of 6350 acres of the burn were seeded.

Projects.Highlights:
In this area, the most serious potential for surface runoff and erosion is from the "Chinooks" which occur often in the area. The "Chinooks" are very warm winds and rains which occur in the spring causing very rapid snow melt. This often results in very high runoff from the uplands and could cause severe erosion and major damage downstream.
Seeding of area of slopes less than 30%: hard fescue 1.5 lbs/acre, alta fescue 1.5 lbs/acre, and perennial ryegrass 2 lbs/acre. Seed mix for slopes of 30 to 60%: hard fescue 1.5 lbs/acre, Alta fescue 1.5 lbs/acre, perennial ryegrass 2 lbs/acre, sweet clover 1 lb/acre, and standard crested wheatgrass 2 lbs/acre.
Fertilizer recommendations: If grass seeding was accomplished in sufficient time for germination in the fall, 67 lbs of 45% urea per acre aerially applied in the fall is recommended. If germination in the fall is not likely the fertilizer recommendations are for spring aerial application of 200 lbs 16-20-0 per acre at the time of spring snow melt. Fertilizer must be applied when soil is moist to obtain response.

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, only rehabilitation report
Recommended to fertilize with ANS (ammonia nitrate sulfur) with 30% nitrogen, 1% phosphorus, and 6% sulfur in the fall at a cost of $6.80/acre (application rate is 50 lbs of actual N per acre).
Extreme variations in elevation (2,000 to 7000 ft) and habitat type indicated that two seed mixes needed to be used.
Seed mix 1 (lower elevations) - Potomac orchardgrass 2lbs/acre, Drummond timothy 0.5 lbs/acre, Durar hard fescue 1 lb/acre, Primar slender wheatgrass 3 lbs/acre, and White Dutch clover 0.5 lbs/acre.
Seed mix 2 (high elevations) - Whitmar beardless wheatgrass 2 lbs/acre, Norden Crested Wheatgrass 2 lbs/acre, Toper Pubescent wheatgrass 4 lbs/acre, Durar hard fescue 1 lb/acre, Drummond timothy 1 lb/acre, cereal rye 20 lbs/acre, and dwarf yellow sweetclover 0.5 lbs/acre. Cereal rye to be applied separately to the drainage bottoms (237 acres) at the rate of 20 lbs/acre..
Temporary fencing - was constructed to keep cattle off of the reseeded area for two growing seasons.
Sheep are permitted to graze during the winter months on the steep breaks along the Snake River. To keep sheep off newly revegetated areas, they were to be rerouted.
The east edge of the fire adjacent to the Snake River was spotty and generally light, created by the fire backing slowly downhill.
One year followup evaluation:(in file) Success of seeding on non-commercial timber sites was excellent. Burned elderberry, maple, and ceanothus were all resprouting. On the commercial timber sites above 6000 ft plant vigor of seedlings was much lower than those at lower elevations. This was attributed to the cooler conditions and shorter growing season.
9-7-74 revisit of fire.
The success of the seeding on noncommercial timber sites was excellent. Burned elderberry, maple, and ceanothus were resprouting. Large prostrate yellow sweetclover plants were numerous on the heavy burned spots. Seeding at 6000 ft on commercial sites was not doing as well, plant vigor was much lower. The difference was attributed to the cool weather which prompted a short growing season and less fertile soil conditions. Two rains fell on the fire area before it was seeded. The heavy burn areas crusted and formed a moisture barrier layer.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: Critical values for Cultural Resources under a Burned Area Emergency Response assessment are defined as Cultural resources which are listed on or potentially eligible for the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP), Traditional Cultural Properties, or Indian Sacred Sites on NFS lands (FSM 2353, June 2020). Potential threats to critical values include: - Looting facilitated by increased visibility in a post-fire landscape. - - Damage from OHV incursion and disturbance. Increased sheet-wash erosion can degrade archaeological features and remove artifacts from site contexts. a. Threat of Looting: Four archaeological sites (53-213, 53-307,53-336, and 53-433) are susceptible to looting because 1) they no longer have vegetation to conceal artifacts and features or restrict access, and 2) they are adjacent to recreation areas, along roads and trails, and/or have a history of looting. Artifacts typically sought after by collectors have been noted in exposed areas. The theft from sites that are potentially eligible for NRHP would result in irreversible loss/damage. Threats from looting on these sites are POSSIBLE with a magnitude of consequences of MAJOR posing a HIGH risk. b. Threat of OHV Incursion: Four archaeological sites (53-213, 53-307,53-336, and 53-433) are threatened by OHV incursion. OHV incursion in this part of the forest is common. The loss of vegetation increases the risk of illegal OHV trespass that has the potential to disturb surface deposits causing damage to the integrity and research potential of the site. The threat of OHV incursion is VERY LIKELY with a magnitude of consequences of MODERATE posing a VERY HIGH risk. c. Threat of Erosion: Eight archaeological sites are susceptible to post fire erosion and runoff, as well as flooding as they are located downslope/downstream of burned slopes (moderate SBS) modelled to have significant increases in runoff, erosion, and flooding. Known subsurface artifacts could be exposed if capping sediments are eroded or carried off-site. Some of these areas are also near roads and recreation areas, which could increase the risk of looting if artifacts become exposed. Watershed response is POSSIBLE to VERY LIKELY with a MAJOR magnitude of consequence posing a HIGH to VERY HIGH risk. (Ratings represent a summary for all eight sites.)

Gold Fire Miles of Stream Channels by Order or Class PERENNIAL 0 INTERMITTENT 1.19 EPHEMERAL 1.18
Gold/Rosa - Increases in runoff from moderate SBS areas resulting in increased overland flow, sheet flow and rockfall: Known archeological sites within the Gold fire footprint lie in areas of low and moderate soil burn severity. The Probability is possible that sites will experience damage from increases in runoff within moderate SBS areas. The Magnitude of the threat is moderate as the site types represented within the burn area are susceptible to the irretrievable loss of unknown features or artifacts. The Risk therefore is intermediate and not subject to BAER treatments. Sites within the Rosa fire footprint are within low and moderate SBS and the Probability is unlikely that they will experience damage from increases in runoff. The Magnitude of the threat to sites within the Rosa fire is minor due to the site types represented. Magnitude of the threat to sites within the Rosa fire is low and no BAER treatments are recommended. None of the sites considered for analysis within either fire footprint are likely to experience significant damage or destruction due to increased runoff, and per watershed modeling, such events occurring within or adjacent to known site locations would be unusual. Should sites experience any form of damage from increased runoff, it is improbable that any individual components (features or artifacts) damaged will impact future eligibility for the National Register of Historic Places. No treatments are recommended. b. Gold/Rosa - Looting as a result of reduced vegetative cover: Looting of archeological sites is an ongoing concern and reduced vegetative cover affords greater visibility of artifacts which may be of interest to looters. For sites analyzed within both fire footprints, the Probability of looting is possible due to reduced vegetative cover, although sites are generally inaccessible. The Magnitude of the threat from looting is moderate as certain artifacts and site components may directly impact the NRHP eligibility of the site. Therefore, the Risk of looting to sites within both fires is intermediate due to the irretrievable loss of material culture. The majority of sites with reduced vegetative cover are historic mining sites, which often contain many different types of artifacts. These artifacts may help ascertain site date and function, however the importance of these sites often lie in their location and their features. None of the sites visited in the field during this rapid assessment contain artifacts that, if removed from the site, will impact the sites... eligibility for listing onto the National Register of Historic Places. No treatments are recommended and the best way to protect the sites is for natural revegetation to obscure the site components.

Gorda-Rat fire -watershed evaluation file
From report "Rat revisited" by Max Copenhagen:
Even though higher than normal winter rains, fire area looked great. Not as many road problems as expected. Densely seeded eyebrows looked good, but probably didn't do much good in terms of slide reduction. Ryegrass coverage was better than expected. Growth of ryegrass was patchy, but it was hard to day why, either drift or soil conditions. On an overall watershed basis rehab seeding provided plenty of additional cover to improve stability. My philosophy continues to be that we as the rehab team should develop the best technical prescription and risk analysis possible within the time frame, and then let managers add or delete treatment areas due to political considerations. I have no problem with it, I just don't want to be a part of it. Probably overestimated the effects (predicting the worst case)
It was decided that all firmly anchored log jams plus large logs should remain in the channel to help maintain channel stability. Large organic debris forms a relationship with the stream channel, playing a crucial role in channel morphology and sediment routing. These effects are usually long-lived, exceeding 200 years for redwood debris. Removal of log jams that have become an integral part of a stream channel can release large amounts of sediment and increase mean water velocity, resulting in a destabilizing effect upon the channel and possibly triggering debris torrents.
Nacimiento watershed - fire evaluation (applicable to many situations concerning N and S slopes) North slopes: good leaf drop replenishing surface litter good mosaic of burn on north slope. Riparian areas are intact Resprouting coming in strong South slopes: Dry ravel occurring in over-steepened drainages Small channels are filling prior to storms and therefore probably will result in moderate flows. Significant amount of sediment will get to reservoirs.
The entire burn area was extremely sensitive to landsliding and about 50% of the coastal area is recently active or active landslides in serpentine and schist rock types. The clayey soils particularly where they occur over serpentine are extremely unstable. Historically, the Big Sur coastal front has had catastrophic landslides and erosion following a fire rainfall sequence.
For both high to moderate burn intensity areas, particularly under chaparral cover types, the repellency was very variable in degree of intensity. Surface soil crusting (platy-like structure) was also severe in many places and appeared to be most pronounced on surface soils that burned very hot on steep slopes.

Projects.Highlights:
No treatment reasons:
A mosaic of burn intensities was created on a landscape with stable geology, and soils that were resistant to erosion. The fire burned on steep ground that was situated near the top end of the drainage. Low drainage densities in the area, combined with low fire intensities in the wetter areas would result in very little impact to stream channels.
Infiltrative soils, surviving soil organic layers, and rock talus on the majority of the area should result in low erosion potential.
Revegetation of the area with short-lived non-natives was expected to be difficult due to the short growing season and cold soil conditions.
Burned area was within the Strawberry Wilderness.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: A total of five (5) previously recorded eligible or unevaluated archaeological sites for listing on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) were identified within the burn area. Several pre-contact sites that are eligible or unevaluated for the NRHP are located outside of the fire perimeter downstream along Sulanharas Creek and may be at an increased risk of flooding. There is a threat of damage, loss of historic context and contents due to damage to sites from hazard trees, erosion and sedimentation, and looting or vandalism to cultural resources on the Shasta-Trinity National Forest. a. Hazard trees- There is a threat of damage, loss of historic context and contents due to hazardous trees falling on cultural resources on the five sites located on USFS system lands within the fire perimeter. Due to the nature of the cultural resources, the probability of damage or loss is Unlikely. The magnitude of consequences is Moderate. In most cases, damage to cultural resource sites represents an irretrievable loss of traces of the past. Cultural resources are non-renewable, and damaged sites and features prevent their potential to provide important information about the past to current and future generations. Due to the nature of these cultural resource sites, a moderate consequence rating appropriately addresses the likelihood of these types of damage based on their nature and potential for significant impact. The resulting risk is Low. o BAER funds are NOT requested to treat these risks.... - b. Erosion and sedimentation- There is a threat to the... -cultural resources eligible or potentially eligible from listing in the NRHP from increased runoff, erosion,... -and debris flows after wildfires. Field observation and burn severity models on slopes above these sites reflect areas within the fire perimeter are not at risk of erosion/sedimentation due to vegetation loss and landscape position. No cultural resources are located directly below areas at risk of debris flows, however increased runoff downstream of the fire is a concern. Those sites located downstream are generally high enough above the creek to be at a lower risk of flooding and would not result in large scale obliteration of these sites but could damage certain features or displace artifacts if flooding occurred. Therefore, the... -probability of damage or... -loss... -is Unlikely. The... -magnitude of... -consequences... -is... -Moderate. In most cases, damage to cultural resource sites represents an irretrievable loss of traces of the past. Cultural resources are non-renewable. The resulting... -risk... -is... -Low. o BAER funds are NOT requested to treat these risks. However, road treatments will reduce sedimentation into cultural resources along Sulanharas Creek. c. Unauthorized artifact collection-... - There is a threat... -of loss of historic context and contents due to unauthorized artifact collection at three cultural resources eligible or potentially eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP). The fire has exposed two historic sites and one pre-contact site that may be at risk from unauthorized artifact collection. This exposure makes artifacts and features susceptible to damage from unauthorized collection. ... -However, the... -probability of damage or... -loss... -is Unlikely, because the pre-contact site is extremely remote with no road or trail access, and the historic sites contain minimal artifacts that could be collected. The... -magnitude of... -consequences... -is... -Moderate. In most cases, damage to cultural resource sites represents an irretrievable loss of traces of the past. Cultural resources are non-renewable. Removed artifacts from historic contexts degrade the meaning of historic sites and features and their potential to provide important information about the past to this and future generations. The nature of unauthorized collection means that impacts resulting in total irretrievable loss of a site or feature are expected but... -unpredictable... -and also... -are likely to occur over time. A moderate consequence rating appropriately addresses the likelihood of these types of damage based on their nature and potential for significant impact.... -The resulting... -risk... -is... -Low. o BAER funds are NOT requested to treat these risks. Forest staff should monitor cultural resource integrity and evidence of unauthorized collection.

Projects.Highlights:
Road work WAS done with non-BAER funds.
Contour Lop and Scatter/Contour Log Material: This combined treatment was proposed for 168 acres on granitic soils where access for other treatments is difficult. Small diameter fire killed trees (<8 inches dbh) will be felled, cut into 5 foot lengths and placed on the contour. The branches and tops will be cut up and spread around. The objective is to create as much soil cover, preferably on the contour, as possible to act as sediment traps and break up sheet and rill erosion. Using small lengths of logs will make it unnecessary to dig shallow trenches to seal the logs. This treatment should allow for faster production rates compared to the normal contour falling treatment. The use of this treatment is concentrated in watersheds serving as domestic water sources or tributaries to Swillup Creek. Due to the very short implementation time period (weather related), only 120 acres were accomplished.
Strip Mulching-Hand: Strip mulching (2 tons/acre rate) with certified weed-free straw was proposed for 60 acres on granitic soils in the high and moderate burn severity areas. The purpose of the treatment is to provide suitable ground cover where there presently is none. The extent of this treatment is confined to sensitive areas near stream channels and swales, on granitic soils. Mulching in strips across slopes has proven to be a more cost effective method of applying this treatment. Strip widths of 15 feet alternate between mulched and unmulched areas. The use of this treatment is concentrated in watersheds serving as domestic water sources or tributaries to Swillup Creek. Due to the very short implementation time period (weather related), only 10 acres were accomplished.

Projects.Highlights:
Roads and Trail Treatments:
NFSR 34N76 (sections 32 & 33, T35N, R 4E and sections 4 & 5, T34N R4E) experienced adjacent high burn severity. The current road drainage is not expected to accommodate the expected increased flows. Additional rolling dips are recommended along this section of road especially downgrade of existing culverts. Approximately 24 additional dips are recommended. One drainage crossing is undersized and not expected to handle increased flows and debris. It is recommended that the existing 18 inch corrugated metal pipe (CMP) be replaced with a 30 inch CMP to accommodate the expected increased flows. Rolling dips will need to be surfaced and need keyed riprap for armoring dip outlets. Riprap material is available onsite. NFSR 34N76A (section 5, T34N, R4E) has burn severities and potential runoffs that are expected to cause roadway damage to the transportation facility. One rolling dip is recommended just downgrade of the intersection with NFSR 34N76. Riprap material is available onsite for outlet armoring.
NFSR 34N76E (section 5, T34N, R4E) also has burn severities and potential runoffs that are expected to cause roadway damage to the transportation facility. One rolling dip is recommended just upgrade of the intersection with NFSR 34N76. This will protect any runoff on the road from being transferred onto the collector road NFSR 34N76 and damaging both roadways. Riprap material is available onsite for outlet armoring.

Projects.Highlights:
Seed rate was 14 lbs/acre. A total of 27,000 lbs of seed was applied with the following seed mixture: slender wheatgrass 56%, regreen 9%, smooth bromegrass 9%, western wheatgrass 9%, annual ryegrass 7%, orchardgrass 6%, and alsike clover 4%.
Seeding rates were monitored using flooring tiles with adhesive on back of the tiles. Helicopter pilot used a GPS unit to establish flight lines. Initial floor tile readings indicated he was not flying close enough to past flights and there was a strip of unseeded area. Pilot was notified but he did not make enough adjustment, resulting in portions of burn area not being seeded. This may have been due to lack of accuracy of the GPS unit, pilot error, flying too fast or too high, or wind conditions.
Helicopter hovered over the seed bucket while it was filled.
Most of the seed has sprouted and is growing after area received several light rains. No heavy intense rains in summer so little soil erosion. Aspen and oak sprouting is occurring.
Two soil erosion monitoring sites were set up in hot burn areas and were to be monitored annually.
Original recommendation by BAER team on this fire was not to do anything. There was a lot of rock cover and it was for the most part a low intensity burn with low hydrophobicity. Forest supervisor over-ruled.

Proposed seed mixture was: Orchard grass 3#/acre, crested wheat grass 6#/acre, fawn fescue grass 4#/acre, yellow sweet clover 1#/acre, Ladak alfalfa 1#/acre, and cereal rye 15#/acre
Cereal rye was part of the mixture to introduce a species that will germinate and grow with the first fall rains. Cereal rye will provide a measure of protection the first fall and will start regrowth early the next spring. In addition to its early growth, the cereal rye also acts as a nurse crop to the perennials, helping to assure successful establishment of a vegetative cover, and then disappearing from the stand in 3-4 years.

Projects.Highlights:
Suppression cost of $17,463,219 includes costs for Beaver Lakes, Siah Lake, Wendover, and Bears Oil. The Lolo portion of the Hopeful II Fire was $2,720,619. The Clearwater portion of these fires is $14,720,600.
Sediment Potential: 21,800 cubic yards / square mile. Results are from Disturbed WEPP. Modeled high severity fire in the uplands and riparian; 20-45% slope; 20-45% ground cover; 0-10% rock; Fenn modified climate. This is a worse case analysis. Most of the fire will have no increase in erosion or sediment.
Adjusted Design Flow, (cfs per square mile): 110 cfsm. For design storm analysis, we used a 15 minute, 25 year storm that occurred in Sleeping Child Creek in 2001. This storm produced a 110 cfsm runoff in a 1.8 mi2 burned watershed (Site 14), which was greater than a 500 year runoff event. This watershed was selected for the design storm because the runoff was water only (not debris) and the watershed was small (Less than 2 Mi2), where impacts are most likely to roads or other facilities. It is possible, that the Hopeful II Fire could receive a similar storm with similar watershed response where burn intensities are high. Storm runoff should be adjusted downward in watersheds where burn intensity is less than high. Road drainage in watersheds less than 2 Mi2 should be designed to handle these flows. In watersheds 5 to 20 mi2, the design storm should be approximately 23 cfsm (Parrett and Others, Fire Hydrology, 7/2003).

Projects.Highlights:
Storm patrol was almost constant after the fire due to series of thunderstorms in Sept. and Oct. Also heavy rainfalls during Jan. required almost constant monitoring of roads. Patrols cleaned out culverts, kept drainage ways open, and made sure dips were cleared. Usually were on patrol during and after the storm. On some roads, esp. access roads to radio towers, there was concern about safety of the public. Put in gates. Patrol mainly does repairs between storms. Patrols are the best cost/benefit treatments. They can prevent damage, save a lot of dollars.
Rip rap was placed below culverts. Trails were winterized by constructing waterbars to improve drainage.
Early warning system consisted of rain gauges that were connected to a radio signal transmitter that is able to transmit the rate of rainfall. Signal sent to appointed emergency director. Rain gauges are strategically placed in burned watersheds that are threats to downstream communities.

The Iron Peak Fire started from a lightning strike and was discovered on August 21, 2024, and burned 544 acres. The strategy for managing the fire has been full suppression, and 100% containment of the fire was declared on August 29. Due to the small size, location, and lack of critical values, an informal assessment of resources in the same drainage as the fire scar for BAER critical values was conducted and found no critical values at risk from post-fire events. From a map exercise the only critical value identified in and downslope of the fire scar is a non-motorized trail. However, this trail is non-existent on the ground, has had no documented maintenance for decades, and consequently is not a receptor for protection from post-fire event damage. Therefore, there will be no request of funding for treatments with the Iron Peak Fire.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Horse Creek Connector Trail #718: Threats are increased erosion resulting in damage or burial of trail segments and exposure of possible cultural materials or features along the trail section; exposure increases the risk of damage and looting to newly uncovered cultural material. The probability of damage or loss is considered possible due to the low to moderate soil burn severity along sections of trail. The magnitude of consequence is considered major because cultural resources cannot be replaced (irreversible) and moderate burn severity occurs along 0.36 miles of the 1.8 mi burned trail. The risk to this value is high and no treatments are recommended. b. Selway Pack Station: Threats are increased potential of debris flow onto alluvial fan, burying or damaging features and structures at the pack station. The probability of damage or loss is considered unlikely due to an unburned area around the pack station, the elevated position of the structures above the channel, and the <20% likelihood of debris flow at this location under typical rainfall. The magnitude of consequence is considered major because cultural resources cannot be replaced and debris flow impacts to the pack station would be irreversible. The risk to this value is intermediate and no treatments are recommended.

Seeding rate was 13 lbs/ac (50 seeds/ft2. 3.Mulching was deemed successful in preventing accelerated erosion on all slopes. 4. Seeding as well as native species regeneration showed little response the first year. The sterile hybrid "QuickStart" germinated well and persisted better than others. Seeding was not successful in the short term in suppressing noxious weed expansion. 5. Cheatgrass increased in both control and treated areas, possibly due to better winter and spring precipitation. The team believed that direct fire effects reduced cheatgrass populations. 6. The team believed that herbicide treatment of cheatgrass was successful in killing 60-89.5% of cheatgrass. Treatment was best in early season.

Storm patrols were along the PCT. Area seeded was the Smith Canyon watershed which was subjected to high intensity burn. Seeding would reduce the risk of flash flooding originating from Smith Canyon. Historical record of major thunderstorms and flooding in the area. In 1985, a storm event sent a wall of mud 11 ft high down Smith Canyon.
The forest sampled the high intensity burn areas in the headwaters of Smith Canyon and attempted to germinate the sample using the protocol documented in the Botany Report from the Ackerson Complex Fire. The sample was planted and watered; after 7, 10, and 14 days nothing emerged, assumed no viable seeds left.

July 17, 2006: July 6, 2006 there was a very high intensity rainstorm that covered the fire area with significant amounts of precipitation. (no site specific rain data available) This rainstorm caused severe soil erosion especially along portions of the Hodag Creek Trail #701 and the South fork Trail #80. Several of the previously constructed trail waterbars were either filled, over-topped, or washed-out. The very high potential for a post-fire erosion event as noted in the initial BAER report unfortunately occurred before adequate natural revegetation had established. There is potential for significant additional soil erosion associated with the trail system and the resulting sediment yield into the tributary streams of the South Fork of the Flathead River (key Bull Trout habitat).

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a) There is a Very High Risk (Very Likely/Major) to cultural resource sites within high and moderate Soil Burn Severity and Very High Risk (Very Likely/Moderate) within low Soil Burn Severity where tree mortality is high. BAER guidance limits threat identification generally to moderate and high soil burn severity. However, there is a very high risk identified for five sites within low soil burn severity due to high tree mortality and expected damage from falling trees on precontact structures. A total of 165 cultural resources were identified within the Laguna Wildfire BAER analysis boundary. Of the 165 sites in the assessment area, 160 (97%) are considered BAER critical values (i.e., archaeological sites listed, eligible, or undetermined/unevaluated for the National Register of Historic Places). These include 63 precontact structures (pithouses, unit houses, and towers), 93 artifact scatters (precontact or multicomponent time period), and nine historic infrastructure sites (corrals, telephone line, spring box, mine shaft, and rock features). Threats to cultural resources in the Laguna Wildfire footprint identified in the critical values analysis include sheet erosion and tree throw. Minimal erosional threats were identified based on hydrologic modeling and in-field site post-burn assessments. The primary threat to cultural resources in the Laguna Wildfire footprint is extensive surface disturbance resulting from trees falling within sites.

Projects.Highlights:
Land Treatments: Land Treatments consist of wood-straw mulch plus PAM-12 mulch, and PAM-12 mulch only. The mulching areas are located in the upper watershed source areas within the burn, on steep facing slopes. The purpose of the mulch is to protect soils on steep slopes from raindrop impact, to reduce the event energy at the watershed-head source areas, reduce hydrophobicity, increase water infiltration, minimize soil erosion and debris-particle entrainment in the runoff at the source areas, and promote re-vegetation from seed germination and seedling survival.
Wood Straw Mulch plus PAM-12 mulch ... fine-textured silty clay loam soils located on 62 acres are proposed for PAM-12 mulch; 20 acres within the 62 acres are proposed for WoodStraw mulch, thus have double treatment on the 20 acres of both WoodStraw and PAM-12 mulch. The 62 acres are located on slopes 35% to 100%, on north facing timber slopes in high burn severity, with soils having high water repellency. Wood straw mulch will provide litter cover protection from raindrop impact for many years following treatment on the treated 20 acres, allowing extra time as vegetation reestablishes since timber areas take much longer to rehabilitate following a fire. PAM-12 will reduce soil hydrophobicity, increase water infiltration, and provide soil moisture for seedling germination and survival. is appropriate for these areas because the wood straw is stable on steeper slopes.
PAM-12 Mulch ... 149 acres are proposed for PAM-12 only mulch. These areas are located in two separate watersheds on burned over PJ with very rocky, fine-textured soils having loam and silty clay loam textures. Slopes are 40% to 100% with moderate burn severity, and on soils having moderate water repellency. Pinyon Juniper woodlands and mountain brush vegetation areas rejuvenate faster than timber areas; however, because there is greater surface rock content, there is greater runoff and reduced water infiltration than there would be otherwise. Therefore, the PAM-12 will help reduce soil hydrophobicity, increase water infiltration, and provide soil moisture for seedling germination and survival.
Seeding ... 62 acres of high burn severity are proposed for seeding. Topsoil has been eroded off this unit during two separate storm events that took place in September 2009, thus removing native, intrinsic seed source. Without a native seed bank, rehab will occur very slowly, thus allowing this unit to continue to be an emergency threat to major storm events in the future, resulting in potential flash floods to Blind Canyon. Seeding will help replace native seed lost during the topsoil removal and allow this unit to add protection to the watershed and help retain both short term and long-term soil productivity. The PAM-12 mulch has been shown to increase water infiltration, and provide soil moisture for seedling germination and survival.

Projects.Highlights:
1300 acres seeded with rye @ $5.40/acre (8 lbs/acre), 12000 acres seeded with Blando brome @ $6.73/acre (3 lbs/acre)
One year after burn - monitoring showed good cover of brome (approx. 3600 lbs/acre. Seed production was estimated to be 3000 to 4000 seeds per sq. ft.
In District Ranger's words "we are convinced of Blando brome's usefulness as a rehabilitation species in chaparral communities"
Used Blando brome because it is a naturalized native and already existed in the Santa Lucia wilderness. Reasons Blando brome was selected: 1. It is not known to have strong allelopathic effects, ryegrass does. 2. It was already naturally occurring in the native plant communities. 3. It was felt that 3-pounds per acre would put enough seeds per sq. ft. to reduce soil loss and produce adequate amounts of seed for future years. 4. It may persist longer than ryegrass thereby extending the useful life of the seeding effort and adding habitat diversity to the ecosystems.
Avoided seeding areas with knobcone pine, lightly burned riparian areas, and areas already having a natural seed source such as grasslands and oak grasslands.
From preliminary report, vegetation considerations for reseeding (in file): There are no guarantees that seeding will be successful. The weather patterns after seeding are very crucial to overall success or failure. High intensity rainfall can wash the seeds down the slope before they can germinate. A drought period, after early rainfall has germinated seeds, can cause grass seedlings to die before maturing and setting seed. The first year benefits from reseeding are not as great as in the second year. Normally the ryegrass plants which survive the first winter and spring, set seed and leave much more new seed on the ground than the normal 8 lb/acre. Hence by the second winter period there is some soil protection from the first years ryegrass straw litter, plus a lot more potential ryegrass plants. By the third year, however, the vigor and density of new ryegrass plants is usually greatly reduced due to competition from sprouting brush and the fact that a lot of nutrients released into the soil after burning are used up by the ryegrass.
Monitoring results in "other notes" section under Los Padres (Las Pillitas)

Due to uniform size and texture, of the pellet coated seed, it flows more evenly through the seeder with better distribution. 3. Seed will germinate as quickly or faster than raw seed. 4. Relatively small amounts of nutrients are placed with each seed in the germinating root zone.

Road Drainage Reconstruction General Description: The roads surveyed within the Panther fire were found to have issues with their drainage system due to the expected increase in flows. The minimal treatments required to remedy these issues are: 1. Drain Dips (with or without armor) ... Roadway dips modify the road drainage by altering the template and allowing surface flows to run off the road to prevent any excessive erosion of the surface. The armor consisting of rip rap is placed where runoff could possibly cause erosion to the road surface and fillslope. 2. Culvert Cleaning ... Includes the cleanout of catch basin culvert inlets, outlets, and the drop inlets. Also included is the replacement of lids covering the drop inlets. Cleaning culvert pipes and replacing the missing and damaged lids over the drop inlets will enable the drainage system to pass flows more intended design flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 3. Culvert Repair - Using mechanical means to open up culverts to improve flow or cutting off sections too damaged to repair. This will improve culvert flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 4. Catch Basin Expansion ... Expanding existing catch basins in size and remove debris in the channel above the inlet. The expanded catch basins will handle more sediment and removing debris will reduce the chance of the culvert plugging. 5. Install Slotted Risers ... Install slotted risers on the inlets of culverts to allow the culvert to pass water as the catch basin fills with sediment. Fill Size Reduction ... Reduce the fill volume over undersized culverts and construct a channel over the culvert. The channel will normally have rip rap to protect the remaining fill. This keeps the flow and sediment in the channel and reduces road related sediment and total fill failure. 6. Fill Slope Protection ... Place geotextile and rip rap on fill slopes where water flow over the fill is expected. This will reduce erosion and sediment delivery down stream. 7. Ditch Cleaning ... The cleanout of drainage ditches is required to remove debris that impede the flow or deflect it out of the ditch onto the road surface. Clean ditches will ensure that the flow reaches drainage structures. 8. Grading Roadway ... Removing wheel ruts in the road surface, re-establishing the road cross slope, out slope or in slope to ensure the flow goes into a drainage structure or is allowed to sheet off outside edge of the road without concentrating the water. This reduces road related sediment. Roadway slope improvement ... Out sloping or in sloping the road surface to ensure the flow goes into a drainage structure or is allowed to sheet off outside edge of the road without concentrating the water. This reduces road related sediment. 9. Culvert Additions ... Add additional culverts to drainage fills or upsize the existing culvert where the expected increased flow is more than the existing culvert can handle. Reduces the chance of fill failure and associated sediment delivery down stream. Also allows replacement of fire damaged pipes and down drains to maintain existing drainage capacity and flow dissipation.

Projects.Highlights: Natural Resources (NR): Botanical resources: Botanical survey data is minimal in the area impacted by the Pizona Fire. It is unlikely that this area will naturally return to a Pinyon Pine dominated forest within the near term (100+ years). Other native plant communities will likely recover slowly, as the area naturally had low cover of perennial grass and forb cover. The area has a low risk of being invaded by invasive species of high-priority for management. There were no previously known infestations, and MIST was utilized. Overall disturbance from suppression activities was relatively low, as most of the perimeter did not have any form of line constructed. The area within the fire perimeter is dry and not likely to support establishment of most priority invasive species (such as tamarisk, perennial pepperweed, and knapweeds) which need more moisture to establish, grow and reproduce. Spike camps, hand lines, UTV/ATV tracks and Heli-spots could see some introduction of new invasive species, but effects are likely to be limited. Spike camps and helispots were located in relatively resistant old growth Pinyon Pine and Sagebrush scrub vegetation communities. Areas with moderate are more susceptible to new invasive species infestation. The highest potential (although still low) for new invasive species infestations in this area is from overland travel by UTV/ATV... s.

Project review with implementation team (in file): Most effective treatment was straw mulching on the contour. Onsite sediments and ashes were stabilized with only minor losses, no rills on the slopes, and no downslope sediment accumulations. Straw bale dams were also effective, but sustained some damages that needed to be repaired before the next runoff season. The least effective treatment was aerial seeding with a variety of domestic wheat.
Log chutes were an additional factor in rehab planning. The log chutes were used by historic loggers to move logs down to the railroad. The fire created water repellent soils which could significantly increase the overland runoff. This could cause the structures to develop into a cross-slope gully system. Each chute goes across the hill slope on a diagonal, which effectively collects runoff from the watershed above and diverts it into the chute. Overland runoff could accumulate enough hydraulic head in the chutes to cause serious erosion and gullies. With minor disturbance to their historic attributes, the chutes could be treated with watershed structures that would protect the watershed and preserve their character.

Projects.Highlights:
Main concern was trails. Heavy rains stopped the fire, but caused damage. Many rains have followed. Trail work needed to be completed due to: watershed above the trails was damaged and will result in increased flows, little reveg is taking place in hot burn areas, high water flows off the burns will continue for months and years, and w.o. protection the trails may be lost. Work was not completed due to an early snow in October. Trail was at 9-10,000 ft on a north facing slope.
Treatment - installed waterbars using rocks and small trees. Removed berms along the outside of the trails so water would drain off the trail. Where side drainages crossed trails, armored with rock to help hold soil in place. Installed rock retaining walls on some steep sections of the trail.
Costs were high for trail work because of site access. In Gila Wilderness, access required driving 15-35 miles to trailheads, then hiking 7-10 miles on trails before reaching damaged fire areas.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: A total of ten heritage sites have been previously recorded within the Madre Fire perimeter. Seven of these are pre-contact sites expressing features such as moderate to light-density lithic scatter, bedrock mortars and milling stations and one roasting pit feature. Additionally, two sites are multi-component, expressing pre-contact bedrock mortar/milling station features and/or lithic scatters along with historic habitation remains and refuse. The last site is a pre contact rock art site that lies completely on Carrizo Plains Ecological Preserve [CPEP] (CDFW land). Portions of one of the multi-component site and one pre-contact site also lie on CPEP land. Lastly, three additional sites (one pre-contact rock art, one historic ranch and one historic lookout) were visited to confirm no suppression damage had occurred and fire had not reached the sites, or in the case of the Branch Mountain Lookout, was visited to apply fire protection measures as a preemptive protection measure. Each of these three sites were found to be unburned. Over the course of the fire suppression and repair effort, LPNF Resource Advisors and Archaeologists- Francis (Fran) McCormick & Pete Wisniewski were able to conduct eleven post-fire assessments and/or general suppression and fire condition assessments on LPNF sites on agency administered lands in the fire area. As the Soil Burn Severity data suggests, low severity fire was witnessed at nearly all sites with only one site expressing some low to moderate severity. The assessments conducted support the decision to not conduct a full-scale Burn Area Emergency Response (BAER) assessment for Heritage Resources. This decision recognizes that the high percentage of low severity fire represents a very low to negligible threat to resources. As a result, no BAER treatments on Heritage sites are necessary.

Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources: There are numerous cultural resources within the fire footprint and immediately downstream drainages with anticipated post-fire effects. However the probability of damage to the cultural resources is unlikely from post fire runoff and soil erosion effects, and the magnitude of consequence is moderate. The overall risk to the cultural resources is low and no BAER treatments are recommended. Due to increased visibility of select cultural sites within the fire perimeter due to the burn effects, the probability of damage to those sites due to informal collection and or voluntary destruction is possible. If damage were to occur at any of the cultural sites the magnitude of consequence would be major making the overall risk to the resource high. BAER treatments are not recommended.

In channel felling policy: if trees are leaning, or there is suppression damage, then trees are removed or positioned where they will be effective in changing gradient or stabilizing channel.
In file Marre 1st winter damage survey by Earl Ruby and Rob Griffith 3 transects set up in Zaca watershed. Average ground cover density for all plots was below 15%. Grass seeding treatment was termed not effective in all three plots. Planning Evaluation: 3 important assumptions 1. Wildfire and subsequent flooding has been a natural process in these watersheds at regular occurring intervals for long periods of time. 2. Burn-induced flooding is therefore a natural event in this ecology, rather than an emergency situation. 3. The degree of emergency created by the burned watersheds must be evaluated in terms of onsite and downstream values that could be destroyed, damaged, or threatened by flood runoff.

Projects.Highlights:
Good narrative of fire rehabilitation project included in file.
Contour felling (not listed in treatments) - was done in 2 rows on the streamside banks 5 to 30 ft away from the channel bottom. Contour tree felling was partially effective depending upon the amount of log touching the ground. The tree falling contract called for 80% of the log to touch the ground, but in many cases this was the exception rather than the rule.
Log dams - In burned out stream channels, trees were felled perpendicular across the channel to create "V" notch weir dog dams. The purpose of this dam was to reduce water velocities plus trap sediment. 85% effective. Of all treatments, log dams were the most effective in adding to stream stability and keeping soil on site.
The winter of 87-88 was very droughty. A little rain occurred during Nov. with a heavy rain the first week of Dec. The dry, cold winter was hard on the annual grass seeding. The heavy rain in Dec. produced channel sour, rilling on the slopes (partially due to the hydrophobic soils) and heavy amounts of sheet erosion. Grass establishment in the brush fields was poor and ineffective. In the streamside zones, grass only grew at elevations below 3800 ft. Grass establishment appeared on east and north aspects with varying degrees of success. On streambank slopes less than 40%, grass was established. Steeper banks had no catchment of grass. Grass density on streambanks ranged from no success to 30% cover . Most of the cover was from barley and soft chess. Rattail fescue was sparse.

Road Drainage Maintenance Purpose of Treatment: The purpose of these treatments is to increase culvert capacities, install water bars (rolling dips) and road side slope armoring (gabions) to accommodate increased water flows and associated bedload and debris, and restore road template drainage. The objectives for accommodating increased flows are to: 1) stabilize and protect the existing transportation facilities; 2) decrease the chances of washing road fill into adjacent streams; and 3) minimize road failure induced flooding that could impact human life and safety. General Description: The emergency stabilization recommendations for Forest Roads 30931 and 30029. are as follows: 1) 240 feet of 24 inch culvert placement. 2) 214 square yards of gabions. 3) Harden 3 low water crossing. 4) 15 cross drains (rolling dips). 5) 1 closure gate. Location (Suitable) Sites: Forest Roads 30931 and 30029. Design/Construction Specifications: 1) Survey, design, and contract administration by USFS. 2) Forest Service Specifications for Construction of Roads and Special Contract Provisions.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: Several archeological sites exist in the area, and field verification was prioritized to those in moderate and high burn severity areas that were easily accessible. The following sites are those that were assessed in the field that were determined to have elevated risk. a. Alunite Mine 42PI00629: This historic mine site is at risk of damage to the site integrity from increased erosion, and falling trees. The probability of damage or loss was determined to be possible as the site is located on a slope greater than 30 percent in an area of moderate and high soil burn severity. The magnitude of consequence is major as the hillslope erosion and sedimentation will affect the site... s aspects of integrity that contribute to the site... s National Register of Historic Places eligibility. While there is a High Risk evaluated at this site, no treatment is recommended due to lack of site accessibility. b. Sawmill Road 42SV02898: This is a historic corduroy road for which site integrity is threatened by increased erosion, sedimentation and/or falling trees. The probability of damage or loss is likely as increased hillslope erosion is expected in addition to water channelizing due to loss of vegetative and forest floor cover which would damage the portion of the site in the channel. While this would not likely be the first larger flood event this site has seen, this is the first fire to this extent in recent memory which would compound risk of damage. The magnitude of consequence is moderate, because damage of the portion of the road in the channel would not impact the sites eligibility for the National Register, but loss or damage would significantly affect the historic value. The resulting risk is High, though a stacked engineering treatment is anticipated to be sufficient in protecting this critical value and no further cultural protection treatment is recommended. c. Prehistoric long term camp lithic scatter 42SV04373: This site is at risk from increased erosion and sedimentation, looting due to exposure of the sites from the burn and proximity to the trail, and/or falling trees. The probability of damage or loss is possible as the site exists within moderate and high soil burn severity and is close to a 50-inch motorized trail. The magnitude of consequences is major as impact to this site features and artifacts would irreversibly affect the site... s aspects of integrity, result in a loss of information important to prehistory, and affect the site... s eligibility for the National Register. With a High Risk, treatment recommended is straw application for both erosion control and concealment, directional felling off the trail leading into the site is also recommended to prevent motorized traffic to the site. (H1). Monitoring will be performed to measure treatment success (M1).

Seeding Project: California Gnatcatcher Critical Habitat Rehabilitation: The BAER Assessment Team recommends seeding approximately 75 acres on the lower slopes of El Cajon Mountain with a coastal sage scrub seed mix, comprised of locally collected seed, to restore designated critical habitat for California Gnatcatcher. This represents about 10% of the designated critical habitat that was burned in the fire. These 75 acres are selected because they are the best planting sites- in the past these areas had the most robust stands of coastal sage scrub. These 75 acres are also considered to be the most vulnerable to invasion by non-native plant species and are the areas where coastal sage scrub habitat is most likely to be lost due to type conversion. California Gnatcatchers typically have territory sizes of 2-5 acres so restoration of this habitat has the potential to support 15-20 pairs of birds.
Seeding this fall will re-establish native vegetation on the lower slopes of the burn area and will help to stabilize soils. Coastal sage scrub will start to regenerate, and treating the area immediately after the fire will improve the success of the revegetation effort as it will be initiated before non-native grasses and other weeds become prevalent in the treatment area. This will reduce the risk that invasive and noxious plants will spread in the burned area. Due to the frequent fires in the Monte Fire area over the last 15 years, the coastal sage scrub habitat is at the ... tipping point... ; without restoration this habitat is very likely to be lost due to type conversion. Per the Burned Area Emergency Treatments Catalog, mulching with wood straw or wood chips may accompany seeding to improve effectiveness (USDA Forest Service 2006).
California Gnatcatcher populations and habitat have been much reduced throughout Southern California due to recent fires and resulting type-conversion. Although there are 169,000 acres of designated critical habitat for California Gnatcatcher in southern California (USDI Fish and Wildlife Service 2007), the habitat maps typically include many areas that do not contain key habitat elements for the species, and many areas that are mapped as critical habitat are not suitable due to type conversion to grassland. In coastal areas, much of the California Gnatcatcher habitat has been lost due to development. The California Gnatcatcher is essentially a coastal species, and most National Forest Systems lands are at too great an elevation or do not have suitable habitat for this species. Areas on the lower slopes of the San Gabriel and San Bernardino Mountains, where this species formerly occurred, no longer have suitable habitat as it has been lost to type conversion. The only sizeable population of California Gnatcatcher on National Forest System lands is located on the Cleveland National Forest in the San Diego River watershed. This area also has good connectivity to adjacent gnatcatcher populations near Lakeside.
Approximately 15,000 acres of designated critical habitat are present on Cleveland National Forest lands, but of those acres only about 2,000 are actually suitable habitat. The lower slopes of the Monte Fire represent at least 10% of this suitable habitat. All of the other designated critical habitat in the San Diego River has been affected by the Cedar and Witch fires so is currently in either a degraded condition or is in the process of recovering from the recent fires.
Post-fire restoration of coastal sage scrub for California Gnatcatcher was completed by the Cleveland National Forest after the 1993 Eagle Fire, and after the 2007 Witch Fire. The areas targeted for those restoration efforts were north of the Monte Fire along the San Diego River. The Eagle Fire burned in May and high shrub mortality was expected to result from this spring burn. Seeding was completed in fall 1993 and monitored in spring 1994. High seedling densities of seeded species was detected on treatment plots, and very low natural recruitment was observed on untreated plots (White, T.C. et al 1995). Due to delays in obtaining funding and applying treatments, no results are available at this time from the Witch Fire restoration effort that was implemented in 2009. In addition the long lag time between the Witch Fire and the restoration work will make re-establishment of coastal sage more difficult due to the increased competition from weeds. Starr Ranch Audubon Sanctuary, which is adjacent to the Cleveland National Forest in Orange County, has completed coastal sage scrub restoration on their property with excellent results (Audubon California 2006).

Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Site 06102600182 Devil... s Backbone Trail is a potentially eligible site and is threatened by post-fire increased erosion, debris flow and fire weakened tree fall that will damage or destroy the trail and result in irreversible damage to a documented cultural resource. The probability of damage or loss is Likely from fire weakened and killed trees adjacent to the trail on steep slopes within moderate to high SBS and >50% PVM, and potential for erosion to the trail tread. The magnitude of consequence is Moderate as the site is potentially eligible to the National Register of Historic Places, and loss of trail segments may impact the eligibility of the site. Every cultural resource is unique and cannot recover once damaged. The risk rating is High. BAER treatments are recommended, working in conjunction with Recreation and their objectives to protect NFS trail infrastructure. b. Site 06102600275 Mining Site is a potentially eligible site and is threatened by the potential for looting due to exposure from the site being burned over, as well as inadvertent damage from other BAER treatments proposed to protect human life and safety, which could result in irreversible damage to a documented cultural resource. The probability of damage or loss is Possible due to exposed artifacts on the surface, and large pits in the area needing to be filled or covered to mitigate human life and safety concerns. The magnitude of consequence is Major since artifacts are exposed on the surface, as well as subsurface features being at risk to disturbance if local materials are used to fill pits. The site is potentially eligible to the National Register of Historic Places, and damage to the site may impact the eligibility of the site. Every cultural resource is unique and cannot recover once damaged. The risk rating is High. BAER treatments are recommended, working in conjunction with Recreation to monitor their BAER implementation as well as mulching and checking the site. c. Site 06102601992 Bear Falls Site is an eligible site and is threatened by loss of data through looting now that it is more exposed from the fire, and negative impacts to Tribal government relationships if the site is looted or damaged. The probability of damage or loss is Likely as this site is located in a severe burn area, exposed, and in a high traffic area within view of the Rogue River Trail. The magnitude of consequence is Major as this site is eligible to the National Register of Historic Places and is in excellent condition. Damage to this site may impact the eligibility of the site, and looting at the site would result in an ARPA case. Every cultural resource is unique and cannot recover once damaged. The risk rating is Very High. BAER treatments are recommended. d. Site 06102601984 Rogue River Trail is an eligible site, and Site 0610261993 Clay Hill Trail is a potentially eligible site, and both are threatened by loss of large sections of the trail from increased post-fire erosion, debris slides, sloughing and destruction of the tread from fire weakened trees tipping and ripping out tread. Loss of large sections of the trail would result in irreversible damage to a documented cultural resource. The probability of damage or loss is Likely for both sites. The Rogue River Trail passes through numerous steep sideslopes and active drainages where the steep slopes experienced moderate to high SBS and >50% PVM. In addition, the Clay Hill Trail switchbacks through an active ephemeral drainage numerous times in an area that experience moderate to high SBS and >50% PVM. Typical winter rains and combined with increased erosion and debris flow potential post-burn make it likely that significant trail loss will occur. The magnitude of consequence is Major as the Rogue River Trail is eligible, and Clay Hill Trail is potentially eligible to the National Register of Historic Places, and loss of large sections of the trails may impact the eligibility of each of these sites. Every cultural resource is unique and cannot recover once damaged. The risk rating is Very High. BAER treatments are recommended, working in conjunction with Recreation and their objectives to protect NFS trail infrastructure.

Land Treatments: Objective The purpose of this treatment is to maintain ecosystem integrity by treating selected sites where burned susceptible habitats have been invaded by knapweed as well as the nearby infestations serving as source areas to the invasions. By reducing the amount of weed seed in the area, and treating new populations, native plant communities can have time to recover with less competition form non-native invasive plants.
Methods Treat burned areas within or adjacent to source weed populations in the Pinchot and Pettibone fires, including with 16 releases of biological control agents summer 2004 using the organisms shown below (4 in Pinchot and 12 in Pettibone). Effects of bio-control agents are addressed in the USDA Weed EIS (1988).

-cattle and wildlife grazing can be mitigated by closing area to cattle, closing of water sources, and using a proper seed mix of less interest to grazers
-seed the burn on an early snow so later snows can cover the seed and push them into the loose spring soil; no heavy rain storm occurred after the fire (thru winter) so planting could still do some good in retaining soil on site -Lesser slopes to be planted with 12 lbs/ac: 2lbs/ac sweet clover 2 timothy 4 Canadian Wildrye 4 hairy vetch

Projects.Highlights:
This fire occurred in the municipal watershed of Bonners Ferry, Idaho.
Design Storm Magnitude, (inches): 12.2. The emergency is related primarily to tributary events... |peak runoff and massive delivery of sediments to and through Myrtle Creek. Flooding in Myrtle Creek is not a primary concern. The design events are 1) long-duration, moderate intensity late-fall rain (with a shallow snowpack; and 2) a mid-winter ... rain-on-snow... event. The latter is characterized by the area holding an essentially ripe mid-winter snowpack and driven by several days of a warm moist maritime airmass intrusion where the high water vapor content (not necessarily rain itself) provides energy through sublimation to convert large melt inputs. Any rainfall passes direct to the system compounding the runoff. Note, high-intensity thunderstorm events are not the primary disturbance factor.
Adjusted Design Flow, (cfs per square mile): n/a. Mainstream flooding is not the issue.
E. Cost of No-Action (Including Loss):
The costs of no-action are indetermined since they are not primarily resource-based; but rather are associated with the integrity and public health of the municipal water collection, delivery, treatment, and distribution systems.
Untreated, it is estimated that sediment loading from the fire has the potential of increasing the delivery of sediment to Myrtle Creek on the order of 31/2 to 4 times the mean annual loading that occurred prior to the fire. In addition, this loading is expected to delivered as ... pulses... rather than distributed over time; and that perhaps 60 percent of the storm derived sediments may be delivered to the vicinity of the domestic water intake system. The potential damages are loss of integrity and operation of the intake and the delivery system, overwhelming of the treatment facilities, and introduction of turbidity and pollutants beyond the capabilities of the system. The risks are expected to be at very high levels for the first five years following the fire in the untreated condition, with progressive reductions in risk over the next decade.
Given that the potential for large rapid inputs of sediment to Myrtle Creek are estimated in this assessment Assuming the damages to include loss of productivity of the land, loss of the access for commerce and other activities of the watershed, the partial loss of bull trout habitats below Myrtle Creek, the loss or reconstruction of the Bonners Ferry water intake and delivery system; modification or new construction of treatment facilities; and the threat to public health; the no-action costs have the potential in the magnitude of tens of millions of dollars. The risks remain to be significant, but the responses are
F. Cost of Selected Alternative (Including Loss):
The effective and timely application of the proposed action is estimated to reduce the sediment loading to 11/2 to 2 times the mean annual pre-fire loading with further significant progressive reduction of risks after the first year.
There is a storm monitoring Power Point Presentation in the project file. Few specifics are given.
