Projects.Highlights:
Proposed post-fire monitoring (funding request of $15,000 was turned down)
One issue that inhibited the BAER analyses for the Narrows fire was available data on post-fire natural vegetation recovery and associated soil erosion rates for the burned area. The paucity of information resulted in only a best, professional estimate. With the current fire occurrence "rotation" on the Angeles apparently moving into the more remote and highest soil erosion rate areas with an older burn history, it is imperative to be able to have concrete data to accurately assess the most effective treatment measures especially now since these remote areas drain into urban areas which were not present the last time the area burned.
This plan will be designed to develop test plots and monitor the natural recovery rate of the plant communities within the burned area as it relates to burn intensity. These communities could include but are not limited to low elevation chaparral, high elevation chaparral, conifer north slope, conifer south slope, and conifer seeded. Monitoring will be on a set duration (3 months) and data will be collected including per cent coverage and species present. Soil erosion rates will also be monitored with silt fence stations which will be visited monthly.
Channel clearing involved removing vegetation (Mescal Cr.) and was done in conjunction with channel armoring.
Sandbags were placed as deflector channels to protect campground and also residences.
Rock dissipaters were placed below culverts.
Heritage Resource documentation included the recordation of 20 sites and an analysis by a hydrologist of damage risk. Flood Watch patrols (treatment) included early warning systems such as radio-activated sirens linked to stream gauges, and area closures and public information/notification.

Projects.Highlights: Land Treatments: Areas with bare soil will be seeded to reduce the likelihood of noxious weed expansion and enhance habitat for sensitive and candidate butterflies. Key native forb species will be selected for this seeding. Seed will be broadcast this spring on bare soil areas and raked in. Approximately 15 acres will be seeded. The area will be fenced to exclude cattle which will improve germination and seedling survival. The species include native forbs which are important butterfly food sources: rough blazing star, dotted blazing star, purple coneflower, yellow coneflower, black-eyed Susan, purple prairie clover, and white prairie clover. Seed will be applied at approximately 2 lbs/acre.

H. Treatment Narrative:
Heritage Resources:
Remove the railroad logging wheel to a secure site for later curation at a suitable facility. While it is common to prevent damage to heritage site by concealing the object on-site, this artifact is both difficult to conceal and already known to parties with an interest in removing it from the National Forest. At the moment, post-fire activity has sufficient people in the area that this is discouraged. But this will no be the case in a few weeks. The Forest Service road crew can move the artifact to the Ranger District Office. The Fresno Flats museum in Oakhurst which includes displays about railroad logging may be a suitable site for its later display.
Off-Site Resources:
A letter sharing the information on potential ash and floatable debris and its likely impact areas should be provided the local affected residents, operator of the diversion to the ponds at Cold Spring Creek and to those responsible for local roads and the County Roads. This would be done in a timely manner to enable residents and/or the County to conduct any independent assessments to guide their mitigation measures.

These structures are designed to provide for channel bed stability, not collection and storage of sediment.

Projects.Highlights:
Information from the Forest Plan Monitoring and Evaluation Report 1992. Overwhich Fire burned in Oct. 1991, from escape from a prescribed burn. The fire rehab team planned seeding, but was prevented from seeding in the fall by weather. Seeding was accomplished on May 21, 1992.
On June 25, 1992 an intense rainstorm occurred. Overland flow caused gullying within 150 to 200 feet of ridgetops - ie new channel head on account of environmental factors. Its interesting that the channel head movement would have been almost instantaneous over the length of channel extension, so it... s a case of a single large event rather than incremental channel head migration. An estimated 250,000 cu yds of material moved down four tributaries to Overwhich Creek. Gravel, cobbles, boulders, logs, and other woody debris was deposited at the tributary mouths, and sand and finer sediment continued down Overwhich Creek. A significant portion of the fish of Overwhich Cr were killed, including bull trout and western cutthroat trout.
There was a lot of monitoring to determine if roads or timber harvest contributed to the event. Findings included that one of the gullied tributaries began in an unroaded undeveloped drainage with less than 30 acres of high intensity burn. Clearcuts apparently did not contribute. Roads apparently increased the magnitude of debris torrents by about 20%, because roads temporarily dammed flows then released higher peak flows when they failed, and also contributed road fill material.

No treatment: even though most of the area experienced high intensity burn, most of the slopes were gentle (5 to 35%). Lacking steep slopes, the likelihood of significant erosion or measurable sedimentation of the streams below the fire was very low.
The decision to leave the fire in an "uncontrolled" status until a season-ending event occurs has a risk of negating the ability to implement rehabilitation measures in a timely manner. When a fire is left in an uncontrolled status for an extended period, the line officer needs to make provisions to conduct the needed survey of emergency watershed conditions so that recommended treatments can be implemented prior to the first damage-producing storms. Due to safety concerns and access restrictions, implementation of rehabilitation prescriptions are likely to be more costly if implemented prior to declaration of control.

Projects.Highlights:
Interviewees include Dave Brewer (Hockderffer BAER leader), George Robertson, and Jeff Hink. Penny Luehring visited this rehab area in Oct. 96.
The Peaks Complex consists of several fires: Hockderffer, Walnut, and Freiliend (sp?). Three main areas (Hills) were treated; Hockderffer, Walker, and White Horse. These were all in the Hockderffer Fire. The S slopes had high intensity burns in ponderosa pine habitats on Vitrandic Ustochrepts, and Typic Argiborolls soils. N slopes were also high intensity burns in mixed conifer (pipo/psme) on Eutric glossoboralfs. Hochderffer and Walker geologic materials are basalt and cinder. White Horse is mostly cinder with limestone inclusions.
George Robertson noted that before treatment could begin the hard rains started. Nothing could be done well or safely in that kind of weather or on the very steep slopes. He did note that he wished they could have contour felled on the lower 1/3 of the slopes where slope% was smaller and the soils were deeper and more productive (higher slopes too rocky and steep). The late seeding (rains) was pretty ineffective compared to seeding in early July, seeding on snow cover, or seeding in spring/June. However, the final 'effectiveness' has yet to be determined.
There is an elk fence in the bottom lands of the burn that is 2 hog fence panels high and encompasses 300 acres (Not part of BAER). Jeff Hink and Jim Raulph (?) are doing some monitoring of aspen regen. The area closed off is so large it is disrupting elk movements so they often break through it. Some places are munched pretty good but the effect of exclusion can be seen. Game and Fish is thinking of a 75% reduction in the herd numbers in this area.
Will Moir and Julie Zimmerman (RMRS) have been doing plant cover/species diversity studies on non-salvage logged areas, after burns. It is unknown whether their plots land on any of the seeded areas or not. Julie said they figured the slopes were what were treated so their plots are more on the flats. Of those species planted and those found by Julie, only the western wheat seems to be abundant. (most other seed species do not show up on her burned plots)
Aerial seeding (BAER) of the fire was seeded with western wheatgrass, mt. Brome, blue flax(N), and regreen (sterile wheat).
Fire suppression rehab seeding: "Seed dozer lines, hand lines, and other disturbed areas with the seed mix specified below. The seed will be applied by a mechanized seeder mounted to an ATV or hand seeded. Seed should be applied to the area prior to dozer or hand work to facilitate 'planting' of the mix." Mixed conifer/pine type (N=native, N*=native that hybridizes easily, rest are introduced): western wheatgrass Arizona fescue (N) slender wheatgrass (N**) spike muhly (N) mountain lupine PJ type Utah sweetvetch (?N) sand dropseed (N) needle and thread (?N) Indian ricegrass (N) sideoats grama (N*) western wheat incident command post and others intermediate wheatgrass small burnet smooth brome western wheatgrass

Projects.Highlights:
Very comprehensive emergency rehabilitation narrative included (in files). Includes resource reports from soils, hydrology, cultural resources, and vegetation description.
Seeding is recommended for areas of high intensity burn except where erosion potential is low due to rocky soil. Seeding is also recommended on moderate intensity burns on steep slopes. No seeding treatments are proposed in low intensity burn areas.
The purpose of the seeding is to minimize loss of highly mobile nitrate nitrogen, and accelerated soil movement and subsequent loss of site productivity or damage to downstream developments. Additional benefits expected include providing a nurse crop for developing on-site germinants, and increasing the recovery time of the sites to produce forage.
Criteria for seed selection: 1. Effectiveness in minimizing erosion and capturing the available nitrogen released by the fire. The mix should include adapted species that are easily and rapidly established to provide, along with on-site species, at least 30-50 percent of the potential site understory cover by the end of the second growing season.
2. Availability - the species selected must be commercially available in adequate quantities
3. Biodiversity - the species selected should not replace or out-compete native species, reduce their ability to adapt to local environments or their rate of establishment, growth, or flowering.
4. Cost/Benefit - the species selected should be reasonably priced and meet the cost/benefit requirements outlined in the emergency rehabilitation guidelines.
Forest zone seed mix: (light)
Bluebunch wheatgrass 4 lbs/ac, cereal rye 6 lbs/ac, and yellow blossom sweetclover 1 lb/ac.
Most significant watershed factor is the absence of surface water, only ephemeral streams. Eastside fire. Most significant erosion problems are associated with roads, due to their compacted surfaces, linearity, and location in the bottom of the drainages.
Monitoring program was intended to address the following: 1) What is the rate of site recovery with and without rehabilitation seeding? 2) What plant cover can be expected on different sites under different conditions? 3) What species are most successful at stabilizing sites?

Roads and Trail Treatments Purpose: To improve road drainage and prevent material from plugging culverts, reducing the risk of washouts, loss of access to the Condor Recovery Center, and downstream damage.
Treatment: Culverts will be upgraded through replacement, addition of risers, rip rapping culvert inlets, and installing k-rail barriers. This combination of treatments will be implemented at critical stream crossings on Squaw Flat Road, Lake Piru Road, Dominguez Canyon road on Forest Service and private lands and roads within the Sespe Oil Fields on Forest Service lands and private lands.
Treatment: Road drainage will be improved by out sloping road surfaces, installing cross drains and rolling dips, and paving steep road sections near stream crossings. This combination of treatments will be implemented on Squaw Flat Road, Lake Piru Road, Dominguez Canyon road, and roads within the Sespe Oil Fields on Forest Service lands and private lands.
Treatment: Gabions walls will be installed at several locations on the Squaw Flat Road to stabilize failing fill slopes.
Treatment: Road drainage structures will be maintained during storm events to prevent plugging.
Accomplishment: All of the above treatments have essentially been accomplished on a total of 23.5 miles of roads in the Sespe oil fields and 3 miles in Dominguez Canyon. About 5% of the work in Dominguez Cyn. remains and should be completed by the end of this month, July 2004.

Projects.Highlights:
Cost of seeding broken down in cost per acre for seed ($23.55 with 8.7lbs/ac x 2.71lbs), aerial application ($3.30/ac), and salary support ($1.47/ac)
Penny Luehring visited this site in Oct. 96. Penny noted that due to the rocky soils (less susceptible to erosion, the seeding treatment might not have been necessary. She noted that the flax was not visible and so could have been cut from seed mix.
Dick Fleishman has set up permanent plots inside and outside the seeded areas to measure and photograph recovery, although the report appears to only 1996 data?.
Seeding species include: western wheatgrass 25lbs (native) mountain brome 15 lbs (? If native to this area) blue flax 5 (?) regreen (rye) 5 (introduced)
Two principle treatment sites at Willow Valley (main tributary into West Clear Creak) and Long Valley. Mark Whitney (Wildlife/Resource advisor on fire) describes fire: " Aside from the portions of Long Valley Draw and Willow Valley drainages involved within the fire perimeter, the vast majority of the burn area is relatively flat. An aerial view of the fire presents a mosaic pattern to the landscape burnt by this fire. Intensely burned areas, where trees were totally consumed, are spotty and comprise approximately 25% of the fire area. Another 45% of the area contains trees which were burnt, but still retain their needles. These trees are either dead or dying. An estimated 80% of the fire area sustained a ground surface fire which eliminated most all heavy fuels (downed logs) and snags. Those heavy fuels which were not totally consumed by the fire remain totally charred (case hardened)." "Care will be given to guard against seeding in and immediately adjacent to West Clear Creek Wilderness."

Projects.Highlights:
Mention of this fire principally due to the various studies done on the area. DeBano, Ffolliott, and Baker established three small watersheds within the burn area representing severe burn, moderate burn, and unburned control, to assess the effects of wildfire on hydrology, soils, timber and forage production. Sims looked at the effects of the fire on water quality. Campbell, Baker, Ffolliott, Larson, and Avery used the area to evaluate Wildfire Effects on a Ponderosa Pine Ecosystem: an Arizona Case Study. Plant populations were evaluated in 2 different masters studies, J.T. Beaulieu (1975) and B.P. Oswald (1981). Will Moir and Julie Zimmerman have done some reconnaissance in their efforts to find good study areas.
From the literature it appears that no fire rehab was completed, only suppression rehab

Projects.Highlights:
Straw mulch was applied to improve germination at a rate of 1 ton per acre, though not listed.
Field reconnaissance of the BAER work during winter has shown relatively high success. The aerial and riparian seeding has generated a 89% coverage rate. Riparian areas that were seeded and mulched have a coverage rate of 98%. Channel structures were very successful in trapping and holding on site approximately 500 cu yds of mobilized sediment. Gate installed successfully kept winter traffic off the road and prevented damage to the road, road cutbanks, and loading of stream channels with road related sediment.
Monitoring - BAER course - Julie Nelson (from abstract) Seeded areas were revisited in Fall of 1995, four years after the fire. Aerial seeding of cereal wheat and hand seeding of blue wildrye, meadow barley, and Zorro fescue were evaluated. No wheat was found four years after the fire, though team members had observed it to be plentiful the first 2 years after the fire. Blue wild rye abundantly occupied the riparian and lower slope communities four years after the fire. Zorro fescue and meadow barley were found in scattered locations.

Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, only a rehabilitation report
Rocky Burn was reviewed on 8-9-74. (report dated 8-26-74). Also have 2nd year evaluation dated 7-31-75.
Seed mix: ladak alfalfa 2lbs/acre, sainfoin 3 lbs/acre, hard fescue 1 lb/acre, and bulbous bluegrass 5 lbs/acre. Bulbous bluegrass was not showing an excellent stand.
Commercial forest land - orchardgrass 3lbs/acre, Timothy 1 lb/acre, and white clover 1 lb/acre. Orchardgrass and timothy were performing well, but white clover was not. Seed mixes are designed to deposit 60 to 70 seeds per sq. ft.
Several stream bottoms were over-seeded with Italian ryegrass (10 lbs/acre). Produced a quick cover along the streams and critical bottom areas. Hardwoods planted along the stream bottom were not performing well.
Livestock were present on the burn seedlings. Plant pullup reduced cover to about 60% on most of the burn, when it could have exceeded 80%. Most of the stream bottom and critical sideslopes had received heavy livestock use. Root systems on all perennial plants were poorly developed and plant pullup excessive.
Salvage logging should be done last on the stream channels and sideslopes to allow as much root development as possible.
Skips and overlaps in the aerial seeding were observed. The light fluffy ash (or surface soil) is an excellent seedbed, but prompt seeding is needed. Precipitation on this layer of ash prior to deposition of seed would materially decrease the probability of establishing adequate ground cover.
Fire started when a rubber tired log skidder caught fire when being moved between timber sales.
Commercial forest land occupied 75% of the burned area. It once was dominated by ponderosa pine which has been removed over the years mainly by salvage logging. It is now dominated by Douglas-fir poles and small saw-timber at lower elevations, and white fir small saw-timber and poles at upper elevations. Most of the stands were so dense that ground vegetation was extremely sparse or lacking.
Sediment check dams - 50 dams/mile (based on 2 ft high dam toe to crest on a 2% stream gradient). Dams should be constructed of permanent material such as native rock. Some key points are providing an earth seal on the upstream side of the structure to prevent movement of water through the dam which could result in failure, and providing a long enough apron on the dam so that water flowing over the crest will not gouge out the stream channel.
Stream channel cleanout should be done before fall storms and done by hand, so as to avoid disturbing streambanks. Natural, solidly imbedded material, that is not likely to be moved or cause problems, should be left in place.
Non-commercial sites 1st yr. Evaluation (1974) - burned oak was resprouting, but no bitterbrush sprouting from old plants. Of the seeded species, only the bulbous bluegrass was not showing an excellent potential stand.
2nd yr evaluation: (1975) - burned oak was sprouting profusely. No new sprouting on the bitterbrush plants. Aerial seeding has reversed itself. There was now a heavy stand of bulbous bluegrass, and only fair stands of fescue, and only traces of the other seeded species.
Commercial sites: 1974- seeded species averaged 83% 1975 - seeded and fertilized after salvage logging. Results were bare ground 21%, litter 13%, native spp. 16%, and orchard and timothy 50%
Silvicultural comment from Lewis Nicholson: the native grass and seeded species indicate the reforestation job can be done but it will be difficult. Pubescent wheatgrass has been used in some seed mixtures. This grass is rhizomacious and makes reforestation next to impossible once established. Not only that, it is low in forage value. I would recommend that this grass species be left out of all grass seeded mixtures.
Wildlife comments from Bernie Carter: we put quite a bit of money in rehabilitation of streamside zones, shrub and tree plantings, but we do not seem to provide the necessary protection from livestock to protect these important streamside management units. I would much rather see us put the dollars in protection fence, permittee maintenance, if he wants to graze the burn; rather than in shrub plantings and let the cows get fat on them. Besides, I think in most cases native plants will rapidly reoccupy the site - reducing the need for planting shrubs.

Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Gold/Rosa - Increases in runoff from moderate SBS areas resulting in increased overland flow, sheet flow and rockfall: Known archeological sites within the Gold fire footprint lie in areas of low and moderate soil burn severity. The Probability is possible that sites will experience damage from increases in runoff within moderate SBS areas. The Magnitude of the threat is moderate as the site types represented within the burn area are susceptible to the irretrievable loss of unknown features or artifacts. The Risk therefore is intermediate and not subject to BAER treatments. Sites within the Rosa fire footprint are within low and moderate SBS and the Probability is unlikely that they will experience damage from increases in runoff. The Magnitude of the threat to sites within the Rosa fire is minor due to the site types represented. Magnitude of the threat to sites within the Rosa fire is low and no BAER treatments are recommended. None of the sites considered for analysis within either fire footprint are likely to experience significant damage or destruction due to increased runoff, and per watershed modeling, such events occurring within or adjacent to known site locations would be unusual. Should sites experience any form of damage from increased runoff, it is improbable that any individual components (features or artifacts) damaged will impact future eligibility for the National Register of Historic Places. No treatments are recommended. b. Gold/Rosa - Looting as a result of reduced vegetative cover: Looting of archeological sites is an ongoing concern and reduced vegetative cover affords greater visibility of artifacts which may be of interest to looters. For sites analyzed within both fire footprints, the Probability of looting is possible due to reduced vegetative cover, although sites are generally inaccessible. The Magnitude of the threat from looting is moderate as certain artifacts and site components may directly impact the NRHP eligibility of the site. Therefore, the Risk of looting to sites within both fires is intermediate due to the irretrievable loss of material culture. The majority of sites with reduced vegetative cover are historic mining sites, which often contain many different types of artifacts. These artifacts may help ascertain site date and function, however the importance of these sites often lie in their location and their features. None of the sites visited in the field during this rapid assessment contain artifacts that, if removed from the site, will impact the sites... eligibility for listing onto the National Register of Historic Places. No treatments are recommended and the best way to protect the sites is for natural revegetation to obscure the site components.

Projects.Highlights:
Treatments: Aerial seeding - 630 acres with cereal barley, contour tilling of slopes to a depth of 12-18 inches, LEB's on steep (>35% slopes), contour strip mulching with straw, and straw mulching below and above roads.
Field review: Contour tilling (700 acres) appeared to be an effective way of increasing infiltration and reducing run-off. In effect the tilled areas served as mini-catchment basins on the contour of the slope. Accumulation within the first of the three furrows tended to have as much as 3-4 inches of sediment trapped. This was determined by locating the ash level in the furrow. Spacing of the contours ranged from 15 to 30 ft depending on the slope and the burn intensity. There was little evidence of rilling between the till strips. Most of the erosion appeared to be sheet. Soil moisture appeared to be greater in the tilled areas. Silt fence in grass area showed about 1 inch of sediment. Seemed that most of the sediment trapped was generated in the first couple of storms. Used road crew to implement. A small crew was able to accomplish a large area in a short time. Limitations: stand density and downed material prevented tilling. Equipment breakdowns slowed things down. Safety hazards especially trees that could enter cage.
Cereal barley applied at 98 lbs/acre. The seeded acreage was in riparian areas and adjacent steeper slopes. It germinated in Oct. but was set back by snow. After a year, it appeared to be 3-5 inches in height and was trapping other material such as pine needles and falling debris. The 2nd year barley came up about as thickly as the first, in a somewhat clumpy pattern due to the seed heads not shattering. This year the cattle ate off the seed heads, but much seed passed more or less undigested through the animals. The 3rd year the barley stand was thinner and noticeably clumpy, often sprouting from old cowpies or along cattle trails. Where salvage logged, the disturbance seemed to promote continued sprouting of the barley. By 1997 barley was down to thinly scattered plants. The great majority of the biomass was from a mixture of soft chess brome, ripgut brome, and filaree, with smaller quantities of other annual grasses, gooseberry, snowberry, native and other forbs, yellow star tulips, and rushes and moss in resurgent seeps. This more native plant community covered about 50-75% of the soil surface.
LEB's were built on steep hillslopes. Silt fence in this treatment had about 1/2 inch of accumulated sediment. Area was also grass seeded. They did not show any sign of creating gullies or channeling water to foster erosion.
A logger noted that he saw an initial flush of sediments with a good amount of charcoal during the first storm, but from that time on the streams ran clear.

Projects.Highlights:
Narrative referenced a monitoring report to be submitted to the BAER Coordinator but unknown if ever completed. Monitoring in the form of photographs and inspections took place over the summer, and retaken in September.
Installation of warning signs was coordinated with the State Highway Dept.
All straw bale structures were installed by June 30, and were filled/overtopped with sediment by August. 5 structures had 1-2 straw bales washed out, and 1 structure had bales stolen. Some structures experienced water flowing around the structure and should have been built wider. Overall belief was the straw bale structures worked well.
1 Earthen catch basin filled with sediment, but the main highway culvert remained free of sediment and debris; the highway experienced no flow over the road.
Contour log structures were built in a short time by a prison crew due to Forest crews involved in suppression activities elsewhere. Some logs were not in contact with the soil and flow had gone underneath the logs. They felt it would have been more productive to install fewer logs but spend more time on proper installation.
Seeding was done by helicopter with a bucket with no agitator. Blue grama was a major seed component and did not feed through the bucket very well because they contain awns. Addition of sand to the seed mix helped in seed flow.

First seeding was a failure due to lack of rain and intense January rains that washed most the seeds from the slopes. A series of subtropical storms hit the area beginning on Jan 9. The Harrison debris basin filled and overflowed depositing a minor amount of sediment in streets and on lawns on Hampshire Ave. A second storm a few days later, before the debris basin was cleaned out generated a wave of sediment that damaged about 31 homes on Hampshire Ave and Golden Ave. A third storm generated another wave of sediment further damaging home plus 2 others. A fourth storm damaged 7 more homes.
Folder includes news articles covering the flood events and public outcry as to who was to blame. Also good pictures of damage done to homes by the mudflows.

Projects.Highlights:
Short narrative included in file.
Area burned contained young plantations, small sawtimber, and old growth forest. Only 10% of the area burned at high intensity, with 30% burning at moderated intensity. Also turbidity concerns and loss of angler days.
It was decided only to seed selected channels and not to seed the unstable steep slopes based on the following: 1. The steep slopes are above the natural angle of repose, and the seeding of grass will not stop the raveling . 2. Woody vegetation like trees and shrubs will anchor the traveling slopes and it was felt that grass would not be a long term solution and that it would compete with the return of trees and shrubs. 3. Stream channels were selected for treatment based on their burn intensity, proximity to class 1 or 2 streams and their sediment storage capacity. Concluded that soil and sediment would reach the channels due to steep slopes and gravity ravel problems. It was recommended that the channels and culverts be kept open to insure that the sediment flows through and is not stored in the water system.
Level 3,4, and 5 roads were to be patrolled in the winter to prevent plugging of culverts and ditches from burned debris that had been loosened. Road surface insloping of level 2 roads would maintain water on the roads.
Culvert replacement - On road 2303 there is a channel that has headwalls with slopes in excess of 100%. The road at this channel has a 20-ft fill with a 24 inch culvert, which is highly likely to fail. An additional culvert, 36 inches in diameter, would be placed 5 ft below the road surface to allow for drainage when the lower culvert is plugged.
Seed mix for area 35 ft on each side of the channel (8.5 acres/mile): Alta fescue 9 lbs/acre, annual rye 5 lbs/acre, Highland Bentgrass 3 lbs/acre, and orchardgrass 3 lbs/acre. Mixture represents a total of 543 pure live seeds per sq. ft. Of that annual rye represents 23 pure live seeds per sq. ft.
The unit of measure for impact to fish habitat is Lost Angler Days. Factors influencing this unit of measure include sedimentation and turbid water, loss of riparian habitat, and floating debris in the reservoir.
It was recommended that killed trees be salvaged within one year. An estimated 45 MBF/acre of net wood can be salvaged for a yield of about 55 MMBF.

Projects.Highlights:
In file, Siskiyou National Forest Wildfire and Recovery Monitoring Report (covers Silver complex)
Of the total acreage burned, 51,540 acres were on Wilderness lands. It was recommended that no aerial or land-based rehabilitation treatments would be prescribed in the Kalmiopsis Wilderness.
Wilderness area has a high natural sediment production from slides and soil erosion on steep, unstable landforms of faulted sandstone, greywacke, gabbro, and ultramafic rocks. These high rates were present before the Silver fire and will continue regardless of the loss of vegetation by fire. Increases in rate of sedimentation due to fire was extremely difficult and expensive to measure in these very steep mountainous landforms.
A large part of 24000 acres of the Silver fire in the Chetco River basin was burned by wild fires in the 1890's, and again in the late 1930's. Other parts of the Wilderness were burned during these periods. Evidence of these earlier fires was present in the form of snags, charred downed logs, and numerous seral stages of vegetation in the 5 to 75 year age classes. Survey of the burned area has shown that natural plant recovery has occurred in the past, providing an adequate plant cover.
Natural sprouters, including Sadler's oak, Pacific rhododendron, and golden chinkapin, present in much of the area will show significant increases in ground cover within 3 yrs. Pinemat manzanita will take longer, but is a very effective erosional cover. Douglas-fir, sugar pine, western white pine, white fir, and Brewer Spruce, with survivors locally abundant in the area, will regenerate heavily on newly exposed mineral soils.

Projects.Highlights: Provide justification why NO TREATMENT was chosen. Effects of the fire do not appear to be sufficient to result in significant alteration of runoff or erosion rates in the watersheds located above the two potential values at risk. Only 80 acres appear to have burned at high severity, as indicated by significant consumption of organics on the forest floor. However, indications of hydrophobicity were infrequent and, where present, were of low intensity. Further, the high severity acres were not concentrated spatially but were spread out over nearly a dozen small ephemeral drainages. Therefore, runoff intensity is expected to be similar to pre-fire runoff and would not be altered significantly enough to place the culvert crossings on 24N30A at a higher risk of failure. Only a very small portion of the burned area is located in the Silver Creek watershed and soil burn severity on that portion was generally low. Some ground cover was consumed but the burned slopes have high rock content and appear resistant to mass wasting events. Assessment indicated little or no increase in the risk that a debris flow or rock slide that could damage the water works would occur on those slope above the risk that was present pre-fire. The Special Use Permittee has been advised of the BAER team... s findings.

Road Drainage Reconstruction General Description: The roads surveyed within the Siskiyou fire were found to have issues with their drainage system due to the expected increase in flows. The minimal treatments required to remedy these issues are: 1. Drain Dips (with or without armor) ... Roadway dips modify the road drainage by altering the template and allowing surface flows to run off the road to prevent any excessive erosion of the surface. The armor consisting of rip rap is placed where runoff could possibly cause erosion to the road surface and fillslope. 2. Culvert Cleaning ... Includes the cleanout of catch basin culvert inlets, outlets, and the drop inlets. Also included is the replacement of lids covering the drop inlets. Cleaning culvert pipes and replacing the missing and damaged lids over the drop inlets will enable the drainage system to pass flows more intended design flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 3. Culvert Repair - Using mechanical means to open up culverts to improve flow or cutting off sections too damaged to repair. This will improve culvert flow and reduce the chance of plugging. 4. Catch Basin Expansion ... Expanding existing catch basins in size and remove debris in the channel above the inlet. The expanded catch basins will handle more sediment and removing debris will reduce the chance of the culvert plugging. 5. Fill Size Reduction ... Reduce the fill volume over undersized culverts and construct a channel over the culvert. The channel will normally have rip rap to protect the remaining fill. This keeps the flow and sediment in the channel and reduces road related sediment and total fill failure. 6. Fill Slope Protection ... Place geotextile and rip rap on fill slopes where water flow over the fill is expected. This will reduce erosion and sediment delivery down stream. 7. Ditch Cleaning ... The cleanout of drainage ditches is required to remove debris that impede the flow or deflect it out of the ditch onto the road surface. Clean ditches will ensure that the flow reaches drainage structures. 8. Roadway slope improvement ... Out sloping or in sloping the road surface to ensure the flow goes into a drainage structure or is allowed to sheet off outside edge of the road without concentrating the water. This reduces road related sediment. 9. Culvert Additions ... Add additional culverts to drainage fills or upsize the existing culvert where the expected increased flow is more than the existing culvert can handle. Reduces the chance of fill failure and associated sediment delivery down stream. Also allows replacement of fire damaged pipes and down drains to maintain existing drainage capacity and flow dissipation.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: A total of 143 cultural resource sites were identified within the burn area of the Telephone Fire. Of these, 59 are eligible and 34 are unevaluated or potentially eligible and managed as eligible until formal evaluation occurs. Post-contact sites include lookouts, wooden troughs, sawmills, mining sites and features, and refuse scatters. The pre-contact sites are generally lithic scatters and quarry sites. Multicomponent sites include both pre- and post-contact components. Site locations that fell within high and moderate intensity were prioritized for assessment, as well as Priority Heritage Assets (PHAs). A total of 7 sites were initially selected for review based on burn severity and potential for erosion. A decision was made to concentrate efforts on the PHA and area of potential public safety concerns. Neither site rated high in the risk assessment. One site rated low due to no real change in post-fire conditions while the second was deemed of minor consequence if damaged.

Projects.Highlights:
Rock fill work never completed but 10 cu. yds of rock were stockpiled by road 40N42. A grade-out rock fill was to be built.
Rock dip was put in to assure that channel runoff passed over the armored portion of the fill below the road.
Four rock walls were constructed along Specimen road to keep the road from washing out where runoff collects and drains towards the creek.
Rice straw wattle treatment was not accomplished due to early snow. Contour felling (see Activity section under Specimen fire)
Two 5 ft rock check dams were constructed in two gullies in order to trap eroded dry ravel material before it reached Specimen Cr. Construction depends on the availability of rock. Important to key in. Height was 2-3 ft. Energy dissipator located downslope. Need to armor the whole thing, because water can flow through them.
12 natural looking stone weirs were constructed in the channel that leads to Specimen Cr. to trap materials and sediment. Height was 6 ft. They helped form natural pools in the streams, increased storage capacity. Constructed to last only a few years.
6 log jams were constructed in the 2 forks of Specimen Cr. above the steelhead habitat.

A formal BAER assessment was not completed because the fire was small in size (i.e., 713 acres). Although there were values at risk threatened including recreational resorts, campgrounds, private residences, powerlines, and infrastructure associated with the Flaming Gorge Dam, none of these values were affected by the fire. In addition, based on field observations, burn severity was mostly low and moderate in a few areas. The type of vegetation present (i.e., ponderosa pine, lodgepole pine, aspen, and sagebrush) will resprout within a few years.

Projects.VegType: ponderosa pine, Douglas-fir, white fir, juniper, and oaks.
Projects.PropThrtDescr: Threat of damage to towns of Sacramento and Weed.
Projects.Highlights:
No 2500-8 report, but good rehab accomplishment report.
Three factors greatly influence fire behavior: fuel, weather, and topography. In the Spring fire, fuels were a mixture of species with light fuels such as pine needles and grass contributing to the rate of spread and heavy fuels including mature trees and slash contributing to fire intensity. The weather was hot and dry with an extreme shortage of moisture during the preceding winter. Winds were extreme. Topography was steep and broken.
Seed mixes for aerial seeding (helicopter carrying a Sling King seeder): Mixture 1 - Ponderosa pine zone at 8.5 lbs/acre - orchard grass (24%), timothy (6%), perennial rye (29%), and intermediate wheatgrass (41%). Mixture 2 - Pinyon-juniper zone at 9.5 lbs/acre - Russian wild rye (26%), weeping lovegrass (10%), Pubescent wheatgrass (32%), perennial rye (16%), sand dropseed (5%), and yellow blossom sweet clover (11%)
Results of reseeding were good. Gentle summer rains continued throughout July allowing the new grass seedlings to become established. Torrential thunderstorms came in Aug. And Sept. removed 2 inches of topsoil from some slopes, but enough grass had become established to hold a great deal of soil in place. By the summer of 1975, there was 60% ground cover on most of the burned area.
Contour terracing - designed to retain a 5 yr, 30 minute precipitation of 1.5 inches. Total of 825 acres. Terraces were insloped with interior baffles installed to prevent lateral movement of water within each terrace. All terraces were discontinuous and staggered on adjacent contours to prevent overloading of the lower terraces in the event of spillage. Results - little on-site erosion occurred and water reaching the channels was practically free of turbidity.
Check dams (constructed using gabion baskets) - results were favorable. Stopped sediment from reaching the community of Weed. Several structures were full of sediment and the rest were filling. Channel degradation had stopped.
Only have an incomplete accomplishment report on this fire.

Projects.Highlights:
Seed mix proposed for use was 40 lb/ac winter wheat
Rock rip-rap was used for channel stabilization to prevent scouring of stream. It was estimated that some 3 miles of stream channel would be subject to scouring above an existing stabilized headcut that was vulnerable to renewed activity resulting from increases in peak flow.
Earth road berms were used to minimize access to areas that were aerially seeded.
Contour felling was completed along canyon toeslopes, and on steep sideslopes below road culverts where surface flow was likely to be concentrated.
Approximately 7,569 acres of highly erosive sideslopes were aerially seeded to restore ground cover to at least 50%. These slopes were exposed to high fire intensities which reduced existing ground cover to less than 10% which consisted of mostly rock and scattered large woody material.

Projects.Highlights:
Immediately after the fire, an intense thundershower resulted in 11 debris flows in the West Fork of Mill Creek drainage. Four were quite massive blocking the West Fork road, covering culverts and ditches, and depositing and estimated 5850 tons of sediment in the stream channel ( with additional deposits on floodplains and terraces). Yet burn severity was low over 95% of the fire.
Blasting was done to create a channel where debris flows had filled the creek.
Contour felling was cut back from original request due to overly rocky terrain.
The Survey Team conducted a review of implementation to evaluate the project, documented in a 2520 memo to the District Ranger 10-4-91.

Projects.Highlights:
Treatment (non-Wilderness) - non-persistent seed mix - soft white winter wheat 10%, annual ryegrass 75%, Saifoin 15%, Wilderness treatment seed mix - hand seeded - locally collected native seed - Idaho fescue 15%, Prairie Junegrass 40%, blue wild rye 30%, Sandberg's bluegrass 30%.
Road - depressions installed in the road surface over streams, to allow the water to flow across the road if the culvert plugs.
Trails - had drainage structures consumed by fire in the medium and high intensity burn areas. In many areas, logs which supported the down\hill side of the trail bed were totally consumed, as were flexible rubberized diversions.
Appendix 1 of report included seeding prescriptions, rationale, seed source, and species selection criteria (in file). Rationale - seeding vs non-seeding: Recommendation to seed high intensity fire zones falling within dry forest, and cool forest coarse vegetative types is based on the potential for extreme erosion of volcanic ash soils on 40-50% slopes and that of granitic soils on 50-60% slopes. Soil erosion adversely affects biological productivity and should be prevented before it becomes a long-term and potentially irreversible problem. No seeding was recommended for low and moderate burn areas. No seeding was recommended for the following coarse vegetative types: rocky forest, escarpment, scabland, and meadow. Because limited contact between seed and soil could be anticipated in these vegetative zones, the success rate of seeding would be low.
Species selection criteria - non-wilderness: Soft white winter wheat (Triticum aestivum) persists for up to 3 yrs with progressive decline in seed production. Its relatively large seed size insures excellent distribution when applied aerially. Annual ryegrass (Lolium multiflorum) is a long season grass that does not contribute significantly to ladder fuels. This species has demonstrated a persistence of 2 to 4 yrs. Sainfoin (Onobrychis viciaefolia) is an attractive, non-persistent legume commonly grown for forage in Scotland. This species benefits soils through nitrogen fixation. All traces of this species disappeared within 5 yrs of seeding. Red fescue (Festuca rubra) is a non-sod forming long lived perennial bunch grass. The rapid establishment and extensive root system will provide long term soil stabilization. The persistent green crown is highly fire resistant, greens early in the spring and remains until early winter. Areas of Red fescue were found persisting on steep, highly erodible soils after the Tower Mtn fire.
Seeding selection criteria - wilderness Blue wild rye (Elymus glaucus) - is a fast developing, short-lived, cool season, native perennial bunchgrass. Typical habitat includes prairies, open woods, thickets, and moist to dry hillsides at elevations in the Blue Mtns up to 6000 ft. It has high seedling vigor, high seed production, and a strong ability to reseed disturbed areas. Idaho fescue (Festuca idahoensis) - is a common and important native cool season perennial bunchgrass. It has a broad ecological amplitude, but does best in 14-24 inch precipitation zones on moderately deep to dep silt loam to clay loam soils. The species has good herbage production, but low annual seed production. Although slow to establish from seed, it has a high value as a persistent species in soil erosion control seed mixes. Prairie Junegrass (Koeleria macrantha) - is a long-lived, cool-season native tufted perennial grass. It occurs on higher montane elevations on well drained soils, (precip. 12-20 in),. It quickly reseeds bare areas after disturbance. Seedling growth is slow to moderate. Sandberg's bluegrass (Poa sandbergil) - is a long-lived, low-growing native perennial bunchgrass. It occurs in drier grassland and shrubland habitats across a wide variety of climatic, edaphic, and elevational extremes.

Road and Trail Treatments: T03 - Road Drainage General Description: This treatment will maintain the road drainage in preparation for increased runoff. Road work will be consistent with pre-fire design in most cases and will include outsloping, drain dips, waterbars, overflow structures, cross-drain culverts, debris racks, culvert cleaning, ditch cleaning, roadside stabilization, inlet guards, and template reshaping. This treatment has a high unit cost because it groups a number of individual treatments that are extrapolated across the entire burned area.

Headcut structures; An intermittent stream near Crockett Camp had two five foot high headcuts. The headcuts were on the WIN list for rehabilitation. The fire burned the watershed above the headcuts. The BAER team determined that the headcuts would accelerate upstream movement since the ground cover was burned. The headcuts were treated in the Fall of 2001. The area was examined in 2002 and the headcut treatment was successful. High water flows and sediment movement were evident in the channel above the treatment area.
Road Contract: Roads in the burned area were inventoried for their ability to withstand extra surface and stream runoff due to denuding of the slopes. The county road to the Fouts Springs California Youth Authority Detention Center had many undersized culverts. Since the county did not have the funds to upgrade the culverts, there was a concern that a culvert could plug, despite the channel clearing, and wash out the road. An alternate route to the Center was determined but this road needed to be upgraded to handle winter traffic.
A road contract was developed to improve drainage on eight roads for 13.5 miles. Engineering, with assistance from hydrology, did the construction staking.
Under the contract, most of the roads were outsloped. Approximately 100 road rolling dips were added to insloped and outsloped roads. Twenty-three culverts were either installed or upgraded and 1,180 tons of riprap were added to culvert outlets as energy dissipators to reduce stream erosion. About 0.80 acres of disturbed areas were seeded and mulched. Twenty-three culvert inlets were cleaned or had catch basins constructed. Twenty-five metal end sections were added to culverts. Gates were installed on two roads to restrict wet season access.
After initial reconstruction, Fall storms generated road runoff that caused rills on the hillside. Contract changes were made to add additional drainage structures. Even with closer spaced (50-70 feet apart) rolling dips there was enough surface runoff from the brush field soils to cause rill erosion on the hillside below the road.
A main road to access the Forest... s electronic site was improved to handle road water. A portion of this road traversed serpentine soil. Since this road provided access to the site during wet weather, road maintenance funds were used to rock this section of road. This was a good example of BAER funds improving road drainage to handle fire induced runoff and road maintenance funds to upgrade the road for wet weather use.
End sections on culvert inlets worked very well as only one end section became plugged and caused a minor road washout. C&M foreman Gaddini conducted storm patrols and said ... culvert end sections are very worth the money... . One can only speculate how many culverts were not plugged due to the installed end sections.
Fireline Barriers: Railroad ties were installed to block OHV access to three firelines.
Sensitive Plant Fence: A fence protecting sensitive plants in the Fouts Springs staging area needed replacement of wood corner posts and wire.
Staging Area Barriers: Wood barriers confining OHV riders to staging areas were burned when the fire went through the area. These barriers, plus others, were installed prior to re-opening the area to use. Roughly 20,300 feet of barriers were installed by inmate crews, C&M crews, OHV specialists and motorcycle club volunteers.
Trail Closure Barriers: OHV trails entering the burned area were closed with a Forest Closure Order. To ensure that Forest users did not ride OHV... s in the burned area, the trail entrances were blocked with wood barriers.
Roadside Barriers: Prior to the fire, wood tie barriers lined several roads. These barriers prevented OHV users from leaving the road prism and venturing into other areas. Four hundred fifty feet of roadside barriers were installed along two roads.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: The area of potential effect for cultural resources is NFS land within the fire perimeter. Eighteen cultural resources have been previously recorded on NFS lands in the Turner Gulch Fire, 11 of which were identified as BAER critical values. Two additional sites adjacent to the fire perimeter were also considered as critical values. Critical heritage values are defined as sites that are listed, eligible, or unevaluated for inclusion to the National Register of Historic Places. The Archeologists on the BAER team were able to visit 4 of these sites and due to high fire activity in the southern portion of the fire were not able to visit the other sites. Prehistoric camps threatened by increased erosion and elevated runoff removing intact subsurface cultural deposits. The probability of damage or loss is unlikely because it is within unburned and low SBS. The magnitude of consequences is major because these historic properties are officially eligible or unevaluated for listing on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) due to data potential. Soil erosion may cause considerable damage to a non renewable resource. The risk is intermediate, and a BAER emergency does not exist for this resource. Cultural resources associated with prehistoric lithic scatters are at an increased risk of erosion and increased runoff removing intact subsurface cultural deposits. The probability of damage or loss is unlikely. Sites that were visited during the field assessment had overall stable structure; however, some low SBS has the potential of displacing artifacts based on remaining vegetation cover on the slope. The magnitude of consequences is major. Because these historic properties are eligible or unevaluated for the NRHP due to data potential. Soil erosion may cause considerable damage to a non-renewable resource. The risk is intermediate. No BAER emergency exists at these sites. Historic Property 1- Ute Trail is at an increased risk of erosion and increased runoff removing intact subsurface cultural deposits. The probability of damage or loss is possible because the site assessment found that the corridors cross through unburned, low, moderate, and high SBS areas. Erosion and runoff are possible on the trail, which may displace associated artifacts and/or features. The magnitude of consequences is moderate because the trail corridor is eligible in part due to their association with other cultural resources and retainment of their function. The loss or damage to associated sites would constitute an adverse effect to the corridor... s eligibility. The risk is intermediate. No BAER emergency exists and no treatments are proposed.

Projects.Highlights:
Seeding recommendation:
Certified seed with no noxious weeds. Objective of the seed mix: provide immediate cover but no long lasting carry over.
Channel mix: soft white winter wheat (50 lbs/ac), slender wheatgrass (12 lbs/ac), and yellow sweetclover (2 lbs/ac)
Non-forest mix: soft white winter wheat (50), annual ryegrass 3 lbs/ac, and alfalfa 1 lb/ac. Fertilize with ammonium nitrate sulfate to get 20 lbs of N/ac
Forest seed mix: soft white winter wheat 35 lbs/ac., slender wheatgrass 6lbs/ac, and red clover 1 lb/ac. Fertilize with ammonium nitrate sulfate to get 20 lbs of N/ac.
Alluvial fans are in private ownership with 2-5 homes each and apple orchards. Lower watershed valley bottoms become quite constricted just above the gentle sloping alluvial fans. These constricted locations become the site of debris dams which blow out with tremendous force and little warning. All roads dissect alluvial fans in valley bottom positions.
Log terracing (LEB's) was increased by 14,300 acres. In many areas, this treatment is the only immediate protection from storms and concentration of surface runoff. This treatment was implemented in upper watershed catchment basins. Log terraces could have been more dense on some sites than others depending on fire effects, sensitivity of the site, and slope. Objectives of log terraces: 1) trenches above each log are a point of infiltration thru hydrophobic soils. 2) logs are a non-erodible control point where overland runoff can overfall without scouring, 3) logs break up the direct flow of overland runoff downslope, causing a meandering runoff pattern with less velocity and less destructive energy, 4) the formation of dendritic rill patterns is controlled, 5) mobile sediments are trapped and potential sediments are stabilized, and 6) ashes are stabilized by each terrace.
In areas with pumice layers over the soil, alternatives to seeding should be considered, especially if seeded species are not capable of penetrating the deep, dry layer of pumice.
Objectives of grass seeding: 1) bind soil in place 2) prevent soil detachment, 3) penetrate hydrophobic soil layers 4) impede overland runoff and control water velocity, and 5) improve infiltration.
Best stands of seeded grasses were in the moist riparian areas. Least needed there because native plants were in equal abundance. The most effective hillslope seeding was on deep, well-drained soils with less than 2 inches of pumice on the surface. It was apparent that that very large areas in the burn were not effectively vegetated. Observations: 1) large areas in the burn were bare of vegetation before the fire, and are still bare after treatment. This may be due to mobile soil surface, extreme soil temp., and/or deep pumice. 2) Seeded areas only attained a height of 2 to 5" then droughted out. Not effectively stabilizing the sites. 3) Native shrubs and grasses did sprout, with an acceptable density and are doing well. These may become the best stabilizers for the sites, and perhaps a "nurse crop" for other species. 5) the soil profile has an overburden of dry pumice, 6 to 8" deep, over decomposed granite with abundant moisture available for plant use. This site condition alone is harsh enough to prevent all but the most aggressive plant species. The plants that become established and are doing well are those natives that are capable of penetrating the pumice and are able to follow the receding moisture front.

Projects.Highlights:
Q. Approximate Miles of Stream Channels by Order: First Order - 86 miles, Second Order - 14miles, Third through Fifth Order - 19 miles.
Cost of No-Action (Including Loss) and Cost of Selected Alternative (Including Loss) was not provided.
In Trail Creek (NE1/4, Section 36) Road 114 crosses an unstable hill-slope. The fill slope of the road erodes silt size to gravel size materials directly into a Bull trout spawning reach of Trail Creek. The wildfire will increase the erosion from the cutslope and fillslope due to increased overland flow and increased soil dry raveling because of vegetation loss on the cutslope. The proposed treatment is to re-route Trail Creek for a distance of 300 feet directly below the fillslope area, and to mulch and seed (grasses & shrubs) the fill-slope and cutslope. The combination of these two treatments will significantly reduce the risk of fire-accelerated sedimentation into the spawning gravel areas of Trail Creek.
Realign 300 feet of Trail Creek in the SW1/4 NW1/4 of Section 35 in T37N, R23W, approximately 1 mile above Thoma Creek to move the channel away from the base of an existing slump. The treatment will remove a fire-accelerated source of fine sediments from above a documented bull trout spawning area. Geomorphic techniques (i.e.; Rosgen) will be used to create the new channel to allow it to function naturally.

Projects.Highlights:
High intensity fire zone is characterized by the total absence of live tree crowns and total absence of ground vegetation. Soils in the high intensity burn show no residual organic increment in the A horizon and are a mosaic of layers of thick, gray ash and oxidized red patches on the soil surface.
Moderate intensity fire is characterized by scorched tree crowns, > 50% dead tree crowns, and > 50% burned understory shrubs. No litter is evident in the black and gray ash mosaic on the soil surface.
Low fire intensity is characterized by live tree crowns, absence of crown scorching, and a black ash layer on the soil surface. Unburned woody material is present and litter is still detectable in the ash layer. Although blackened, root crowns of perennial plants in this zone appear to be viable. Understory shrubs are >50% unburned in this zone.
Small sediment trapping structures (large woody material) were installed in a headwater stream. A walking type excavator would be used to place the large woody material across the channel where existing wood was consumed by the fire. Using this type of equipment, the tree root would remain attached when it is felled and the could be partially buried. Both of these factors would guarantee successful placement of the grade control structures and would prevent it from washing downstream. Large woody material diameter will range from 12 to 16 inches with a length of approximately 40 ft or more.
Included in report Appendix entitled Wheeler Point Seeding Recommendation: High fire intensity zones mix: soft white winter wheat 45% (35 lbs/acre), annual ryegrass 40% (2 lbs/ac), sainfoin 15% (11 lbs/ac)
No seeding was recommended for; low and moderate fir intensity zones to minimize competition with native species; for rocky forest, escarpment, scabland, and aspen meadow.
Species selection criteria: soft white winter wheat - Persists for up to 3 yrs with progressive decline in seed production. Relatively large seed size insures excellent distribution when applied aerially. It is recommended that local source seed be used to defuse any future claims regarding pathogen sources. This is particularly important since kernel bunt disease has recently caused quarantine measures to be invoked in Texas, Montana, and Washington.
Annual ryegrass - is a long season grass that does not contribute significantly to ladder fuels. Persistence of 2 to 4 yrs.
Sainfoin - non-persistent legume commonly grown for forage in Scotland. This species benefits soils thru nitrogen fixation. All traces of this species disappeared within 5 yrs of seeding.

Projects.Highlights:
Additional reason for seeding and fertilizer was to help reduce the expected infestation of noxious weeds in the intensely burned areas.
Debris catchment structures - logs with diameters >10 inches and lengths greater than 2 channel widths, arranged with one end in the water against the opposite bank, pointing slightly upstream will provide a stable sediment trap. Spacing depends on channel gradient. The distance between structures should be about 3 to 5 channel widths when the stream gradient is < 1.5%, and 1 to 2 channel widths when the gradient is > 1.5%. These instream structures will trap floating debris and sediment and provide more diversity of aquatic habitat.
Seed mix high intensity burn area:
Mountain brome 3 lbs/ac, White Dutch clover 1 lb/ac, Kentucky blue grass 3 lbs/ac, and Redtop 2 lbs/ac Fertilizer (30-0-0-8) applied at a rate of 130 lbs/acre.
Emergency rehab narrative. Aerial seeding and fertilization. Seed mix: orchardgrass 3 lbs/acre, Sherman's Big bluegrass 2 lbs/acre, Timothy 4 lbs/acre, and Dutch White clover 1 lb/acre. Fertilizer mix: 38-0-0-8 at 130 lbs/acre. Equal to 50 lbs of actual N/acre. 3547 acres will be seeded and fertilized.
Contour felling was to be done on 100 acres of slopes >60% in the high intensity burn areas. Riparian planting of willows and cottonwoods was to be done along 2.2 miles of O'Brien Cr., along with instream debris structures. Check dams were installed in 6.1 miles of the headwaters of Stall and sleepy Hollow Creeks.

Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources (CR):For prehistoric (primarily stone & ceramic features), sites, totaling142 in burned area, four were field inspected post-burn. Threats exist from loss of vegetation holding features and artifacts intact poses increased risk of precipitation causing sheetwash and slope erosion. These site were found to be at Low risk. b. For proto/historic site/features consisting of wooden components, a total of 19 were identified within burned area. Eight sites were field inspected. The risk to these sites was determined to be High. c. A pre-historic rock shelter (1754), which is eligible for the National Register of Historic Places, is threatened by high post-fire water flows and erosion. Loss of vegetation poses increased erosion risk. The probability of damage or loss is Very Likely due to the sites location at the confluence of two drainages. Erosion from the bottom of primary wall has already started. Freshly eroded cobbles were evident in drainage bottom below site. Loss of all vegetation from base of site will cause further disturbance with precipitation. The magnitude of consequences is Major based on Irreversible damage to critical cultural resources resulting in considerable or long-term effects. This site is unique in this area and represents the potential for broader learning about the surrounding history of the landscape. See treatment H1 (EDRR). d. Navajo Trail, which is eligible for National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) is at risk of loss of integrity and original route due to suppression activities; blowing ash/sand; erosion from post-fire precipitation. The probability of damage or loss is Likely on areas where the trail is not on a ridge have post fire peak flow increases that are significant, very significant or extreme (i.e., >100% of pre fire flows) for the 50% chance event, making damage very likely. The tread is already starting to disappear in areas with moderate and high soil burn severity. The magnitude of consequence is Major because the Navajo Trail is eligible for the NRHP. Many Navajo/Paiute cultural sites along and associated with the trail were lost/impacted along the trail. Any further damage to this resource would impact broader landscape of information. This would be and added benefit of S2. And P1a (EDRR), if treatments area. 4. Other (CRs): Other non-BAER critical values, such as for Wildlife, Vegetation, Range, etc. were identified during this assessment. Also, non-NFS critical values were identified, such a BLM managed roads. See Critical Values table in project record.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: Of the many cultural resource sites within the fire perimeter, 10 cultural resources assets and locations were selected as priority for the BAER assessment. These cultural assets are threatened by vandalism, looting, and erosion due to loss of vegetative cover. The probability of damage or loss is possible given the loss of vegetation from the fire that has exposed previously unexposed sites and increased accessibility to sites. The magnitude of consequences is moderate because loss of information or diagnostic artifacts could impact eligibility status. The risk rating is intermediate. BAER treatments are not recommended.

Projects.Highlights:
Descriptive narrative included with report (in file). Also good geomorphic interpretations of the different watersheds made following the burn are included in the report (in file).
Low elevation seed mix: (seeds/sq.ft.) Blue grama 3% (5), Sand dropseed 1% (12), Prairie Junegrass 3% (13), Indian ricegrass 25% (6), Sideoats grama 18% (7), Regreen 25% (1), and annual rye 25% (10)
High elevation seed mix: (seeds/sq.ft.) Mountain brome 37% (11), Timothy 5% (15), Sheep fescue 12% (20), Regreen 46% (2)
Contour felling was increased in watersheds above Lama. Intensity of burn in these areas makes this treatment critical in providing sediment storage on the slopes and preventing the sediment from reaching the streams and impacting water quality.
First major storm 6-18-96, resulted in debris flows down Largo Canyon. Large amounts of sediment and woody debris were deposited within the riparian area. In places, the stream had downcut 8 to 15 ft through the sediment now present in the channel bottom.
Second storm event - resulted in little change in the watershed. No additional debris flows resulted from this event.
Because of a wider floodplain, depth of sediment accumulation in Lama Canyon was not as great as in Largo.
Effectiveness of BAER treatments:
Log dams - Initial estimate of effectiveness was 70 to 80 percent. Some of the channels where these structures were placed were scoured deeply as the structures blew out and the flow continued downstream.
Contour felling: The initial estimate of effectiveness was 50 to 80%. It was observed that some of the smaller diameter logs were pushed downslope to the channels and contributed to the debris dams. Other contour logs were pushed downslope on one end and are now angled towards the valley below, reducing their effectiveness.
Aerial seeding: No germination has yet occurred even though there was sufficient amounts of rain. The first sign of germination of seed was noted on 6-28-96. Germination on steep slopes was noted behind standing trees and on the uphill sides of surface rock fragments.
Assessment of watershed conditions 2-3-97: Summer monsoon rains caused significant sheet and rill erosion from steep slopes in the upper ends of Largo, Lama, and Garrapata canyons and the stream channels and riparian areas have been heavily damaged. In spite of treatment measures implemented, the intensity and duration of the summer rains produced runoff that effectively overwhelmed the in-channel treatments and removed the structures from the 1st order channels where they were installed. Those that remained in place were filled beyond capacity and in most cases the channel has been downcut by storm runoff to a level ranging from 8 to 12 ft below the original grade.
LEB's were still effective. Lack of small limbs and organic debris to fill the space beneath these structures and seal them at ground level was identified as a limiting factor.
Slashing was effective, except for this material disappearing as people take it for firewood.
Aerial seeding now is effective in providing vegetative cover for soil protection, especially in cooler, moister sites such as north and east aspects. Steep, south facing slopes where seed germination was limited still provided source areas for runoff and sediment delivery to stream channels. Natural vegetative recovery in the form of re-sprouting of understory vegetation and the regeneration of oak and aspen stands has contributed significantly to the vegetative recovery of the area. Trees that were scorched and displayed a tan or reddish tinge still had a chance to survive.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) eligible sites: Approximately 92 eligible or assumed eligible archaeological sites for listing on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) were identified within the burn area and a total of 29 sites were identified and visited for field assessments. Watersheds denuded by the fire can cause erosion, debris flow, damage to sites from hazard trees, looting or vandalism due to increased visibility and storm run-off, which can completely displace archeological surface artifacts, cut through archaeological sites damaging cultural deposits, or undermine historic buildings, structures, and features. Surface artifacts can be moved or buried by erosion degrading their integrity and spatial relationships. These impacts may destroy cultural resources or alter the context of surface and subsurface cultural remains vital to any scientific analysis or interpretation of past human behaviors and activities. The probability of damage or loss is possible for all sites, because watersheds denuded by the fire can cause erosion, debris flow, storm run-off, or damage to sites from hazard trees and surface artifacts can be exposed and are susceptible to looting and vandalism. As a result, the magnitude of consequences is major. The resulting risk is high.

The probability of damage or loss is UNLIKELY because impacts to site would not cause any expected damage. The magnitude of consequences is MODERATE because damage would cause considerable or only term effects. Risk is LOW. Treatment options considered installing rock fall fence and/or proactively scale rocks to prevent impacting site. No recommended treatments. Note that an adjacent engineering treatment will support protection of the site. 45MS134 Historic Site includes increased access and visual exposure of artifacts. The probability of damage or loss is VERY LIKELY because the location is directly adjacent to the trail and very visible. The magnitude of consequences is MINOR because any potential looting would not impact on the integrity of the site or loss of significance. Risk is LOW. Treatment options considered are seeding, closure of site, and/or masking of artifacts. No recommended treatments. Note that natural revegetation is expected to recover thus masking the site. The adjacent trail is also proposed to be closed for the first year.

Projects.PropThrtDescr: Threat to timber and range segments of the local economies.
Projects.WtrQualThrtDescr: Threat to fish habitat
Projects.SoilProdThrtDescr: Risk of loss of soil in timber stands was high. Potential for introduction of non-native grass spp.
Projects.Highlights:
Extensive narrative and burn intensity maps included in file.
Major concerns involved the potential effects of the salvage operation.
Fire activity was spotty, leaving many unburned areas within the fire perimeter. An estimated 18% of the area was burned at a moderate or high intensity.
Rock fragments covered nearly 50% of the soil surface within the fire perimeter. A storm system which brought nearly 1 inch of rain to the area in a 3-day period had little erosional effect. Stream channels (Sawmill and Dairy Cr.) in the fire area were already in poor condition before the fire due past and present road construction, logging, and grazing practices.
Four cattle allotments were damaged, including 22 miles of boundary and allotment management fence along with several range improvements. These direct losses caused by the fire would bring about additional impacts through the loss of grazing fees and economic value to permittees and the community.
Recommendations: Contour felling on the lower third of slopes in moderate high burn intensity areas using 20% of the 6-10 inch class size trees. Keep grass seeding to a minimum because the effects of seeding on sensitive plants is unknown and because fire intensity was low for the most part. Keep livestock off for two years. Snags should be retained. Save and protect 5-10 of the best live trees per acre as a seed source.
Hydrological point of view - over the long term, the spotty nature of the fire combined with the large amount of light and moderate burn, accomplished a significant reduction in fuels and would lead to a rejuvenation of some species of native vegetation that would benefit the watershed. From evidence of fire scars and vegetation types, the site is adapted to fire and would tend to recover rapidly from fire effects. Because of the amount of rock fragments on the surface (50-60%) it was questionable how much additional erosion protection would be provided by grass seeding. The Forest Service roadless area and the BLM Research Natural Area of Silver Cr.has been little affected by man . In this area the hydrological effects of the fire were positive. There was a 300% increase in the amount of large woody debris (LWD) in the main channel. Amounts of LWD, up to 2 pieces/100 ft of channel were in place and would function to dissipate the energy of high flows, trap sediments, and scour pools, thus providing fish habitat. It was recommended that no salvage or rehabilitation activities be undertaken in this drainage. Areas of the Silver Cr. Watershed that have seen human activity including road construction, and location, timber harvest, and grazing were in unacceptable condition before the fire (assigned a 25% threshold, the lowest). Fish habitat quality was in poor condition before the fire and fire effects would further aggravate the poor conditions. Salvage needed to be planned to avoid increasing sediment delivery to channels above already expected rates. This would mean adherence to threshold levels, minimization of road construction, no ground disturbance adjacent to stream channels, leaving all standing trees (dead or alive) within 100 ft of any channels to provide future LWD recruitment, designating skid trail systems and other mitigation measures. Road management objectives in the area needed to be re-evaluated. The current transportation network of roads located in every draw has greatly contributed to the poor stream conditions. In many cases, the stream channel is reduced to nothing more than a ditch. In some cases the road is the stream channel.
Seed mix recommended for high burn intensity areas:
Sandberg's bluegrass (Poa Sandberg) 1.5 lbs/acre, Blue bunch wheat grass (Agropyron spicatum) 7.5 lbs/acre, and orchard grass (Dactylis glomerata) 4 lbs/acre.
