Sediment Potential: The amount of eroded sediment from hillslopes and stream banks that is delivered into stream channels depends on surface roughness from landscape features such as surface rock content, slope, downed woody debris, litter, microtopography, and other ecosystem characteristics. From the WEPP Cloud results of modeled catchments of interest there was a maximum increase of 11 lbs/acre/yr (0.0055 tons/acre/yr) of sediment delivery, a minimum of no change post fire, and an average increase of 3.6 lbs/acre/yr (0.0018 tons/acre/yr) across a mosaic of all burn severity classes.
Cultural and Heritage Resources: Precontact sites within the fire perimeter are generally characterized by lithic scatters (i.e., sites containing debitage, stone tools, and/or ground stone) rock cairns and culturally modified trees. Historic-era sites include dendroglyphs (tree carvings), cabin remains, can/refuse scatters, cairns and roads/trail. Cultural sites can be adversely effected by post-fire erosional processes, vandalism, informal artifact collection, flooding, and debris flows. Archaeological sites are a non-renewable resource and impacts to sites can be much greater during the period immediately following an initial burn then during the fire itself. As such, identifying threats to sensitive cultural resources is a critical part of the BAER process. The Crazy Creek Fire perimeter encompasses 249 previously recorded cultural resources. Post fire, field assessment determined that looting is the primary threat to resources within the fire perimeter. Given the scale of this fire and the number of sites involved, the BAER heritage team ran the initial site list through a series of four filters, to identify the critical values with the highest potential for post-fire impacts. These filters included 1) site eligibility, 2) burn severity, 3) distance to a road (looting) and 4) assemblage composition. With these filters applied 12 eligible - or unevaluated - sites were identified in moderate or high severity burn units, within 100 meters of a maintenance level 2-5 road. These 12 resources are grouped into three sets of critical values for the purposes of this BAER assessment. Heritage Assets ... Location 1: the 060700573 archaeological complex is composed of 22 previously recorded sites that have been consolidated into one site record. The site boundary for this complex of smaller, task specific sites is great than 600 acres. The southern, timbered margin of the area burned hot during the fire, exposing numerous precontact artifacts immediately adjacent to a 3 digit road. Given the proximity to the road it is ... Likely... that artifacts will be collected by the public which would result in ... Moderate... impacts to the site complex - which keys out as a ... High... probability of damage or loss. The heritage team recommends treatment code H1 to mitigate the risk of looting in the form of two gates on the -500 road. A gate on the eastern and western end of the -500 road will provide an effective deterrent to recreational use and minimize looting within this archaeologically rich landscape. Other Heritage Assets ... 11 Sites: the recommended treatment for the remaining sites is ... no treatment.... Site specific assessments will be made at each of these eleven sites in the spring to assess vegetation recovery and its impact on ground visibility. This determination is predicated on the assumption that these less visible resources will be protected by the current fire perimeter closures and natural vegetation regeneration Salters... s Cabin: no treatment required. Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources: ... cents Damage to sites from Hazardous Trees, Erosion, Sedimentation, and Looting Approximately 25 archeological sites that are unevaluated for listing on the National Register of Historic Places (NRHP) are located within the Dillon Fire perimeter. Of these sites, nine were identified to be within 50m of high or moderate burn severity. One site was identified during pre-field review as likely being inaccessible. Two sites were identified to be on private property. The remaining six sites were identified as Critical Values and an attempt was made to visit. Limitations included time constraints, access issues, miss-plotted GIS, and safety concerns. One site was positively identified, four were not re-located, and one was not visited. The sites are situated within smaller areas of high and moderate burn which are surrounded by low or unburned areas. The mosaic aspect of the burn left many trees intact thus the imminent threat from a tree strike was not identified near the site locations. Readily available material for new needle-cast and leaf litter was observed in site areas and sites were not near well-traveled roads thus looting threats were not identified. The general location of the sites on flats or ridgetops did not lend themselves to impacts from erosion or sedimentation. The probability of damage or loss due to tree strike, erosion, sedimentation and/or looting is determined to be unlikely. Damage to cultural resources results in an irreversible impact to an element, or elements, of their eligibility to be listed on the NRHP. Cultural resources are non-renewable and irreplaceable, and the magnitude of consequences is determined to be major. The resulting risk is intermediate.

Projects.Highlights:
Extensive narrative included in file. Good section on ecology/vegetation.
Seed mix for 5430 acres in moderate and severely burned land within the Davis and Swamp Cr. drainages: Winter wheat 10 lbs/acre, orchard grass 3 lbs/acre, yellow blossom sweet clover 2 lbs/acre, and Rhizoma alfalfa 1 lb/acre.
Seed mix for 1901 acres of severely burned land: winter wheat 15 lbs/acre, orchard grass 2 lbs/acre, and yellow blossom sweet clover 2 lbs/acre.
Most moderate and severe burning took place in timbered areas on steep, north-facing slopes.
Positive side for major runoff events - higher water velocities associated with such events would aid in flushing stream gravels of fine sediments resulting in improved spawning habitat. This is part of the natural stream process. Negative side - is the condition of drainages before fire. Many of the tributary drainages especially in the Starvation Ridge area exhibit a lack of riparian vegetation and large organic material, trampled banks and aggravated channels.
Several samples of shallow mantle failures were noted on the south aspect of Table Mtn. These features appeared to be localized phenomena resulting when water saturated soils lost their cohesiveness and flowed for short distances downslope. Soil saturation to the point of slope failure becomes more of a concern when transpiring trees are removed.
Density flows, avalanches of dry ash and fine soil, were noted at several locations throughout the burn area, usually in association with hotter burned sites. Material will stabilize when soil moisture increases. These processes as well as fire are an integral part of the site ecology and there is little past evidence of catastrophic damage to the soils.
On one site that was investigated after the fire 0.3 inches of rain fell within a 24 hr period on a hot burn site. The surface ash layer was still intact, dry and slightly crusted; while a band of moisture 1.5 inches thick was noted in the mineral soil just beneath the ash and above the hydrophobic layer. No signs of surface runoff were noted. Thus a more gradual wetting of the soil surface during spring snowmelt should not pose a serious threat of increased surface flow or erosion; particularly on the sheltered north aspect slopes where the majority of the hot burns occurred.
In narrative, interesting determination of the lost value of spawning steelhead is given.
Range - Two full growing seasons of rest from livestock grazing will be given. Then if the hot burn areas have a minimum of 50% ground cover, livestock grazing will continue on the treated areas.

Projects.Highlights: 1. Mobile home park had suffered episodic flooding prior to the fire. The watershed above was 87% burned and a degree of additional high risk. 2. Ground application of hydromulch was deemed very effective. It held up well during Sept. storms, and erosion was felt to be less than pre-fire rates. Log erosion barriers were similarly felt to be very successful. 3. Research (San Dimas) installed monitoring sites to determine effectiveness of wood chips vs. pellets and straw mulch. Team expressed concerns about heavy equipment on the site. 4. Achieved a good response from seeding where it was done in coordination with another treatment, ie. Log barriers. Where seeding was the only treatment, success was spotty. 5. Believed channel debris removal was very successful. 6. Straw bale check dams were highly successful in trapping sediment and slowing flow. An additional 60 acres were treated with rock grade control structures by the AZ Dept. of Transportation. 7. Road maintenance treatments were deemed successful. 8. My calculated costs differed slightly from the data sheet. Uncertain as to why.

Projects.Highlights:
Much of the burned area was on south aspects on medium to highly erosive soil types (rhyolite and andesite). A storm on Aug. 8 1989 created gullies in low gradient, 1st order streams as well as farther downstream. There was also a great deal of rilling on bare hillsides at the very top of slopes. A mild winter with a light snowpack provided little soil moisture recharge. Two summer thunderstorms occurred in early Aug. of 1990. Grass seeding had resulted in 30 to 50% cover , but the soil absorbed very little moisture. These two events filled log sills (sediment delay structures) in 3rd order streams. They also filled and breached hay bale structures built in 1st order streams. A very intense rainstorm occurred on Aug. 24, 1990. An engineering rep observed 25 ft of road bet that was cut back by runoff in a 2nd order stream channel. This event not only filled, but totally buried (3-6 ft) a series of log sills on a 3rd order stream with 1 inch plus material for hundreds of feet. Hay bale structures were either breached or washed out. Hillslopes had large amounts of rilling and gullying creating steep gradient bare soil areas. Even though on-going fire salvage logging operations had some of their erosion control measures completed, most of the skid trails had gullies from 6 to 18 inches deep, regardless of ripping, waterbars, or earthen dams. Hay pastures three miles downstream were covered with sediment.
Additional treatments after these storms were prescribed. Including grass seeding on 6.5 miles of 1st order stream channels that have gullies and large bare soil areas (mostly upper portions of water shed). Grass seeding on 6.3 miles of alluvial material in mostly 2nd order and larger streams (lower ends of the watersheds).
In file - Earl Ruby's Final, as built report for log sill dams, straw bale dams, silt fences, and tree felling in channels. Includes treatment photos

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Increased risk from post fire conditions exist to proto/historic heritage sites consisting of wooden/combustible components. The threat to these cultural resources is loss of vegetation that leaves sites exposed to weather events. The probability of damage or loss is likely since some damage has already occurred, and mitigation/salvage will not result is recovery of the resource. The magnitude of consequence is major since damage to archaeological sites is substantial and irreversible. Although the risk is major, no treatments are recommended since organic features cannot be mitigated. b. Increased risk from post fire conditions exist to heritage sites in low/unburned soil burn severity. Loss of vegetation poses increased disturbance risk from weather events. The probability of damage or loss is possible since some ground cover has been lost but not entirely. The magnitude of consequence is major since loss of archaeological sites is irreversible. The overall risk is high, but no treatment was recommended since the sites are unburned/low soil burn severity. c. Increased risk from post fire conditions exist to heritage sites in moderate/high soil burn severity especially those within and adjacent to drainages. The threat to these values is loss of vegetation, increased erosion rates, and increased peak flows. The probability of damage of loss is likely due to the sites being in drainages and within moderate/high soil burn severity. The magnitude of consequence is major since damage/loss to archaeological sites is substantial and irreversible. The overall risk to these resources is very high. Seeding, straw wattles, signage, tree felling, road closures, and monitoring is recommended for these sites. See treatments section for additional information.

Table 3: Miles of Stream Channels by Order or Class PERENNIAL 15.5 INTERMITTENT 49.2 EPHEMERAL 2.8 CANAL/DITCH 0.5
Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Heritage Assets ... Location 1 is an archaeological site situated at the base of a basalt cliff in the Whychus Creek drainage. Two potential fire associated impacts are considered here: 1) Elevated hillslope erosion and potential scouring of terrace due to increased post-fire hydrologic responses and 2) Informal collection of sensitive artifacts/voluntary vandalism of pictographs. Each type of damaged is considered below. i. ii. Physical post-fire threats: The fire consumed most of the vegetation in the site area, which could increase the rate of erosion through alluvial and colluvial processes along the face of the basalt cliff. The lack of vegetation may also destabilize the creek-side terrace where the site is located. Elevated channel runoff due to the post-fire conditions has the potential of inducing terrace scour. Considering post-fire hydrologic modeling results coupled with field assessments of the site, the probability of damage or loss is unlikely. The magnitude of consequence is moderate. The overall risk for this site due to physical processes is low and no BAER treatment is recommended. Looting and Vandalism: The most sensitive portions of this site have been systematically excavated by looters for decades. This site is adjacent to a recreation site, which has resulted in informal artifact collection for a long period of time and fire effects due to the Flat incident have further exposed this resource. The probability of damage to the resource by this threat is possible. The magnitude of consequence is major, making the overall risk rating high. No BAER treatment is recommended. b. Heritage Assets ... Location 2 site... s composition is extremely similar to Location 1. As such, it shares identical threats to the resource and the same treatment considerations. This location is also in the Whychus Creek drainage; however, it is within the recent Alder Springs fire footprint, which did not reburn in the Flat Fire, yet still faces the potential threats of post-fire related conditions from the Flat Fire as it is located roughly 500 feet downstream of the incident... s boundary. Physical post-fire threats: The site location is closer to the stream channel... s active floodplain within a destabilized terrace. However anticipated increases in post-fire runoff and hillslope erosion are minimal for the area, therefor the probability of damage at this location is possible. The site has a higher density of intact deposits, and therefor any damage to this resource would have a magnitude of consequence of major. The overall risk to this resource is high. No BAER treatments are recommended. Looting and Vandalism: Impacts to the rock art panels and artifact assemblages are considered possible, while the magnitude of consequence would be major, as these panels and artifacts are a non-renewable resources. The overall risk to this resource is high. No BAER treatments are recommended

Aerial Mulching Treatment Objective The purpose of the treatment is to restore watershed functions formerly provided by ground vegetation, canopy, and duff layer that were lost due to the fire. By reducing the amount of surface runoff, this treatment would have beneficial protective effects of reducing sediment into streams supplying the water treatment plant at Stevensville, and also protecting Bull Trout habitat. Methods Weed-free straw would be applied with a helicopter at 2 tons/acre on high and moderate intensity burn areas. Treatment sites would be strategically located to prevent eroded soils from entering area streams.

Projects.Highlights: Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. One undocumented cultural site was identified and assessed during the assessment. This site is potentially eligible for the National Register of Historic Places. This site is located in an area of low soil burn severity and has limited drainage area above it. It is a rock art site, with a resistant sandstone cap located above the rock art which will further protect the site. Loss of integrity of this site could potentially occur from erosional processes or damage from hazard trees, but the probability of damage or loss for the site is unlikely. The magnitude of consequences associated with loss or damage to the characteristics of the site that contribute to site eligibility is major. The site has a risk rating of Intermediate, with no treatments proposed to address the site as a cultural Critical Value.

Projects.Highlights:
Cost of aerial seeding broken down to $5.20/lb. Regular mix, $0.49/lb annual rye, and $3.12/acre for aerial application.
George Robertson said he would do things differently if to be done again. Since nothing can grow if the soil isn't retained, and since the native seed doesn't seem to establish well he would go ahead and plant the introduced species.
In Oct. of 96 Penny Luehring visited this and other fire rehab areas and did an evaluation. She noted that the legumes could be left out of the mix since there seemed to be ample supply of lupine, locust, and Peavine available onsite (San Francisco Peaks area). Flax (LINUM) did not grow well and so could be left out of the seed mix. She also noted that there doesn't seem to be a need for a seed mix of more than 4 species, consisting of 1 annual (rye, regreen) and a couple perennials.
Fire rehab plan asks fire suppression to "Fall snags on Horseshoe Hill on contour or perpendicular to the slope to break run-off." This was not noted by any interviewee so don't know if it was done. This is contour slashing not LEBs. Incident rehab team on fire suppression rehab was Scott Ewers and Ken Jacobs. Jeff Hink said he was Fire Situation Leader with Jim Bedlion as IC.
Curley (1980) was reburned by this fire. Reburn was not an issue of fuel loading but that everything was so dry. (Jeff had never seen it so dry that bark was a fuel.) Fire would spot through these lower fuel areas.

Projects.Highlights:
In file: report - by Milke Amaranthus, "Surface erosion in intensely burned clearcut and adjacent forest with and without grass seeding and fertilizing in southwest Oregon"
Very few winter storms resulted in less storm patrols than anticipated.
Cordoning - cordones of conifers or hardwoods were planted on the steeper exposed slopes.
Geotech - jute netting
Preliminary observations of the effectiveness of treatments were conducted on 2-17, 2-24, and 3-4 of 1988. Approximately 37 inches of rainfall fell from Sept 87 thru Feb 1988 (about 60% of normal). Rainfall was evenly spaced and gentle. Straw erosion barriers - minimal erosion had collected behind the structures.
Contour felling - Density of the contour-felled trees was too low. The number of structures should have been about 27, at a spacing of 40 ft by 40 ft. Very little soil was trapped behind these structures. Possible reasons are: below average rainfall and low intensities, structures\res were constructed on gentle slopes (<30%), and post-fire infiltration rate was greater than the rainfall intensity.
Observing downcutting in burned channels with increased flows following the fire. Check dams -(burlap sacks filled with soil) - they were not holding up well due to rotting and abrasion by rocks. Need to use stronger bags. Straw bale check dams - were placed in channels with minimal streamflow. They were intended as temporary grade stabilizers to prevent downcutting in the channel until vegetation began to recover. They were holding up very well
Single fence checkdams with erosion cloth - were generally effective in controlling channel gradient and trapping sediment. Water passes thru the filter cloth fairly slowly, so water flowed over the top of the dams.
Straw mulching on the contour - done in strips, both straw and alfalfa. Alfalfa was less likely to blow away because it became matted and resembled natural needle mulch. The alfalfa decomposes faster than the straw. Spread at 1/2 inch, treatment was effective.
Aerial seeding - difficult to evaluate the success of seeding so far.
From Amaranthus report: Majority of surface erosion was associated with a large storm that dropped 10.5 inches of precipitation during the period of Dec 1-9. Grass and fertilizer treatment reduced surface erosion 31% in the clearcut and 50% in the adjacent forest. Differences in surface erosion for treated and untreated areas were not significantly different, however, because of high variation. Difference might have been greater had grass coverage been more extensive before the first major storm. No surface erosion was observed in seeded and fertilized blocks after Dec. 9, suggesting that rapid increase in vegetative cover from Dec. until May 1988 apparently was effective at preventing surface erosion. Low surface erosion values in untreated blocks after Dec. 9 are probably due to infrequency of large storms, in combination with increased occurrence of natural vegetation and armoring of the soil surface. It is likely that accelerated surface erosion that accompanies periodic intense fire represents a large portion of long-term surface sediment yield of otherwise forest-covered slopes. The study indicated that although large increases in surface erosion occur, susceptibility is short term and depends upon timing of vegetative recovery and storms.

Projects.Highlights:
Roads and Trail Treatments:
Road and culvert work includes installing drain dips (approx 230), removal of culverts and replacement next year with upsized culverts (12), culvert replacement with upsized culverts and overflows (20), culvert removal and replace with bridge (1), ditch cleaning (2.4 miles), installation of small trash racks/sediment basins to protect cross drains (20), rock spillways at two bridges (2), removal of burned bridge at Red Creek crossing. These improvements will be installed on roads 1881, 330, 330-A1, 1832-A2, 771, 330-B1, 1832, 1800, 1883 and 1821. One culvert will be removed and replaced by a bridge. This is necessary due to the large amount of bedload that this stream carries which the fire will only exacerbate. This site has been identified in an ongoing EIS for Copper Creek and fish passage for bull trout is critical here and cannot be accomplished with a culvert. Where feasible, culvert removal with upsizing next summer is preferable to allow for passage of debris and flood flows. While this requires mobilization twice it does protect our investment on these roads during the critical time period. Where culvert removal and waiting cannot be done due to public safety during winter use, culverts will be upsized accordingly to handle flood and debris. Fish passage is critical for bull trout on several of these and a bottomless arch is being proposed for one of the culverts.
Trail work will include installing 285 drainage structures on 26.5 miles of trail, six wooded culverts and 155 feet of puncheon. Drainage structures are necessary to reduce sediment delivery to streams. Replacement of the 155 feet of puncheon is necessary for both drainage and safety reasons. These partially burned puncheons present a real hazard to horse and foot travel.
Hazard Tree Felling: Due to the high recreation traffic this area receives an aggressive hazard tree felling program is being proposed to reduce the risk of loss of human life. Larger trees within one tree length of forest system roads 1882, 330, 1882, and the Copper Creek campground will be felled. Trees that are greater than seven inches, damaged or killed by fire, and pose an immediate threat to public safety or property will be felled. To minimize the risk to fellers, a mechanical feller buncher will be used where possible. Use of feller buncher also reduces costs.
Hazard tree felling will also occur along the 26.5 miles of trail. Due to the historical nature of the mainline trail this will be done by hand. Only those trees that pose an immediate threat to public safety will be felled. Because a feller buncher cannot be used here the cost per acre will increase.

Rye grass was planted in the Ventana wilderness and observations have indicated it was very short-lived. Native grasses completely dominated the rye grass in 5 yrs. and it disappeared. Used coated seed (fertilizer), doubled lbs/acre of seed so reduced rate of seed application by 1/2..

Cultural and Heritage Resources: The Lower Sugarloaf fire perimeter on USFS Land comprises six known historic resources. Of those sites, three sites were eligible for the National Register of Historic places and thus eligible for BAER evaluation. One was inspected for BAER evaluation, which provided the framework to extrapolate effects of post-fire threats. a. There is a threat to a historic recreation campground within the burn perimeter due to both erosion and sediment displacement as well as increase potential for vandalism, looting, and fire weakened trees to damage the site. The probability of damage or loss is unlikely because the site is not within the area of influence of erosion and sediment threats and due to geographic location keeping the site hidden from the road even with post-fire vegetation loss, vandalism and looting are not expected. Additionally, the SBS was low at the site, so fire weakened trees are unlikely to cause damage. The magnitude of consequence is minor because loss of information or diagnostic artifacts would not impact eligibility status. The risk rating is very low. BAER treatments are not recommended.

Projects.Highlights: Potential Restoration Needs Potential restoration needs were discussed after field reconnaissance and primarily centered around seeding to address erosion and weeds. Fire effects differed based on terrain, pre-fire vegetation, localized past treatments (chaining, mastication, prescribed fire, etc.), and burn patterns. Numerous monsoon storms have passed over the fire within the first weeks after ignition. One primary area dominated by pinon-juniper and oak shrub in one of the headwater tributaries to Big Bucktail Creek was identified as a treatment area where seeding could benefit recovery and weed competition. The GMUG is planning to aerially apply, over approximately 400 acres, seeds already at hand once conditions are favorable in late fall/early winter with the arrival of snow. Similar treatments are also proposed by the BLM with acreage downstream from FS land. A field visit is planned for November to see if additional vegetative recovery is ongoing, especially after plentiful monsoon moisture provided favorable conditions in the otherwise drought-prone landscape. Furthermore, fence repairs may be needed, especially between Forest Service and BLM land. Based on findings from this and other planned reconnaissance in 2025, the GMUG may submit future funding requests through the Burned Area Rehabilitation (BAR) program.

Roads and Trail Treatments: Road treatments are (1) closures on roads to protect public until snagging is complete and roads are safe, (2) snag falling and clearing on 37 miles of road in High and Moderate Severity burned area (11% of roads in fire) for the safety of the public and employees implementing BAER treatments, (3) ditch and culvert protection (clean inlets and ditches of wildfire debris, protect crossings with grade sags and T-risers), and (4) winter storm patrols in lieu of treatment for unforeseen plugging of road drainage with wildfire debris. Main access roads through the fire and roads that must have winter maintenance must be safe and open all winter. There are no trail treatments proposed.
The roads planned for active treatment are not able to be closed and are primary access for administrative and public use. The BAER implementation team will install temporary closures on 10 roads, complete hazard tree removal on 37 miles of road (estimated at 20 trees/mile), install grade sags/T-risers or pull back unstable fills at approximately 34 sites, and clean ditches and culvert inlets on 146 miles of road. Two-person Storm Patrol teams will drive roads 2-4 times per month this winter, and three teams will perform flood emergency road maintenance during 3 storm events. These measures are targeted at the emergency road measures made necessary by wildfire effects during the first winter, and are above the ordinary road maintenance requirements on the 332 miles of roads located within fireline boundaries.
This request includes funding for engineering design and administration of road drainage treatments, especially those requiring contract specifications (Eng Design & Admin). Other implementation costs are built into line item treatment costs.

Projects.Highlights:
Visual monitoring of 4 silt fences that were constructed to hold back sediment from entering ephemeral and intermittent streams. (in file)
Following observations were made: 1) Hydrophobic soils persisted and could be easily identified in areas with manzanita, and Mariposa soils
2) Needle cast from pine trees and leaves from oaks provided an excellent protective layer to the soil.
3) Barley grass was anywhere from 3-5 inches in length and also helped catch other material and to impede the flow of runoff.
4) Bear clover staubs caught pine needles and branches and helped to create a more tortuous path for runoff.
5) High winds and saturated soils had brought down a lot of trees, branches and bark which helped provide good soil protection
6) Rill patterns had developed on many steep slopes and accelerated erosion was apparent.
In file, 3 page narrative by Earl Ruby describing the effectiveness of treatments (2-9-93)
Hi-lites Barley seeding seemed to be an effective treatment, with approximately 6 to 10 plants per sq. ft established.
Tilling was a successful and effective treatment on the lower 1 mile of road that is permanently closed and being removed. Most of the above normal rain infiltrated, with little evidence of overland runoff. Grass seed planted on roadbed has sprouted where sunlight has warmed the soils. Where the road enters the floodplain, it has effectively absorbed both rainfall and runoff from adjacent sideslopes.

Hydrology: Estimates are given for the change in peak flow (cfsm) from pre-fire to post-fire. For the 2 year, 6 hr, 0.75" storm, prefire peak flow is 0 cfsm post fire peak flow is 10 cfsm. For the 10 yr and 100 yr, the pre and post numbers are (10 yr, 0, 125 cfsm) and (100yr, 0, 261cfsm). Calculations are by John Potyondy for the Lowman Complex fire and were done using the SCS Runoff Curve Number method.
Good vegetation recovery assessment was based on two other nearby fires, one 3 yrs past and the other 21 yrs past. The fire three years past had a total cover of about 50%, including litter moss and rock for 20%, and vascular plants for 30%.

Projects.Highlights: Debris Flows: The highest likelihood of post-fire debris flow is the largest area of high soil burn severity on the steepest slopes in the fire. There is past debris flow visible on satellite imagery within the burned area demonstrating a history of debris flows. The 1-year return interval event (15 min rainfall intensity at 26 mm/h) shows a 60-80% probability of debris flow with a volume estimate of 1,000-10,000 m3 in the section above the 620 trail. The volume can be an over-prediction in this landscape, but it does show that a debris flow could damage the trail and prevent ingress/egress. The slopes above the remainder of the 620 trail and 403 trail are 0-40% probability basins under the one-year recurrence interval storm.

Projects.Highlights:
All treatments were for fire suppression. Wilderness revegetation included 100 acres of firelines at a cost of 2750/acre.
The fire burned the west side of Palomar Mtn., and around. Extensive dozer lines were put into the wilderness. Winds pushed fire up into Big cone Doug. Fir. A 3 inch rain put fire out, but caused some flooding damage to Hwy 76 (clogged culverts). All dozer roads were rehabed. Major concern in wilderness area. Track excavator was used to pull material back over roads. Seeding was done by hand. Re-contoured slopes, planted shrubs, treatment was successful.
Finer shrubs like chamise work best when pulling back over road (hold soil in place better). Larger material like scrub oak does no good when cut after fire. Actually is harmful, big stuff doesn't make good ground contact and can cause channeling of water.

Projects.Highlights:
Prescribed treatments were developed with wilderness values in mind. Contour felling in highly visual areas would be completed by blasting rather than chainsaws. There is an associated in cost per acre of treatment to try and stabilize soils while keeping the wilderness character intact. The use of native martials and the non-traditional methods to reestablish necessary ground cover should be utilized in the wilderness area rather than choosing the no action alternative. As difficult it is to decide treatments in wilderness areas, the BAER team felt that some treatment was necessary to protect against unacceptable loss of soil productivity and water quality degradation both on and off site.
Single log sediment traps - reduce stream velocity, create a stair step effect, reducing the erosive power of the streamflow
Rock dikes - to prevent further or new downcutting in a stream channel. Depending on the composition of the original streambed, size and shape of the rock used, method of installation, rock dikes can be installed so as to be flush with the original streambed, or up to 12 inches in height.
Log erosion barriers (Inyo definition of LEB's) - installed in the same fashion as contour felling, with the only difference being the placement of the material. Installed on gentle slopes and would provide an area to catch and store sediment that may move from steeper slopes.
Mulching - in riparian areas, straw mulch applied at 2 tons/acre along 0.5 mile of stream channel (100 ft)
Grass seeding - recommended species and rates of: 1) Elymus glaucus -blue wildrye at 6 lbs/acre, 2) Bromus carinatus California brome at 4 lbs/acre, 3) Vulpia myros - Zorro fescue - barley at 40 lbs/acre. Seeding was to be done in only the riparian areas of intermittent and ephemeral streams.
Do not have interim or final report, so do not know what treatments were accomplished.

Projects.Highlights: Needless to say this was a huge, complex fire with substantial risk to property. 1. The fire partly occurred on the Tonto NF. 2. The stream order summary was by perennial and intermittent. I put the perennial as an order 1stream and did not show any other streams. The narrative listed 548.3 miles of intermittent streams. This was on NFS and private land only, not the other federal. 3. Roads and trails shown in the summary are for the NFS and private lands only. 4. The design and adjusted design flows showed huge ranges; 80-245 for design and 125-1500 for adjusted design flows. I averaged the range to come up with flow inputs shown. 5. Tree felling shown in the treatment section was for spotted owl habitat improvement. It also included seeding with native plants in the cost. The seeding and tree felling was not itemized so I could not separate out the costs and add them to the seeding line for instance. 6. The first "other" shown on page 4 is protection of a fish hatchery to protect the inlet and stabilize area around it. The narrative described it as jute/excelsior erosion cloth. The second "other" is heritage site protection. Again the type of treatment was not described.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: a. Lewis and Clark National Historic Trail: Threats are increased erosion resulting in damage or burial of trail segments, loss of trail due to loss of vegetation as trail markers, and exposure of possible cultural materials or features along the trail section; exposure increases the risk of damage and looting to newly uncovered cultural material. The probability of damage or loss is considered possible due to moderate and severe soil burn severity along sections of trail, moderate erosion hazard ratings across 96% of the fire, and that the BAER assessment survey was unable to locate the trail. The magnitude of consequence is considered major because cultural resources cannot be replaced (irreversible) and moderate to high burn severity along 0.89 miles of the about 2 mi burned trail. Avoidance areas concerning this part of the trail for the Mire Fire were created based on the GIS/GPS data that has been on record denoting the route of the trail as it passes north of Saddle Camp junction. This section however, was not able to be located on the ground despite the corresponding GIS data that was originally recorded in the early 2000s. Due to past fire activity, deposition of vegetation material, disturbance by logging and possible negative effect from past fire events, the section of the trail within the Mire fire is likely fragmented and holds little integrity. The risk to this value is low and natural recovery is the recommended treatment.

Projects.Highlights: From interview with Dave Brewer 1/14/99: -Chalender RD -entire fire was seeded with no great effort at avoiding small amt of private -fire was mostly on a cinder cone with fairly moderate slopes -seeded steep slopes (400 acres) with 12 lbs/ac (1lb sweet clover and 11 lbs grass mix of orchard grass, smooth brome and intermediate wheat) -had intended to seed leveler areas (857 acres) with 3lbs/ac (2lbs yellow sweet clover and 1lb mix of orchard grass, smooth brome, and intermediate wheat) BUT the sweet clover so small it came out too fast that they just kept dumping in more of the grass mix and probably ended up seeding these areas much like the steep slopes- at about 10 lbs/ac -this high seeding of the leveler grounds upset the timber crew interested in pine regen -had good rain within a day or two of seeding (about 1"/hr) -one event that summer did move some soil, filling one small tank and causing some rilling and erosion but not bad -that summer from the higher hills the burn looked like one great green patch; an elk magnet that still has good hunting -seeding worked well mostly due to low slopes and good rains after seeding

Projects.Highlights:
P. Dominant Soils: Soils in the Red Bluff fire area are primarily loamy sand to sandy loam textures Soils are generally shallow to moderately deep on the mountain side-slopes or ridges and moderate to deep in the lower elevations. Higher elevations have moderate to high inherent erosion and debris slide hazards.
Soils in the Shower Bath fire area are primarily loam, loamy sand, and sandy loam textures. Soils are generally shallow to moderately deep on the mountain side-slopes or ridges and moderate to deep in the lower elevations. Higher elevations have moderate to high inherent erosion, mass movement, and debris slide hazards.
Q. Geologic Types: Geology in the Red Bluff Fire area is predominantly pink granite of the Casto Pluton. The Shower Bath Fire area is predominantly in the Challis Volcanics comprised of andesite, latite, tuff and rhyolite. The fire is within the Northern Rocky Mountain Physiographic Province and is characterized by steep rugged mountain terrain. Elevation ranges from over 10,000 feet to 3,000 to 4,000 feet along the Middle Fork of the Salmon River canyon. Major land forms within the fire area include Oversteepened Canyonlands along the Middle Fork and some major tributaries and Mountain Slopelands. Steep slopes are common in the fire area with slope ranges of 65 to 85 percent in the canyonlands and 45 to 65 percent in the Mountain Slopelands. Glaciated landforms such as U-shaped glacial valleys and cirque basins are common in the headwaters of the drainages at higher elevations.
R. Miles of Stream Channels by Order or Class: Shower Bath Fire - 255 miles of stream channel Red Bluff Fire ... 314 miles of stream channel

Table 3: Miles of Stream Channels by Order or Class STREAM TYPE PERENNIAL 2.6 INTERMITTENT 1.0
Sediment Potential: Sediment potential refers to the volume of eroded material that is transported through the watershed and delivered to the outlet which in this case is Lake Pend Orielle. In steep, channelized systems like this one, sediment moves quickly through tight draws and confined drainages with minimal deposition prior to the outlet. WEPPcloud modeling shows sediment discharge increasing from 0.55 to 360 tons/year indicating nearly complete delivery of eroded material downstream. This high connectivity means that sediment generated on hillslopes is not just a localized issue... it becomes a downstream hazard, especially to those that may be in the downhill area.

Cultural and Heritage Resources: There are two unevaluated sites, but no known historic properties located within the War Creek Fire burn area. One of the unevaluated sites is a historic farmstead and artifact scatter. Although this site is within the fire perimeter, the site itself did not burn over. The second unevaluated site is a multicomponent site with a historic farmstead and artifact scatter and a prehistoric artifact scatter. The fire did burn at this site. The features of the site remain in stable condition, and no artifacts found were effected by the burn. The probability of damage or loss across the fire is possible, and the magnitude of consequences is moderate. The BAER risk rating is intermediate and BAER response actions are not recommended.

Projects.Highlights: Noxious Weeds Detection and Treatment (EDRR-BAER): EDRR treatments to prevent establishment or spread of new invasive plants into relatively weed free areas. Noxious weed treatment with herbicide will be conducted under IDIQ or service contract with priority given to known noxious weed infestations in the burn areas such as Leafy spurge, Canada Thistle, Field Brome, Ventenata, Dalmatian Toadflax, Field Bindweed, Bull thistle and Houndstongue, etc. Early detection field reconnaissance will take place in areas with the highest probability of new establishment such as riparian areas (with soil erosion and deposition) and high soil burn severity areas. Primary method of control will be application of herbicide (GrazeOn) with backpack sprayers and ATV with treatments occurring during the most effective time of year to attain maximum translocation of herbicide to the plant resulting in higher success of control. Known weed areas and a buffer on intermittent streams of 100 ft were used to calculate potential increase in weeds and to come up with an estimate on cost. Note: there is always a possibility that weeds will show up anywhere within the fire perimeter. This is only an estimate/starting point of 1,800 acres. Known weeds for the area consists of thistle, primarily Canada Thistle, Bull and Musk Thistle which will be the primary weeds looked at under BAER. Out year treatment, over one year, will be looked at under BAR.
